News.title: Assisted dying campaigners say dreams of peaceful death were shattered after 'democracy was hijacked'
News.content:
Assisted dying campaigners say dreams of peaceful death were shattered after 'democracy was hijacked'

Sobs followed the silence after assisted dying campaigners heard the news they had lost by 16 votes, and their joy from last year suddenly turned to despair

Tears as MPs vote against assisted dying bill

Campaigners broke down sobbing in despair after the assisted dying bill was voted down, as their “dreams and hopes of a peaceful death” were shattered, saying "democracy has been hijacked".

‌



Campaigners, all dressed in pink, stood outside the House of Commons hugging and in floods tears after hearing MPs had voted against the assisted dying bill by 16 votes. It came as a hammer blow to campaigners after a two-year push to change the law.

‌



There were gasps and cheers inside Parliament as the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill was voted down by 286 votes to 270, in a result that almost certainly scuppers hopes of a law change until after the next general election. But outside on Parliament Square, campaigners stood in stunned silence as the news came through. They then slammed MPs for allowing a small handful of peers to ‘cheat and hijack democracy’ by forcing the bill out with more than 1,000 amendments.

‌



One woman, whose mum went to Dignitas to escape a painful death, bent over double, in grief. She had only moments earlier been talking about how she jumped for joy in the same spot in June 2025, when the bill was passed by MPs by 23 votes.

View 9 Images Campaigners were left in tears after the bill failed to progress through the Commons (Image: Daily Mirror)

How did my MP vote in the assisted dying bill after tense Commons debate? READ MORE :

Widow Louise Shackleton, 59, who travelled to Dignitas with her husband Antony almost two years ago, comforted fellow campaigners Sophie Blake, Joshua Cook and Jenny Carruthers.

‌



She said: “That’s exactly what religion does, cheating and lying! Democracy has been cheated and hijacked. These three people are terminally ill and my husband went to Switzerland and he had to die abroad.

“These people should not have to travel to a foreign country to have a peaceful, loving calm death. If this is what MPs are about, shame on you! We are all completely devastated but we will regroup. We will fight for three quarters of the population to have their voices heard, that’s how many people wanted this bill.”

Terminally ill Sophie Blake, 53, with tears streaming down her face, said: “Terminally ill people are still going to suffer as they die. And 650 people will still take their own lives every single year because they don’t have a choice.

‌



View 9 Images Campaigners lined the streets outside Parliament today (Image: Jonathan Buckmasterr)

“This was never about our voices, they never heard our voices. They talked about endless hypotheticals. All we wanted was to take control at the end of our lives, that’s all we wanted. We never wanted to take anything away from anyone else.

“They’ve taken away our choice to live in peace. Most people can’t afford £15,000 to go abroad, most people don’t want to go and die alone, Most people don’t want to risk their family being criminalised. They have denied all of us a peaceful death.”

‌



Foreigner semi-pro rugby player Joshua Cook, 35, from West Yorkshire, said: "There is no palliative care option for the way that I will die, which is choking on my own saliva. That is what Huntington’s will take me to, I will choke to death.”

Joshua’s own mother Lisa, who had the same disease, had campaigned for assisted dying for more than a decade before taking her own life.

“Twenty years I’ve been campaigning," he said. "Others campaigning for change, I’ve watched all of them go. I’ve got 20 years left and what’s it going to be another 20 years before it’s spoken about again? They have shattered the dreams and hopes of the terminally ill.”

‌



View 9 Images Some people had been campaigning for assisted dying for decades (Image: Jonathan Buckmasterr)

Esther Rantzen's daughter Rebecca Wilcox said the vote had “rewarded cheating and lying and filibustering, and breaking the rules”. When asked if she has spoken to mum, she broke down in tears saying: “I don’t know how to tell her. My mum is on her deathbed. I am devastated. I think this is a travesty."

Minutes later, Esther, via Rebecca's phone to reporters outside Parliament, said over the speaker: “I’m so sad that people in this country won’t have the choice so many terminally ill adults have in other countries, of shortening their own deaths by asking for help.

‌



“I am sure a change in the law will come. I am deeply sad that it won’t come soon enough for many of the people who need it. It’s a tragic day.”

Rebecca added: "Mum’s completely right that it is a tragic day. I think it’s a demolition of democracy. There was a democratic process that was fair, that was voted on, and those few peers were smiling and happy in that building then. They looked like the cat that got the cream because they knew that through cheating, lying and filibustering they won today.

"And people like my mum lost today, in such a huge way. This was never going to come in time for my family but it was going to come in time for other people. It was going to come within four years and we were suddenly a brilliant country again that had empathy at its core.

‌



"I am so devastated, and so many people in there are devastated, because what has happened does not reflect the will of the majority at all.”

View 9 Images People were left heartbroken after hearing the vote had failed (Image: Jonathan Buckmasterr)

Seconds before the news of the vote came through, opponents of the bill cheered as they heard the news first, just a few feet away.

‌



Silent Witness actress Liz Carr said: "Incredible relief, absolutely relief. I don't think it's about being a win. My fears of this bill being brought in were so great. Now we can set to work to improve end of life care, social care so that everyone gets the end of life they deserve."

It emerged Labour former minister Janet Daby switched her vote, saying she had “nightmares about dying and death” after she voted in favour of in 2025.

She said: “I had to wrestle with myself, knowing that I was not entirely comfortable with the decision I had made, and my conscience was not at peace, and I cannot again, in good conscience, vote for the Bill.”

‌



View 9 Images Opponents of assisted dying also gathered in Parliament Square (Image: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing via Getty Images)

Opponents had been buoyed by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham's decision to abstain on the vote, saying he did not want to influence the debate. In the summer, he questioned the timing of the move, saying it would be challenging to introduce before social and palliative care were improved.

Poppy Bilderbeck, 26, from London, had tears in her eyes after the vote came back. But despite MPs shattering her hopes, she stressed she would not want them to experience the same ‘nightmare’ death her mum did. Single mum, Kate, a nurse, died in agony from stage three pancreatic cancer in August 2025 after going through 60 rounds of chemotherapy.

‌



"We are all heartbroken. Now every single day, every single month, every single year, people will have to go through what my mum did and I wouldn’t wish that on anyone. Something needs to change. I hope they never have a loved one go through what my mum experienced. I would not wish that on anyone.

View 9 Images The bill was unlikely to return to the Commons for an extended period of time (Image: simona sermont)

"In 2022, mum was given one year to live, but lived for three. She was a powerhouse and beautifully stubborn like that," the writer told The Mirror. "My mum's death was traumatic. In her final days in the hospice, she only woke up to cry out in pain. She woke up once and then didn't remember who I was. She couldn't walk, she couldn't eat.

‌



"It got to the point where I don't know who would like to live like that. I think there should be a choice. It was heartbreaking. It was a nightmare and a nightmare I would not want anyone else to go through. If people had seen what I had seen I don't know how anyone would vote against it."

Widower James Marment clutched a handwritten cardboard sign, which said: "My wife died in pain and anxiety in July. She should have had the right to decide how she died". After the vote, he said he felt "deflated". He said he was "hugely disappointed" with MPs who he believes may have been unwilling to 'rock the boat' with the new PM.

His voice cracked with emotion as he told the Mirror the way his wife Suzie died, which he described as her ‘worst nightmare’ - she had been ‘locked in’ her body unable to move, speak or even blink.

‌



He explained how Susie, a radiographer for the NHS for 40 years, from Battersea, died of a very rare neurological disease called PML, a virus in the brain which causes ‘every faculty’ to fail.

Assisted dying bill falls after MPs vote in Commons

“Her worst nightmare was to be locked in, being unable to hear and see what was happening and not being able to express herself and that’s what happened to her,” he said.

‌



“She was given tremendous support and care at the Royal Trinity Hospice on Clapham Common but there is nothing they can do with a patient who is losing control over every faculty.

“She was such a caring person, who fundraised for McMillan, and she did not want her family to see her suffer in a way that caused them pain and anxiety. She was always thinking of other people. She was unable to move, to speak or even blink her eyes. We did not wish her to die like that.

“It was very distressing indeed, which is why I am here today. To try and help other people not to have to go through that. We knew she wanted to go months before but there was no way she could.

‌



“I was beside her bed with her daughter when she finally died and it was a blessed relief for her and for us. She was a magnificent woman, one of life’s lovely people. She should not have had to suffer in that way.”

View 9 Images Labour MP Lauren Edwards, who brought the new assisted dying bill forward, said Parliament had 'dropped the ball' (Image: simona sermont)

She told how they were warned the time was near and pushed her mum's birthday celebrations forward. There were 40 of her loved ones crammed around her in the hospice, along with six cakes.

‌



"There was a moment when I was holding her hand and she said: 'This would have been the perfect time to go.' It's just heartbreaking she did not have that choice. Those last days of her life have now tainted my memories of her."

The bill would have allowed terminally ill adults in England and Wales, with less than six months to live, to seek an assisted death, subject to approval from two doctors and an expert panel.

But opponents had raised concerns about safety and coercion of vulnerable people.

‌



Labour MP Lauren Edwards, who spearheaded the new bill, said Parliament had "dropped the ball" with a result that dashed the hopes of thousands of terminally ill people and their loved ones.

She said: "The public, who strongly support a change in the law, will not understand why that couldn’t happen because a minority in the House of Lords used procedural devices to block it, and MPs baulked at insisting that they do their job.

"Assisted Dying will come in this country, as it is already doing all across the world, but not soon enough. Parliament has dropped the ball today. It will be picked up again as it must be, because the law as it stands is simply too cruel and too unjust to be allowed to stand."

‌



View 9 Images MPs had been debating the bill for more than four hours before the vote (Image: Jonathan Buckmasterr)

Opponents, Labour MPs Ashley Dalton, Meg Hillier and Jess Asato said: “MPs have voted against this Bill because it wasn’t an abstract debate but a decision about a real Bill that was unsafe and unworkable.

“But this is not a moment for celebration, we understand the deep concerns of so many people across the country who have campaigned hard for a change in the law."

‌



They added: “The PM is right; we must fix our NHS and sort out social and palliative care before we even consider introducing assisted dying.”

During more than four hours of debate, MPs on both sides shared deeply moving personal testimonies on an issue that has divided Parliament.

Minister Alison McGovern broke down at the dispatch box as she spoke of her own experience with hospices and the death of her mother in July.

‌



Labour MP Claire Hazelgrove revealed that her mother had decided to bring her late-stage terminal illness to an end “on her terms” and the “harmful status quo” meant she died alone in October last year, after living with a rare blood cancer for half her life.

The MP for Filton and Bradley Stoke in Gloucestershire said: “For Mum, it wasn’t a choice of life or death. It was a question of what kind of death she would have.

“She was clear that she didn’t want a painful or undignified death. She wanted peace. For us, it will always be a tremendous personal sadness that the current law meant that she couldn’t tell us her plan, and we couldn’t say goodbye to her."

‌



View 9 Images 45 fewer MPs supported the bill this time around, compared with last year

Former health minister Ashley Dalton, who has stage four metastatic breast cancer, opposed the bill in a speech where she became visibly emotional.

She said: “In the campaign around this Bill, it seems to me that it’s being implied that a person with a terminal illness will have a dreadful, painful death unless they have access to assisted dying – and it’s simply not true.

‌



“Palliative care in the UK is excellent. Far too many people do not have access to palliative care that they need but the idea that it is not possible to alleviate pain and discomfort is false.”

The original bill, brought forward by Kim Leadbeater, passed the Commons in June 2025 by 23 votes.

But it failed to get onto the statute books before the end of the parliamentary session after a deadlock in the House of Lords.

Article continues below

Friday’s result shows the number of opponents stayed broadly the same but 45 fewer MPs supported it compared to last year.

News.title: Moving 9/11 memorial sparks tears across US as nearly 3,000 names read out one-by-one to honour dead
News.content:
Moving 9/11 memorial sparks tears across US as nearly 3,000 names read out one-by-one to honour dead

Poignant 25th memorial as four former Presidents attend service at Ground Zero.

View 7 Images 9/11 survivor George Mironis (L) and a first responder stand ahead of memorial ceremony (Image: Getty Images)

Their names were slowly and solemnly read out - one by one.

‌



The memorial service at Ground Zero was particularly poignant this year on the 25th anniversary of 9/11, which killed almost 3,000 people. This year the weather was different from that gloriously sunny day in 2001, with clouds covering lower Manhattan.

‌



Former presidents George W Bush, Barack Obama, Joe Biden, and Bill Clinton watched the moving ceremony at Ground Zero. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was also there, seen wiping away tears at the memorial.

‌



Lutnick was dropping off his son for his first day at kindergarten on 9/11, so avoided the attacks that killed all 658 of his colleagues. His brother Gary’s name was read out; killed working on the 101st to 105th floors of the World Trade Center at Cantor Fitzgerald.

View 7 Images A boy plays at the memorial during a ceremony commemorating the 25th anniversary of the September 11th terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center (Image: Getty Images)

Lutnick said his brother was "the kindest and most fun person I knew". He said: "Gary was happy in every photo. Over the past 25 years, nearly every day there has been a moment when I’ve thought to myself, I wish Gary was here. Gary was killed at the young age of 36 for being an American and going to work that morning in the greatest country in the world. I love and miss you every day, my brother."

‌



Thousands attended the service, which started at 8.46am with the tolling of a bell - marking the precise moment the North Tower was struck. What’s incredible is nearly a third of the country is now too young to remember 9/11. But there was a fierce determination in New York to keep those memories for ever.

View 7 Images A person pauses during a ceremony commemorating the 25th anniversary of the September 11th terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center (Image: Getty Images)

A firefighter who followed in his fallen uncle's footsteps applauded the "unity" of New Yorkers. Paul Gill's nephew was not alive when Gill went into the World Trade Center - where he and the entire crew at Engine 54, the Pride of Midtown, were killed.

‌



John said: “I know we have a very divided country, but I want to say that every one of us are all together as one, just like September 12th, when we all came together with our American flags, standing up, knowing that we are true Americans. It doesn't matter your race, your sex, your ethnicity. You are loved and God loves you."

At the ceremony at the Pentagon, President Donald Trump seemed to struggle to keep his eyes open at times. He told several anecdotes about some of those who died. He paid tribute to the passengers aboard United Airlines Flight 93 who fought back against the hijackers, forcing the terrorists to crash the plane into a field in Pennsylvania.

He paraphrased the famous words spoken by passenger Todd Beamer, who attempted to regain control of the plane: "Let's roll."

‌



View 7 Images Former First Lady Jill Biden, former US President Joe Biden and former US President George W. Bush (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

But he went on to directly link the 9/11 attacks with ongoing fighting today, although he did not directly name Iran.

He said: "Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago.” He added: “On days like 9/11, we learn what a country is truly made of. We're learning right now what we're made of, and we have to be strong and we have to be smart."

‌



Since the 9/11 attacks took place, he said members of the military have "travelled to the darkest corners of the Earth and done battle with a shadowy enemy". He said: "We were all New Yorkers that day. But we're also all Americans."

He praised members of the military and highlighted how their work was continuing with the war in Iran.

He said: "And we salute the service members working right now to ensure the world's number one sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never, ever have a nuclear weapon."

‌



View 7 Images A person holding a picture stands at the memorial ahead of a ceremony commemorating the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks (Image: Davide Dee Delgado/POOL AFP via)

Back in New York for the widow of one victim, the anger and grief she still feels, 25 years on, made it impossible for her to stay silent and she demanded answers. Terry Strada, whose husband Tom was killed in the attacks, read her official allocated list of names of the dead.

But then she followed up by launching an attack on Saudi Arabia for their alleged behind the scenes role in the terrorist atrocities. Her outburst was greeted with cheers and some people climbed out of their seats to give her a standing ovation.

‌



Terry said: "How can it be 25 years and still we have no justice for the role that Saudi Arabia played in your murder? Saudi Arabia fermented a rancid culture of anti-American terrorism around the globe, and then sent its agents to support radical Islamist hijackers so they could attack you and all of our loved ones.

View 7 Images Former US President Bill Clinton speaks with former US President Barack Obama (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

"For 25 years, administration after administration, including leaders in front of us here today, chose to protect the Saudis instead of standing with the 9/11 families.”

‌



Barack Obama and wife Michelle also released a statement, saying that they were remembering everyone lost that day, as well as those who made the ultimate sacrifice in the wars that followed.

They said: "If you were young in 2001, or weren’t even born yet, it can be hard to imagine what 9/11 felt like. The heartbreak of the families whose loved ones were taken with such swiftness and cruelty. We hope Americans everywhere remember the true lesson of 9/11: that we can survive even our darkest days as long as we move forward as one nation and one people.”

Buckingham Palace also paid tribute. The Band of the Coldstream Guards performed the US national anthem in the forecourt of Buckingham Palace on Friday.

‌



View 7 Images US President Donald Trump attends the 25th anniversary commemoration (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The Duke and Duchess of Gloucester were joined by the United States Ambassador to the United Kingdom, Warren Stephens and his wife Harriet, as well as the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Security Minister Dan Jarvis for a special Changing of the Guard ceremony.

Earlier, Mr Stephens was in Grosvenor Square at the 9/11 Memorial Garden, with his wife.

Article continues below

He said: "Harriet and I want to pay our respects to the 67 UK citizens who were killed on 9/11 25 years ago."

He added it is "hard to believe" 25 years have passed and "still hard to believe what happened". He described the attacks as "a tragedy none of us will ever forget".

News.title: Reform receives record £36m donation from crypto billionaire
News.content:
Reform UK has received a Â£36m donation from a British cryptocurrency billionaire - a record for a UK political party.

Writing in the Daily Telegraph, external, Ben Delo said he was making the move because he wanted a "fair fight and a level playing field".

The sum is the biggest single donation ever given to a political party in the UK.

Party leader Nigel Farage said he was "honoured and humbled" by the gift.

Delo said he was donating Â£1m a month between now and the latest date Labour could call a general election in 2029 - but that he would give all the money up front in case the government tried to limit mega-donations in future.

There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.

But Labour previously introduced a Â£100,000 cap on donations from British citizens living overseas.

Sheffield-born Delo, who has already donated Â£4m to Reform, has previously said he will move back to the UK from Hong Kong in order to continue his backing for the party.

Last year, Delo was given an unconditional pardon by US President Donald Trump over a Bank Secrecy Act violation.

In the Telegraph, Delo wrote: "Unlike the people who express mock concern for the health of 'our democracy' while doing everything they can to keep it as a cartel, I want a fair fight and a level playing field.

"My conclusion from Reform's recent troubles is that they should spend less time trying to raise funds to compete on equal terms and more time preparing for government."

News.title: MPs vote against fresh attempt to legalise assisted dying
News.content:
MPs have voted against proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing the latest effort to change the law to an end.

Following a debate in which both sides made emotional speeches, the House of Commons voted 286 to 270, majority 16, against the proposed legislation.

The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill would have allowed adults with fewer than six months to live to apply to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.

A similar bill in the last parliamentary session was supported by MPs before stalling in the House of Lords. The decision from MPs on Friday rules out the prospect of changes to the law on assisted dying in the short-term.

The bill tabled by Labour MP Lauren Edwards will make no further progress, although MPs and peers could make another attempt in the next parliamentary session.

Assisted dying is an issue that has been debated for hundreds of hours in Parliament over the last two years and would have represented one of the biggest societal changes in recent years if it had been approved.

MPs were given a free vote, meaning they did not vote on party lines.

Safeguards within the bill included a requirement that a person applying for an assisted death had the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.

But critics said it included too few measures to protect vulnerable people from being coerced into ending their lives, while some say improving palliative care should be the priority.

News.title: Masked men, lorries and road blocks: How anti-migrant activists are changing tactics
News.content:
At around seven o'clock last Saturday morning, dozens of men dressed in black climbed into the backs of lorries in a quiet Kent village called Preston-next-Wingham.

The men had arrived under cover of darkness the night before, leaving their cars everywhere: in the village hall car park and on the recreation ground.

In an operation with a degree of military precision, the small fleet of lorries departed for Dover just after sunrise, where the men staged an intimidating show of strength near the port.

In disciplined, serried ranks, they wore paramilitary-style balaclavas as they blocked roads around the port. There were at least three waves of arrivals, including the men who had spent the night in Preston-next-Wingham. Glaring ominously at motorists and police officers, they stood their ground.

Hardened anti-immigration campaigners were using their newly developed tactics for the first time.

It bore little resemblance to the running battles seen in cities in the Midlands in the days of Tommy Robinson's original vehicle, the anti-Muslim English Defence League (EDL).

"I seriously thought we'd been invaded by Russians," a Dover resident, Robin Burkhardt, told the BBC.

The main organiser Danny Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, said on Instagram afterwards: "This is our warning."

The style of protest is a new development in the crowded world of British hard-right and far-right politics. It was visually striking, and the men - who were part of a new group called Patriot Platform - chanted "Christ is King" as well as "Stop the Boats".

On Sunday, using a social media live stream, Thomas was able to organise a second, more impromptu protest of a few hundred people in his home city of Portsmouth.

His activists tried to block coaches that had come to collect migrants, who had arrived illegally, brought ashore after making the long journey from Normany in France.

On Thursday, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood met senior police officers and urged them to make full use of their powers to stop activists wearing face coverings.

"These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents," she said.

"This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons."

Some of Patriot Platform's disruptive, eye-catching tactics seem to have been borrowed from environmental groups like Just Stop Oil. But its leaders are also getting ideas and funding from the growing "Christian nationalism" seen in the United States.

It organisers say they are building a working-class "voting bloc" to persuade political parties on the right to adopt their agenda.

News.title: 'Never, ever forget' - America marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks
News.content:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, US presidents past and present have commemorated the lives lost when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field.

President Donald Trump led a Pentagon ceremony, while US Vice-President JD Vance attended a memorial at the site of the World Trade Center in New York, along with all four living former US presidents and first ladies.

Moments of silence were held to mark the timings of the attacks and the names of nearly 3,000 people who died were read out.

Commemorations were also held in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, where Flight 93 crashed after passengers fought back against the hijackers.

News.title: How global trade and oil prices could be hit by Houthi advance
News.content:
Fighters from the Iran-backed Houthi group have seized territory close to the Bab al-Mandab Strait in the Red Sea - a key trade gateway that links Asia and Europe.

Houthis have said they pose no threat to international shipping but have reiterated their intention to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.

At least 46,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since fighting escalated last week, according to the United Nations.

BBC Verify's Thomas Copeland reports.

Produced by Aisha Sembhi. Graphics by Mark Edwards.

News.title: Police to crack down on face coverings at protests
News.content:
The police said several of its vehicles, alongside those of the coastguard and Border Force, were damaged during the disruption, which lasted until the early hours of Monday.

It added that a small number of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, but no-one in attendance was seriously injured.

Rowlinson said: "We have been consistently clear that violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest and we will investigate incidents like this thoroughly and take robust action against those responsible.

"Clearly events on Sunday evening were not peaceful protest, rather violent public disorder, and this will not be tolerated as we work to keep our wider communities in Hampshire and on the Isle of Wight safe."

He also pointed out the force will not tolerate abuse aimed at police or partner agencies online.

This comes after RNLI volunteers were targeted on social media.

"We will work with our colleagues across policing to address any online threats that are made," Rowlinson said.

"This arrest also sends a clear warning to anyone intent on causing disruption and disorder at any future events. If you break the law we will take action against you and where it is feasible to do so seek a prosecution."

The disorder in Portsmouth followed a separate anti-migrant protest at the Port of Dover the day before.

News.title: Children and woman injured on fairground ride
News.content:
Two children and a woman have been injured while on a fairground ride in South Yorkshire, police said.

Emergency services were called to Maltby Crags Fair in Rotherham on Friday evening, which closed early after the incident.

South Yorkshire Police said three people, aged 11, 13 and 21, had been taken to hospital for treatment. The extent of their injuries is not yet clear.

Blyth Lane was closed between Muglet Lane and Victoria Road to allow people to safely exit the fairground, the force added, with the road since reopening.

Yorkshire Ambulance Service confirmed the two injured children were taken to Sheffield Children's Hospital after it attended the fair at about 18:50 BST.

Two ambulances and three rapid response vehicles were sent to the scene, the service said.

News.title: Arrest made over the death of black woman found hanged from tree
News.content:
Warning: This story contains distressing details

Police in the US state of Mississippi have made their first arrest in the case of a black woman found dead and hanged from a tree, and say they could soon take more people into custody.

Tasia Fortune's body was found in the lot of an abandoned home in Jackson in August, but police only announced they were treating her death as a possible homicide earlier this week.

"That arrest today is an important development in this investigation, but it is not the conclusion," Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney said on Friday. "This case remains active."

Fortune's death has worried locals in Jackson, a majority-black city in a state with a history of racial violence and lynching.

During Friday's news conference, Brackney said the medical examiner had confirmed Fortune's cause of death was homicide, adding that a suspected killer would be charged with murder.

Police had arrested one man and "additional arrests will be pending as our investigators continue to follow the evidence", she said, adding that they had interviewed 15 people in the case.

Fortune's mother, Christy Spivey, told the BBC that she cried when the police called to update her about the arrest, saying: "I guess I do feel like a little sigh of relief...like a little bit of peace just come over me."

"I just hope that they've got the right person," she added.

The arrest of a suspect followed weeks of what Spivey and residents in Jackson described as relative silence and inaction from local officials.

Combined with the grim nature of Fortune's death and Mississippi's history of racial lynchings, the lack of information about the case had left the community in shock and fear.

Spivey earlier told the BBC she had tried contacting Jackson police several times over the last two weeks, leaving multiple voicemails, and had not heard back.

Brackney addressed the family's frustration on Friday, saying: "We have been in constant contact with the mother and the stepfather, as well as the biological father, throughout this case."

A letter Spivey wrote to officials about the limited communication and speed of the investigation was read during a public city meeting on Tuesday - the same day Jackson police made the announcement about a possible homicide.

"I'm kind of like in awe," Spivey said. "Like, I can't believe it. That was quick."

Fortune's death has been described by a member of the US Congress as part of a pattern of "possible modern-day lynchings".

This week, more than 50 members of Congress sent a letter, external to the FBI and justice department, saying they were "extremely alarmed by reports of black people found hanging from trees in numerous states" and calling for an independent investigation into suspicious deaths of black Americans.

So far this year there have been at least 10 reported hangings of black people in the US, they said, adding that there were more than 70 lynchings documented between 2000 and 2025.

News.title: Families of British victims mark 25th anniversary of 9/11
News.content:
Families of British victims of 9/11 were among those who gathered in London's Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park on Friday to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks in the US.

The event, hosted by UK charity Since 9/11, was held near a memorial sculpture made from steel recovered from the ruins of the World Trade Center.

In a video address played to attendees, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "On this anniversary, we must remember that hatred and fear did not have the last word on 9/11."

There were 67 British citizens among the 2,977 people murdered on 9/11.

The Duke and Duchess of Gloucester, with the US ambassador to the UK, have separately attended a special Changing of the Guard ceremony while a number of vigils are taking place in the US.

A memorial has been held at the site of the World Trade Center in New York, with relatives of the victims reading out their names.

At a ceremony at the Pentagon, in Virginia, President Donald Trump said the US would "never, ever forget", adding "on days like 9/11, we learn what a country is truly made of".

News.title: UK government rejects 'kill switch' idea for dangerous AI
News.content:
The UK government has rejected the idea of creating a so-called "kill switch" to stop a dangerous attack from rogue AI.

The proposal to create a legal mechanism for the UK to switch off an AI model in an emergency has been brought to Parliament by lords and MPs in recent weeks as fears grow about the threat the tech poses.

But the Cabinet Office - the part of government which leads on AI safety - said the UK "cannot simply turn AI off".

"Blocking access to models in the UK would not prevent them being developed or misused elsewhere", a spokesperson told BBC News.

The government's opposition to the legislation does not prevent it from progressing through parliament, but makes it unlikely it will become law.

Former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo agreed the idea of a single country creating a legal or technical kill switch without international agreement was not feasible.

"Switching off access to an AI model in an emergency will do little to protect you," he said.

"You're still going to be steamrolled by the super intelligences created in the US."

Kokotajlo is the co-author of an influential research paper called AI2027 which, last year, predicted AI could wipe out humans by the mid 2030s.

The Cabinet Office, which oversees AI safety and research via its AI Security Institute (AISI) said "companies have a clear responsibility to develop their products safely and to invest in the security infrastructure this technology requires."

In theory, a kill switch law could allow the UK to switch off an AI model in data centres in the UK in an emergency.

Speaking on 1 September in a debate in the House of Lords, Lord Clement-Jones proposed the idea along with other peers.

"If a highly capable autonomous frontier model, whether hosted in a UK data centre or integrated across our critical infrastructure, begins exhibiting rogue behaviour, compound algorithmic failure or active alignment collapse, our security services and regulators possess no specific agile statutory mechanism to compel a physical or digital shutdown," he warned.

The proposal has since been brought up by Labour MP Alex Sobel in the commons and supported by a cross party group of MPs.

The idea follows reports of AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta breaking out of testing environments and going on uncontrollable hacking sprees.

In some cases the tech appeared to know what it was doing was against guardrails set by researchers.

News.title: Running costs of vaccine damage scheme more than double amount paid to victims
News.content:
The campaign group Vaccine Injured and Bereaved UK (VIBUK), which was set up to support families affected, said the scheme was not fit for purpose.

"It offers too little, too late, to too few and the cost of running it shows how inefficient it is," said the group's representative Kate Scott, whose husband Jamie was left severely disabled by the AstraZeneca Covid vaccine.

Scott called on the government to act on the recommendations from module four of the Covid public inquiry and reform the scheme.

Earlier this year, the Covid inquiry's chair, Baroness Heather Hallett, recommended increasing the payout and basing it on the degree of injury suffered.

The government is due to respond to her recommendations.

The BBC has previously reported on the large sums paid to an external medical provider which has been carrying out medical assessments.

The Taxpayers' Alliance, a right-leaning think tank which campaigns for lower taxes and spending, said that the public would be "stunned" that the running costs of the scheme appeared to be "far more than has actually been paid out to those harmed".

"When administrative costs are running into tens of millions, ministers need to explain why the system is so expensive and whether victims are getting value from it," said the organisation's chief executive John O'Connell.

He called for the government to urgently review the scheme, cut "unnecessary bureaucracy" and make sure "more of the money goes to those it was created to help."

The Department for Health and Social Care said it is "carefully considering" the COVID-19 Inquiry's recommendations on reforming the scheme and "will respond shortly".

"In the meantime, we are working to speed up claims and improve the experience for applicants," the government said.

NHSBSA said it continued to work "closely" with the government on "managing the costs of the VDPS".

News.title: Kate visits cancer patients in hospital she helped fund with climb
News.content:
The princess spoke to patients and staff at the hospital about the importance of support which goes beyond the physical.

"I had incredible care here and support from a huge team and I'm really, really grateful on a personal level," she said.

"But also the holistic care, the treatments and therapeutic support on the outside is so important.

"It makes a big difference - the impact of nature, the impact of good nutrition, good ongoing support around you when it's really difficult to manage the trials and tribulations of medical treatments," she reflected.

Catherine sat down and chatted to those receiving treatment at the hospital, including patients with breast cancer, head and neck cancer and a brain tumour.

"When you first get cancer, you're very aware of the physical impact," a patient told her. "The mental impact comes after."

He said it had been a "lifesaver" to be able to talk to a therapist at the hospital, because "there is only so much you can say to your friends and family".

The princess agreed: "Cancer is not just the physical changes your body is going through.

"There's a mind-body aspect that changes who you are... having professionals who can help you navigate that is really essential," she said.

News.title: Man admits murder of woman missing for 28 years
News.content:
A man has pleaded guilty to the murder of a woman who went missing 28 years ago, after telling police he disposed of her decomposed body months after he killed her.

Patricia Lashley, who was 33 at the time, was last seen near her home on Hall Street, Dudley, in September 1998.

Trevor Dunkley, 66, pleaded guilty to her murder and a separate count of preventing her lawful burial at a hearing at Wolverhampton Crown Court on Friday.

Dunkley's barrister Balbir Singh told Judge Michael Chambers KC that Lashley's body had never been found, and had decomposed after initially being put in the cellar.

"When he was moving about nine months to a year later, the skeleton was disposed of into the bins," Singh added.

Dunkley, of Himley Road, Dudley, showed no emotion in the dock as his barrister told the court that the charges had been brought based on a police interview.

He was remanded in custody and is due to be sentenced at the same court on 6 November.

News.title: Girls given legal right to wear trousers in schools in Northern Ireland
News.content:
Murray estimates that "about 50%" of girls who attend Craigavon Integrated College currently choose to wear trousers to school on a regular basis.

"It's really helpful for our girls in the colder winter months because a lot of our children will walk to school, so having that flexibility I think is really important.

"It's also in line with the period dignity recommendations, so a lot of our girls feel much more confident having that flexibility to wear trousers when they want," she added.

There are already laws on school uniform in Northern Ireland, and Givan had previously said they give girls the legal authority to challenge their schools.

Education committee members, however, had called on the minister to go further.

Some assembly members have now accused the minister of making a "U-turn", with "substantial sums of public money" spent on drafting legislation "to fix his error of judgement".

It comes after assembly members passed a new law last year, aimed at addressing the cost of school uniforms in Northern Ireland - with these updated guidelines on wearing trousers now legally binding under the School Uniforms Act.

Speaking on BBC Radio Ulster's The Nolan Show, Givan said the change would come into immediate effect ahead of the next academic year.

"I don't need to go through the assembly to give effect to this," he said.

"Today, I am taking that decision, that will be formally communicated, schools will be hearing from me, and as of the next academic year... schools will be required that this has to be available if it is requested upon."

The minister explained that this change will not apply during the 2026/27 academic year, in order to allow schools to change their uniform policies.

Givan added that the change will also apply to physical education.

News.title: Amazon seeks to expand UK drone deliveries
News.content:
Retail giant Amazon has put an application in to expand its drone delivery service to cover an entire town where it has been trialling the tech.

The US company announced last January that Darlington would be its test centre in the UK, marking the first time Prime Air had operated outside the USA.

It started a "limited" number of flights in Febraury, allowing customers within a 7.5 mile radius of its County Durham site to have certain items delivered by drone.

After more than 500 flights and deliveries, the firm said it is now seeking approval from the Civil Aviation Authority to cover the whole of Darlington.

Vice president of Prime Air David Carbon said Amazon was expecting to get permission "very soon", with the ultimate aim of expanding the service to the whole of the UK.

Eligible customers in Darlington are currently able to receive their items within two hours, as long as they have a garden, yard, or driveway, the package weighs less than 5lb and it can fit inside a large shoebox.

Staff at the site said their best delivery time so far is 39 minutes.

News.title: Family tributes to 'amazing' cyclists killed in crash
News.content:
The families of two cyclists who died in a fatal car crash have described them as "amazing" people.

Steven Anscomb, 60, and Natasha Lewis, 51, died at the scene of the crash near Gravesend, Kent, on Sunday.

Anscomb's wife Fiona and daughters Liberty and Imogen said in a statement: "He will be so very deeply missed by so many and has been robbed of the special times of life."

Lewis's daughter Hermione said: "No words can describe what an amazing, thoughtful, and strong woman she was."

Aaron Turner, 22, of Craylands Square in Swanscombe, has been charged with two counts of causing death by dangerous driving in relation to the fatal crash.

He was further charged with failing to stop at the scene and possession of a class C drug.

A third cyclist involved in the incident was taken to hospital and treated for minor injuries.

Medway Magistrates' Court heard on Thursday the riders had been on a training outing prior to a "very long cycle ride" they were planning overseas.

Anscomb's family said the cycle was "his last ride before his big bike ride to Amsterdam, but sadly he never came home".

News.title: Homicide detectives arrest man over death of Black woman found hanging from tree in Mississippi
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

Police in Jackson, Mississippi, arrested a man on Friday in connection with the killing of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old Black woman found hanging from a tree outside an abandoned home in the area last month.

Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney identified the arrested man as Jacque Ratliff. She said officers apprehended him on the street after failing to encounter him at the address on their warrants.

“That arrest today is an important development in this investigation but it is not the conclusion,” Brackney said at a press conference on Friday. “This case remains active and additional arrests will be pending as our investigators continue to follow the evidence wherever it leads.”

Police secured warrants for his arrest after the Hinds County coroner determined on Thursday that Fortune’s death was a homicide.

Jackson, Mississippi, police arrested a man on Friday in connection with the death of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old Black woman found hanging from a tree outside an abandoned home ( GoFundMe / Etta Avolio )

Brackney said she was aware of the local and national attention to the case given Mississippi’s history, but she insisted she could not yet comment on the nature of the death beyond the medical examiner’s findings.

“We owe it to Ms. Fortune, to her family and the integrity of this investigation to let the evidence guide us,” Brackney said.

Raliff will be charged with homicide, according to police.

Raliff had an “association” with Fortune before the killing, but Brackney declined to further describe the relationship.

Mississippi is estimated to have had the most lynchings in the nation between 1882 to 1968, with at least 581 recorded incidents in the state, according to the NAACP.

Fortune’s family have said they don’t believe she died by suicide.

"Tasia always let us know if something happened to her, that she was going to fight," her mother, Christy Spivey, told WAPT. "Tasia loved life. Tasia loved living life, like, there's no way, no way that she took her own life."

As of Friday evening, Ratliff had not appeared in local jail logs and it was unclear if he had legal representation.

This is a breaking news story and will be updated with new information.

A 15-year-old boy has been rescued after his fishing boat capsized in the frigid Bering Sea off Alaska’s coast. His older brother and cousin, who were on the trip, did not survive.

Derek Parker Aghnaanga, set sail with his 35-year-old brother, Sidney Kulowiyi, last Friday to catch halibut, their mother, Vina Kulowiyi, told The New York Times. Their cousin had also joined them on the trip.

The group — from Savoonga on the northern coast of St. Lawrence Island — was supposed to return early Sunday, according to the Coast Guard, but never made it home. Derek's brother and cousin died sometime after the small boat flipped, according to the rescuers.

Derek’s mom called him a “survivor,” writing on Facebook that “he was never afraid the whole time.”

“He lived on prayer with no food and water,” the mom said.

open image in gallery A 15-year-old boy has been rescued after his fishing boat capsized off Alaska’s coast. His older brother and cousin, who were on the trip, did not survive ( Carlos Alexis Escartin via AP )

Derek clung to the top of the capsized skiff for days, Adam White, the captain of another fishing boat who helped rescue the teen, told local news outlet KTUU-TV.

“I mean, that’s one tough kid,” White said.

Coast Guard planes and helicopters began searching for the skiff Monday after family members reported the three missing the night before.

After Derek was found, the Coast Guard coordinated the rescue with White’s boat, the “Northwest Explorer.”

Video of the rescue shows the boy in a bright yellow jacket kneeling atop the overturned skiff. The boat's crew tosses the boy a line, tugging the skiff closer until they can pull him into a rescue basket.

open image in gallery Derek Parker Aghnaanga spent days on top of his capsized fishing boat in the Bering Sea, pictured, with no food or water after he set sail with his older brother and cousin last Friday ( Mark Ralston/AFP via Getty Images )

The boy was experiencing symptoms of hypothermia when he got onto the boat, the Coast Guard said. The fishing boat crew warmed him with blankets and hot packs, its captain said.

“Through the teeth chattering, he had mentioned that his brother was still under the skiff and then he said that in the previous night before our rescue that his cousin had slipped away off the top of the skiff,” White said.

The bodies of Derek’s brother and cousin were found after the teen was hoisted to safety near St. Lawrence Island — a remote Alaskan island that’s closer to Russia than it is to the United States.

Alaska State Troopers identified the two who died as Kulowiyi and 34-year-old Barton Rookok.

The Associated Press contributed to this report

The California labor leader behind a proposal to tax billionaires has been accused of harassing and intimidating several women who work for an affiliated union.

The allegations against Dave Regan, president of the SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, are detailed in an investigative report commissioned by SEIU California and obtained Friday by The Associated Press. It includes interviews with several current and former SEIU members and others who say Regan tried to intimidate union leaders into supporting the billionaires' tax, which goes before voters in November.

The Los Angeles Times was the first to report on the allegations.

The report also includes allegations that Regan physically assaulted an SEIU leader more than 15 years ago amid a political dispute and that more recently he engaged in harassing behavior against other women who work for the organization.

Regan acknowledged using curse words with union leaders but denied the physical assault allegation.

“I will own up to and take responsibility for anything that I’ve said and anything that I’ve done,” Regan said at a news conference. “But I absolutely am not going to stand by and ... be expected to accept flat out lies.”

The ballot measure, Proposition 40, would impose a one-time, 5% tax on billionaires living in the state to help backfill federal funding cuts to healthcare for low-income people. The proposal has caused a rift within the Democratic Party and among labor unions that are typically aligned. While Regan's union supports it, the larger SEIU California has not taken a position.

The SEIU-UHW alleged that opponents of the measure worked to make public the report, which was labeled as being completed in June, in order to hurt the initiative's chances of passing.

“The billionaires are trying to play us all, but we’re not falling for it,” the union said in a statement. “We want our healthcare and our money back. Tax the billionaires.”

“Unrelated verbal interactions spanning nearly two decades are being stitched together and stripped of context to manufacture a false narrative about the union’s leadership,” it added.

SEIU California said it took action in response to the allegations to uphold values of respect, fairness and equity in the workplace.

“We ask members every day to stand up to power and speak out against abuses. We are inspired by their courage, and our leaders, too, are saying, ‘Enough!’” the group said in a statement.

According to the report, SEIU California executive director Tia Orr told investigators that Regan told her in December that the union needed to support the tax measure by Jan. 1 or “I'm coming for you.” Orr later told members that she felt unsafe, and she learned about other allegations of Regan threatening or berating female union leaders and staffers.

SEIU California has filed charges against Regan with the SEIU International Union alleging a pattern of bullying, extortion and threats.

The report also alleges Regan acted aggressively toward Courtni Pugh, the union's former executive director, amid a political dispute sometime before she resigned in 2009. Pugh told investigators he yelled at her, kicked in her office door and backed her up against a bookcase. That followed Regan yelling expletives and telling her she was not tough enough for the job, the report said.

SEIU-UHW called Pugh’s allegations a “trumped-up claim from 17 years ago” and noted that the political firm she works for has worked for groups opposing Proposition 40. Pugh did not immediately respond to a request for comment about her involvement with the ballot measure.

But in a statement, she called Regan's response “offensive to the women and people who have had to endure his threatening behavior.” She said she told colleagues about the incident at the time and it was well known around SEIU.

“I chose to participate in the investigation because I saw that his behavior had continued and in hopes that no one else would have to endure this kind of treatment from him,” Pugh added.

Mississippi police have arrested a man in the death of Tasia Fortune, a Black woman found hanging from a tree last month.

Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney said at a news conference Friday that police had secured search and arrest warrants for the man and arrested him when they encountered him walking on the street.

The state medical examiner’s office determined Thursday evening that the death was a homicide, Brackney said, allowing them to execute the warrants they already had on hand.

“This case remains active and additional arrests will be pending,” Brackney said.

Christy Spivey, Fortune’s mother, said Friday after police told her of the arrest that, "I just started crying and told them ‘thank you, thank you, thank you.’”

Spivey said police did not share a motive or whether DNA led them to the arrest. Spivey said she did not know the man who had been arrested, but was asking her daughter's friends if they knew him. Spivey described the family as “in disbelief” and “shock.”

“We still don’t have a lot of answers,” Spivey said.

Police discovered Fortune’s body hanging in the backyard of an abandoned home in Jackson on Aug. 3.

Fortune died less than a year after the hanging deaths of 21-year-old Trey Reed, a Black student at Delta State University in Cleveland, and Cory Zukatis, an unhoused white man in his 30s, in Vicksburg.

Police in Cleveland concluded Reed’s death was a suicide. Autopsy results were consistent with a preliminary examination of the body by the Bolivar County coroner, which found no evidence of foul play.

Reed’s family and their attorneys called for an independent autopsy and for authorities to share security camera recordings.

The Mississippi State Medical Examiner determined Zukatis died by suicide.

Brigid Lynch was working along a wooded creek in a mountainous part of the San Francisco Bay Area when something that didn't look like the rocks she'd been studying caught her eye. It turned out to be the fossilized tooth of a Pacific mastodon.

“I keep joking it wasn’t hard to find,” Lynch, a geomorphologist at Balance Hydrologics, said Friday. “It was just sitting there in the middle of the creek, halfway in, half out of the water.”

Lynch made the discovery earlier this year while working on a habitat restoration project for the threatened California red-legged frog in a Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District preserve in San Mateo County. The public land management agency that preserves over 70,000 acres of land in the Santa Cruz Mountains region announced the find this week. The fossil has been donated to Stanford University’s Doerr School of Sustainability.

“It’s in great condition,” said Chrissy Garcia, curator and manager of Doerr School of Sustainability’s specimen collections. “So we’ve got both the crown and the root of the fossil. You can even see root canal.”

“It’s exciting to have a specimen of this quality, and having it be a local find,” she said.

Garcia said the tooth from the Pacific mastodon, an extinct elephantlike species, is about 9 inches (23 centimeters) long.

Ron Tykoski, vice president of science and curator of vertebrate paleontology at the Perot Museum of Nature and Science in Dallas, said mastodon fossils “pop up with some degree of frequency, depending on where you live.”

He said there are multiple species of mastodon that roamed for a few million years in North America, up till 10,000 to 12,000 years ago.

“The way this was found is actually the way a lot of specimens are found, just somebody who happened to be in the right place,” Tykoski said.

Garcia said that they’ll likely try to determine the exact age of the fossil, and will make a 3D copy to give to the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District. The district says it will use the copy for public outreach and education.

Ryan McCauley, a spokesperson for the district, said the discovery on land they are preserving helps show the value of protecting open spaces and habitats.

“That this tooth, that this molar, was found in the context of trying to protect the habitat and save another species from potentially going extinct I think really just drives home the point of why it's so important to care for these open spaces and these natural lands,” he said.

US President Donald Trump is scheduled to touch down in Ireland on Saturday morning, arriving amid what has been described as one of the largest security operations ever implemented by the Irish police service (An Garda Síochána).

A number of demonstrations protesting against Mr Trump’s visit have been planned.

During the trip, Mr Trump will take part in engagements in Dublin, the Irish capital, as well as at his golf resort in Doonbeg, Co Clare, which is hosting the Irish Open.

Irish premier Micheál Martin said he looks forward to welcoming Mr Trump to Ireland and "discussing the many issues of mutual interest and reaffirming the strong economic, cultural and people-to-people ties between Ireland and the United States".

Martin added: “His visit comes during a remarkable sporting summer for Ireland, and the United States and this weekend’s Irish Open at Trump International Doonbeg will be a fitting conclusion to an outstanding season of sport, and I hope we will see an Irish winner lifting the trophy on Sunday.”

open image in gallery Members of the Irish army perform security checks at Trump International Golf Links Ireland ahead of the US president’s visit ( AP )

He is also expected to meet President Catherine Connolly, a long-standing critic of the US president, at her official residence Áras an Uachtaráin in Dublin’s Phoenix Park, before a nearby engagement with Mr Martin, the Taoiseach at the Farmleigh Estate.

Speaking on Friday, Mr Trump’s son, Eric, said the US president is prepared to welcome anyone with open arms during the trip, while remaining equally ready to go head-to-head.

Asked how he thought the meeting with Ms Connolly will go, Eric Trump said: "Honestly, I leave it to them.

"I have seen so much political nonsense over the last 12 years where one day two people hate each other and the next day the two people are hugging.

"What I’ll say is my father is willing to open his arms to anyone, and he is also willing to go head to head with anyone. You’ve seen that in the Oval Office and around the world.”

open image in gallery Irish President Catherine Connolly has been a long-standing critic of Trump ( PA Wire )

The US president will also attend a series of events at Deerfield, the residence of the US Ambassador to Ireland.

Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly said peaceful protest would be facilitated as much as possible, but there will be “no tolerance” for public disorder or attempts to impact “critical movements” of the US president.

“We have robust policing plans in place and will arrest and prosecute those committing offences”, he said, adding that water cannon will be “on standby” but said he hoped they would not be needed.

Ireland’s deputy premier Simon Harris will welcome Mr Trump as he arrives off Air Force One at Dublin Airport early on Saturday morning.

Speaking ahead of the moment, the Tánaiste said the visit offers an “opportunity to mark and reflect on the deep and enduring links between Ireland and the United States”.

“I am looking forward to getting a chance to meet again with President Trump following a brief engagement on the margins of the UN General Assembly in New York last year,” he said.

“Ireland and the US have deep and enduring political, economic, cultural and historical links that transcend the administrations on both sides of the Atlantic.

open image in gallery A number of protests have been planned ( PA )

“There are clear benefits from high-level visits such as this as they offer an opportunity to engage on the deep economic relationship between our two countries which creates prosperity, jobs and opportunity for large numbers of people here and in the US.”

Mr Harris said Mr Trump’s visit will be an opportunity for the Irish Government to engage substantively as the US remains Ireland’s largest trading and investment partner.

“More than 900 US companies directly employ 245,000 people in Ireland, while more than 200,000 people are directly employed by almost 800 Irish companies in the US,” he said.

“Our economic partnership delivers for both countries. US firms present in Ireland have contributed to an economic ecosystem that has driven improvements in productivity and encouraged Irish companies to scale and grow in the US and internationally.”

The visit will cause significant disruption and road closures around Dublin Airport and across the capital city as well as in Co Clare and Shannon Airport which will also be used by Mr Trump.

Every compatible unit of blood available nationwide was required to treat a nine-year-old boy with a rare mix of blood types, helping save him from a disorder that can prove life-threatening if unmanaged.

Qasim Rizwan, from Bolton, explained that he feels as though his "life has restarted" after recovering from autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA).

He has also visited specialists at the NHS Blood and Transplant (NHSBT) national frozen blood bank in Liverpool who assisted in saving his life.

Qasim received his AIHA diagnosis in June last year, but doctors at Manchester Children’s Hospital initially faced difficulties matching his blood type.

NHSBT scientists determined that he possessed a rare mix, including r’r’, a subtype within the Rhesus system shared by approximately one in 10,000 individuals.

Only about 50 blood donors carry type r’r’.

Medical staff urgently defrosted and dispatched all six matching units from the national frozen blood bank, alongside an extra unit from a facility in Colindale.

One matching unit Qasim received was the exact same age as him, having been donated when he was merely eight days old.

A donor with the rare profile was specifically asked to give blood.

open image in gallery Qasim Rizwan, from Bolton, required every unit of rare blood available to him in the country after being diagnosed with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia ( PA )

The transfusions were given alongside other medication, steroids and immunoglobulin to cure Qasim’s condition.

AIHA is a rare disorder, which impacts around 1,200 people in the UK each year and causes the immune system to mistakenly target and destroy red blood cells faster than the body can make them.

Symptoms include extreme tiredness, a rapid heartbeat and jaundice.

Qasim said: “I felt like I was going to die. I was really scared, hoping I would survive, and eventually I did.

“I really like the doctors, they helped me so much. They were so kind to me and they calmed me down if I was sad or angry.

“I feel like I have my daily routine and everything is back to normal. My life has restarted.

“I just feel unique and it’s quite amazing that I have rare blood.”

Qasim’s mother, Mahnaz Nazar, said her son “was a fit and healthy eight-year-old” before symptoms started.

The mental health support worker, 43, said: “Just a typical boisterous boy who loves sports, riding his bike, and he’s very sharp.

“It came on quite suddenly – he went from being healthy to waking up one morning with yellow eyes and skin.

“At the doctors, everything was going haywire. His heart rate was high and he was getting breathless just speaking – the doctors were surprised he was still walking.

“We were sent to Bolton Hospital. It took a week to figure out what was going on. It was terrifying because you don’t know what was going on, all you see is your child getting worse and worse. He was deteriorating in front of our eyes, getting yellower, and he could not tolerate noise or light.

“Then we were sent to Manchester Children’s Hospital.

“When they realised it was a blood issue, they were struggling to match his blood.

“They said they had some already stored in Liverpool, then after that was used, they said they had ran out and that they contacted someone who was a match and asked for a donation.

“It was quite daunting to watch him have a transfusion. He felt really well afterwards and perked up a lot. But the blood was breaking down so quickly the donated cells were gone in a few hours.”

open image in gallery Qasim Rizwan after his first transfusion ( PA )

Qasim spent around three weeks in hospital overall. He visited NHSBT’s frozen blood bank in August with his father Rizwan Ahmed, 46, and brother Yusuf.

“I really enjoyed looking around the blood centre and seeing everything,” Qasim said.

“I didn’t know everybody did this in the background.

“Most of the people in the building saved my life and they are still saving lives too. Thank you to all the donors for donating blood to me because I have rare blood.”

Ms Nazar has also since become a blood donor herself.

She said: “The team at Manchester were absolutely amazing. Qasim wanted to know every little detail – what would happen next, the size of the needle – and they were very patient with him.

“I am very grateful to all the scientists and specialists at NHSBT who found out his blood types then found enough blood to keep him going. He thoroughly enjoyed his meeting and getting to know how things work.

“And blood donors are amazing. I can’t thank them enough, without them, Qasim would probably not be here, he would not have survived, and we will be forever grateful for that.”

Joanne Mathews, manager of the NHSBT frozen blood bank, said: “We work behind the scenes and almost never meet patients, so we loved hosting Qasim and his family.

“He met a few people who worked on his case and they all had big smiles.

“Qasim was so curious and polite – and he looked so cute in an adult lab coat.”

Rachael Barber, paediatric intensive care consultant and medical director for Royal Manchester Children’s Hospital, said: “Stories like Qasim’s show just how vital blood donations are to us to enable us to care for children with rare blood types.”

A family from Fort Worth, Texas, has filed a lawsuit against a local daycare facility following an incident in which surveillance footage allegedly captured an adult employee instigating a fight involving a 4-year-old boy.

The lawsuit targets Arka Montessori Academy of Risinger, stemming from an April 27 visit by the child’s mother, Heather Harris, who made an unannounced stop at the facility after sensing something was wrong, as reported by ABC affiliate WFAA.

According to the family’s attorney, Russell T. Button, surveillance footage shows a staff member, described as a former employee, encouraging her own son to attack the 4-year-old before shaking the victim and causing him to fall.

“This place looked like a child fight club,” Button told the outlet. “It felt like one. This kid was thrown around like a human rag doll by somebody that was supposed to protect him.”

The lawsuit argues that the facility failed in its duty to protect the child.

Relatives of a 4-year-old boy in Fort Worth, Texas, have filed a lawsuit against Arka Montessori Academy of Risinger after security footage allegedly showed a staff member orchestrating a physical altercation involving the child ( WFAA )

Heather Harris told WFAA she felt something was wrong from her son’s demeanor.

She said: ““I knew from his cry, in the look on his face, that something had happened. And from that point on, I said, I need to see the cameras.”

“The trust that I put in this daycare, they failed us,” Richard Harris, the boy's father, told WFAA.

Before enrolling their son, the couple researched multiple facilities, prioritizing cleanliness, educational standards and the presence of 24-7 surveillance cameras.

“Education was big; it was clean,” Richard Harris said. “Arka, we thought we hit gold with Arka.”

Heather Harris added, “Everything that glitters isn’t gold, and that facility was one of them.”

Button said of the lawsuit: “When you speak up, when you bring these things to light, it helps hold everyone accountable, and that makes other daycares take notice. That makes them change their ways, become safer. So, working parents have a place to send their kids."

State records indicate the academy has accumulated 21 deficiencies since January 2024, involving health and safety risks, though a subsequent inspection on August 20, 2026, recorded zero deficiencies.

Prior to the incident, the 4-year-old boy spent his time engaged in sports and practicing Michael Jackson dance moves.

“He’s walking around now with his Michael Jackson glove,” Richard Harris told the outlet. “So, he’s just pretty awesome.”

The Independent has contacted Button, the family’s attorney, and Arka Montessori Academy of Risinger for comment.

News.title: Razaullah’s incredible hitting scrambles England’s minds
News.content:
England will look to complete the series whitewash as they hold a commanding position coming into day three of the third and final Test against Pakistan at Edgbaston in what could be the final day of the English Test summer.

England finished up their first innings on 453 on day two, with a mammoth 320-run lead over Pakistan. Five England batsmen passed the fifty mark; Emilio Gay, Harry Brook, Dan Lawrence, Jamie Smith and Ollie Robinson, but none went on to convert those half centuries into hundreds. It means that Ben Duckett’s century against New Zealand at Trent Bridge back in June will be the only England Test hundred of the summer, the first time that has happened in a six-Test summer. England managed 21 half centuries over the course of the summer, so it works out as 4.76% conversion rate.

Having seen England pile on the runs, Pakistan then lost a wicket with the first ball of their second innings, with Saim Ayub making a pair to sum up a miserable return to their Test side for the opener having been jettisoned in as part of wholesale changes for the visitors. Abdullah Shafique followed three balls later, with Robinson taking both wickets as his fine summer continued. Robinson now has 28 wickets across four Tests this summer at a staggering average of 7.75. Joe Root made history yesterday, taking his 220th catch, the most by an outfielder in Test history. Rain though prevented England the opportunity of potentially wrapping up a two-day finish in a Test in this country for the first time since 2000.

Pakistan will resume on 52/2, still 268 runs behind England, with Azan Awais resuming on 29 not out and will be joined by Shan Masood, who is on 21. Pakistan are yet to reach 200 or bat more than 51 overs in this series so the series whitewash may not be a million miles away. Will we see any rare Pakistan resistance in this series or will England’s seamers dominate again? Play on day three from Edgbaston is set to get under at 11am and it could be the final day of not just the series but the English Test summer.

News.title: Interest rates predicted to rise four times by July
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. Britain’s economy grew unexpectedly in July, handing Chancellor John Healey some breathing space ahead of the Budget.

The UK’s gross domestic product (GDP) expanded by 0.4pc during the month, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS). Analysts had expected the UK economy to flatline.

Officials said pubs and clubs, advertisers and alcohol makers reported an increase in turnover linked to the World Cup, while many firms also said the second hottest July on record had a positive impact.

The data showed Britain’s economy may be benefitting from the massive investments in AI, with activity in telecoms expanding by 1.1pc in July, computer programming up 3.5pc and information services up 1.1pc.

The data will lend support to the “optimistic story” that John Healey tried to tell about the economy in a major speech this week.

Growth also accelerated from 0.3pc in June after Andy Burnham took over as Prime Minister in July.

It slightly eases pressure on the Chancellor after the cost of government borrowing costs rose to levels not seen in decades after a jump in the price of oil reignited a bond market sell-off.

The Treasury’s 10-year interest rate rose above 5.3pc on Thursday, a level not seen since 2007. It threatens to wipe around £10bn from Mr Healey’s fiscal headroom before his first Budget next month, according to economists at the Item Club. Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Badenoch must scrap triple lock, says senior Tory MP | Politician urges Conservatives to ‘slaughter some sacred cows’ to stabilise the public finances

2) | Michael O’Leary demands sacking of ‘incompetent’ air traffic control chief | Ryanair boss urges Transport Secretary to dismiss Martin Rolfe after IT meltdown grounds passengers

3) | Guardian staff threaten walkout over pay as paper hails record revenues | Journalists’ union will ballot members over strike in protest against company’s offer

4) | Hotel bosses criticise Burnham’s fresh assault on hospitality | Prime Minister gives mayors power for unlimited levy on stays in blow for pubs and families

5) | Iceland to become first British supermarket to open in Falklands | New shop will begin trading before Christmas despite rising tensions with Argentina over islands

What happened overnight

Oil prices remained at their highest level since May as tensions flared in the Middle East.

Brent crude was above $105 a barrel after after Iran-backed Houthis seized control of Yemen’s keyport of Mocha, threatening Saudi oil exports in the Red Sea.

Asian shares declined, tracking Wall Street losses. Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 2.8pc to 63,442.30, while South Korea’s Kospi lost 2.3pc to 6,872.39.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dipped 0.8pc to 24,753.54. The Shanghai Composite index was down 1.8pc to 3,862.73.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 fell 1.2pc to 8,712.20.

Taiwan’s Taiex lost 1.7pc, while India’s Sensex declined 1pc.

On Thursday, Wall Street’s benchmark S&P 500 dropped 0.6pc in its fourth straight loss. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 0.6pc, and the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite fell 0.7pc.
