World.title: Officials report 63% drop in Chiapas homicides: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📉 Chiapas homicides down 63% : Speaking from Tuxtla Gutiérrez, Sheinbaum touted security gains under Governor Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar, saying “people feel safer in Chiapas today than they did two years ago.” Officials reported the daily homicide rate fell 63% in the first eight months of 2026 compared to 2024, with 9,949 arrests and 18.6 tonnes of drugs seized in the southern state since Sheinbaum took office.

: Speaking from Tuxtla Gutiérrez, Sheinbaum touted security gains under Governor Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar, saying “people feel safer in Chiapas today than they did two years ago.” Officials reported the daily homicide rate fell 63% in the first eight months of 2026 compared to 2024, with 9,949 arrests and 18.6 tonnes of drugs seized in the southern state since Sheinbaum took office. 📚 Pencils over screens after poor PISA scores : Responding to this week’s PISA results showing 41.8% of Mexican 15-year-olds scored below basic level in math, science and reading, Sheinbaum announced new math and reading textbooks for teachers and students, and highlighted plans to regulate device use in schools while pushing a “return to pencil and paper.”

: Responding to this week’s PISA results showing 41.8% of Mexican 15-year-olds scored below basic level in math, science and reading, Sheinbaum announced new math and reading textbooks for teachers and students, and highlighted plans to regulate device use in schools while pushing a “return to pencil and paper.” 🏥 CJNG ‘clandestine hospital’ found in Jalisco: García Harfuch confirmed that a property in Tecalitlán used by the Jalisco New Generation Cartel to treat injured members was uncovered during the search for a missing 20-year-old man, who was among eight people freed from the site.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Friday morning press conference in Tuxtla Gutiérrez, capital of the southern state of Chiapas.

At the start of the mañanera, Sheinbaum said that since Governor Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar took office in December 2024, and “with the coordination with the federal [Security] Cabinet,” the security results in Chiapas have been “very good, not just in the reduction of homicides and other high-impact crimes, but also in the perception [of insecurity].”

“People feel safer in Chiapas today than they did two years ago,” she said.

Later in the press conference, security officials presented the latest data on homicides, high-impact crimes and arrests in Chiapas, a state where violence increased significantly in 2024, especially near the border with Guatemala.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were Sheinbaum’s remarks on how the government plans to improve both the teaching and learning of mathematics and reading in Mexican schools. Her comments came three days after the publication of PISA testing results that showed that around four in 10 Mexicans 15-year-olds scored below the basic level in science, mathematics and reading.

Homicides down 63% in Chiapas compared to 2024

National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa noted that the homicide rate in Chiapas remained “quite stable” between 2015 and 2023 before increasing significantly in 2024, a year in which an average of 2.4 murders per day were committed in the state.

She noted that the daily homicide rate in the first eight months of this year was 0.9, representing a reduction of 63% compared to 2024. The year-over-year decline was 10%, according to the data presented.

Figueroa also reported that the daily homicide rate in Chiapas in August — 0.9 — was 64% lower than the rate in December 2024, the month Ramírez was sworn in as governor.

With regard to high-impact crimes, among which are homicides, kidnappings, violent robberies and acts of extortion, the daily incidence in Chiapas in August was 2.7, a reduction of 44% compared to November 2024. The data presented by Figueroa showed that the daily incidence of high-impact crimes rose 8% between August 2025 and August 2026.

Later in the press conference, Security Minister Omar García Harfuch reported that 9,949 people were arrested in Chiapas between Oct. 1, 2024 — the date Sheinbaum took office — and Aug. 31, 2026, for allegedly committing high-impact crimes. Authorities seized 1,545 firearms and 18.6 tonnes of drugs in the state in the same period.

Sheinbaum outlines strategies to improve educational outcomes

A reporter asked the president whether Mexico’s education system needs to be strengthened in light of the PISA results published this week. In testing for the OECD’s Program for International Student Assessment, 41.8% of Mexican 15-year-olds scored below the basic level in the science/math/reading triad, more than double the 19.7% average across OECD countries. Education Minister Mario Delgado on Wednesday addressed the low scores earned by Mexican students by blaming “the excessive use of cell phones and computer screens.”

Sheinbaum asserted that “education in Mexico is getting stronger,” before acknowledging that Mexican students have ground to make up.

“We have to make progress in mathematics. We’re going to have a special textbook next year for the learning of mathematics, to help the teachers and the students,” she said.

Sheinbaum subsequently highlighted that Mexico wasn’t the only country to score poorly in the reading domain of the PISA testing.

She said that “all the countries of the world” scored poorly on reading, “with the exception of four or five, due to the use of digital platforms.”

“[That was] acknowledged by the education area of the OECD. Young people, girls and boys, stopped reading and understanding what they read due to the excessive use of digital platforms, which is something that we’re now addressing,” Sheinbaum said, referring to a plan to implement national regulations on the use of devices in schools.

“[We’re going to] return to pencil and paper, pen and paper, and reading,” she said.

Sheinbaum said the teaching of reading and writing in Mexican schools will also be supported by a new textbook.

She said that the new textbook (or likely textbooks for different grades) will include poems and short stories that girls and boys “should know.”

Clandestine CJNG hospital discovered in Jalisco

A reporter asked García Harfuch about the discovery of a clandestine Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) hospital in the state of Jalisco.

🚔 En rueda de prensa se informó que la Vicefiscalía en Personas Desaparecidas, en coordinación con la Guardia Nacional y la Secretaría de la Defensa Nacional, realizó un operativo en Tecalitlán que permitió rescatar a ocho hombres y detener a seis personas. (1-3) pic.twitter.com/Vbe47OAf8T — Fiscalía del Estado de Jalisco (@FiscaliaJal) September 10, 2026

The Informador newspaper reported on Thursday that the search for a 20-year-old man who went missing in Tlaquepaque in July led authorities to a property in the municipality of Tecalitlán that was used as a clandestine hospital by the CJNG. Informador noted that six people were detained at the property. Eight alleged victims of forced recruitment, including the missing 20-year-old, were freed.

García Harfuch confirmed that injured “organized crime people” were treated at the property. He added that investigations related to the discovery of the property are still being carried out.

World.title: The ultimate guide to contemporary Mexican restaurants in Guadalajara
World.content:
Mexican Independence Day celebrations this month offer a great opportunity to celebrate and rediscover Mexican food, and what better way to do it than through five restaurants that are putting a contemporary spin on traditional Mexican cuisine?

From chilaquiles with poblano chile sauce to eggplant tamales and corn pancakes, here are some of the best contemporary Mexican restaurants in Guadalajara to try right now.

Ixtle

Located in Zapopan, Ixtle defines itself as a kitchen true to its roots: A relaxed concept that takes corn and Mexican ingredients as its starting point, reinterpreting them through international techniques and references.

In the mornings, guests can enjoy innovative dishes such as the Jarocho Breakfast, featuring eggs in hoja santa with longaniza, banana and confit mushrooms, or waffles made from maize accompanied by a blend of caramelized miso, maple syrup, honey, mascarpone and macadamia butter.

Lovers of traditional hot café de olla will appreciate Ixtle’s reinterpretation of a staple of Mexican cuisine — the café de olla latte, served cold with orange peel and a touch of foamy milk.

At night, the menu becomes more elaborate, drawing on a wider range of international influences and featuring dishes that are designed to be shared. The Mediterranean tuna tiradito, served with red peppers in pil-pil sauce and nixtamalized tomato paste, is a must-try.

Best for: Breakfasts with friends or a date night

Breakfasts with friends or a date night Location: C. Miguel León Portilla 478, Santa Fe, 45168 Zapopan, Jalisco

C. Miguel León Portilla 478, Santa Fe, 45168 Zapopan, Jalisco Instagram: instagram.com/ixtle_rest

Teté Cocina de Barrio

Spearheaded by siblings Mario and Karla Papa, Teté has been delighting tapatíos for over a decade through a cuisine that blends Mexico’s culinary heritage with flavors introduced by the different cultures that have settled in the country.

With an approach that prioritizes seasonal ingredients, the menu at Teté not only changes every month, but it is a complete surprise for diners, who do not know what they will have for dinner until dishes start arriving.

Guests are also in for another surprise: Teté does not have waiters. Instead, everyone does a bit of everything, with the chefs themselves guiding diners throughout the meal.

With no waiters and no menu, Teté defines itself as a restaurant that “doesn’t repeat menus, but experiences.” It’s no wonder this unpretentious restaurant in the Moderna neighborhood has made it to coveted culinary rankings around the world.

Best for: Date night

Date night Location: C. Rayón 830, Moderna, 44170 Guadalajara, Jalisco

C. Rayón 830, Moderna, 44170 Guadalajara, Jalisco Website: tete-cocina-de-barrio.mailchimpsites.com

Amorcito Mío

Located in the heart of Zapopan Centro and just steps away from the Zapopan Basílica, Amorcito Mío offers a warm atmosphere and home-cooked-style recipes.

Although the breakfast menu offers international dishes such as sandwiches and paninis, it is simultaneously a celebration of Mexican food, albeit with a twist.

Guests will be surprised by the variety of sauces featured on the chilaquiles menu beyond the traditional red and green. Expect chilaquiles with poblano chile sauce, spicy peanut sauce and a super spicy sauce made from güero chiles and habanero.

To balance the heat, Amorcito Mío offers a varied selection of Mexican breads, including pan dulce staples like conchas, as well as traditional bolillo and birote.

While breakfasts highlight authentic Mexican flavors, the menu shifts in the afternoon and evening to feature wood-fired pizzas and a blend of Italian and Mediterranean dishes.

Best for: Casual gatherings with friends

Casual gatherings with friends Location: Calle 5 de Mayo 275, Zapopan, 45100 Zapopan, Jalisco

Calle 5 de Mayo 275, Zapopan, 45100 Zapopan, Jalisco Instagram: instagram.com/amorcito_mi

Bruna

View this post on Instagram A post shared by BRUNA (@bruna_mx)

With a terrace surrounded by lush gardens and sculptures, Bruna generates excitement from the very first moment, offering diners an almost theatrical experience.

Since opening in 2015, chef Óscar Garza has drawn inspiration from Mexican abuelitas’ recipes and street-food flavors, reinterpreting them with contemporary techniques and an artistic presentation.

Among the dishes that stand out for their meticulous presentation is the chile en nogada, which returns to the menu each year during the patriotic month. Las probaditas de mole, literally meaning “little tastes of mole,” features a rainbow of colors and flavors that pushes the boundaries of classic mole poblano.

If you are looking for something sweet and original, be sure to try the bruleated corn cream, a dessert that blends the traditional flavor of corn with the classic French twist of crème brûlée.

Best for: Special occasions

Special occasions Location: Lerdo de Tejada No. 2418, Col. Lafayette, Guadalajara, Jalisco

Lerdo de Tejada No. 2418, Col. Lafayette, Guadalajara, Jalisco Instagram: instagram.com/bruna_mx

Tikuun Comedor Local

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Tikuun comedor (@tikuun.comedor)

Spearheaded by chef Carlos Espinosa, Tikuun has been open for over a decade, but only recently began receiving the recognition it deserves.

Situated in the trendy Colonia Americana, it features a constantly rotating menu that showcases new preparations and seasonal variations throughout the year. Although the menu draws inspiration from different cultures and cuisines, the restaurant’s manifesto promises a distinctly Mexican essence in each dish.

Standout recent offerings include roasted eggplant with cured nopal, aged cotija, salsa macha made with chia and Kalamata olives, requesón cheese and garlic confit, as well as octopus with recado negro, chinchayote, sweet potato and beet.

The intimate, almost home-like atmosphere allows guests to savor the experience at a leisurely pace, whether ordering a la carte or opting for the tasting menu.

Best for: An intimate dinner with friends

An intimate dinner with friends Location: Emeterio Robles Gil 50, Col. Americana, 44600 Guadalajara, Jalisco

Emeterio Robles Gil 50, Col. Americana, 44600 Guadalajara, Jalisco Instagram: instagram.com/tikuun.comedor

Gabriela Solís is a Mexican lawyer turned full-time writer. She was born and raised in Guadalajara and covers business, culture, lifestyle and travel for Mexico News Daily. You can follow her lifestyle blog Dunas y Palmeras.

World.title: Is Mexico as patriotic as the US? Just look around!
World.content:
I plead guilty. Whenever the Mexican national anthem was played at this year’s World Cup, tears welled up in my eyes. It was pride. Pride that my team was participating in a flagship event of contemporary football — and that, moreover, they were performing so well, for once!

And yes, I was that ridiculous woman. And so was my mother, my sister, and even my mother-in-law, who, although born in the Soviet Union, has been Mexican longer than I have been alive. We all cried in pride. Tears flowed from our eyes in unison: “al sonoro rugir del cañón” — and that was just for the World Cup!

And I know I’m not the only one. The overwhelming response of people celebrating our victories at the Angel of Independence on Paseo de la Reforma confirms it. Thinking about that, I sincerely wonder: Are Mexicans as patriotic as people from the U.S.? This is harder to answer than I initially thought.

Proud of our roots?

Mexico is a megadiverse country. Biologically, of course, but also in terms of ethnic groups. On numerous occasions, I have written for MND about Indigenous neighborhoods that are still alive even in Mexico City, and how we still have a syncretic understanding of our relationship with God and the church. People don’t find that in the U.S., because our colonial pasts were indeed very different.

And as such, our relationship with Indigenous peoples is very different. While in the United States less than 3% of the population identifies as Native American, according to the most recent census, 19% of Mexicans identify with an Indigenous group.

Therefore, Mexico’s relationship with its Indigenous peoples is also different and very complex. Besides being inevitably tainted by racism and pigmentocratic segregation, it is ironically painful to think that we take pride in the 68 Indigenous languages ​​still spoken throughout the country.

This diversity, at first glance, gives us a very strong sense of history and identity that hardly any other country in the Americas shares. However, at the same time, “60.8% of Indigenous people live in some level of poverty,” according to the most recent INEGI survey. This equates to almost 8 million people who, due to a fundamentally racial issue inherited from the colonial period, live in some state of poverty. Painful? Yes. And deeply shameful, too.

Although there are distinctly Indigenous towns — and possibly entire states — throughout Mexico, like Oaxaca, we don’t have anything like a reserve for Native nations, as happens in the U.S. This topic alone could be a doctoral thesis, but it undeniably deserves a mention in an article about national pride. All of which brings me to the next uncomfortable issue.

The issue of malinchismo

Octavio Paz wrote a lengthy essay on this issue in 1950. In “The Labyrinth of Solitude,” the author explores our relationship with “la chingada,” that is, La Malinche: the historical figure who, despite being Indigenous, married a high-ranking officer among the Spanish invaders.

In a word, Paz thinks that our relationship with that first mother, Malintzin, shaped by the European invasion, still weighs heavily on us. Our colonial past not only shames us, but it severely affects our Mexican identity. Ouch. This leads us to what’s called malinchismo: the notion that something is better simply because it’s not Mexican. This extends to nationality, language, everyday products and even systems of thought.

How does malinchismo interact with our sense of national pride? It’s hard to say. It’s a difficult relationship that reminds us of the shame of having been dominated by European invasion, but it coexists in our national history as part of our very identity. I think it all boils down to the fact that it’s a common saying among Mexicans that, nowadays, only people from Puebla want to be Spanish.

That simply does not exist in the United States. On the contrary, it’s a grave insult to be “un-American,” right?

God bless … Mexico?

My partner lived at Penn State for a year because of his dad’s job, and he remembers with a strange feeling that the “Pledge of Allegiance” to the flag was recited every morning. In Mexico, the closest thing we have to that is what Sarah DeVries described as “Honores a la Bandera.”

Although there are points of convergence, our civic culture is more diluted: You don’t see Mexican flags in the homes of ordinary Mexicans. It’s more common to see virgins, saints or crucifixes. On the contrary, it seems, at times, that we forget our national symbols until September, or perhaps when there’s a major global sporting event, like the World Cup.

You’ll hardly find anyone in Mexico saying they’re a proud patriot, or that they’re proud of our troops. We usually never trust the police — let alone the army. Along the same lines, I’ve never heard anything like “God bless Mexico!” Perhaps because we don’t have the legacy of Manifest Destiny looming over our sense of nationalism.

You will find, though, a general feeling of pride in being a Mexican, although we have a very complicated relationship with our colonial past. Our sense of national pride, moreover, still has a very PRI-ist tinge to it — which again, might be material for an entire doctoral thesis on its own.

Proud to be a Mexican

A recent poll by YouGov shows that “70% of Americans say they are proud to be Americans; 16% say they are not.” In contrast, 89% of Mexicans expressed being proud to be Mexicans in the 2020 National Survey of Civic Culture (ENCUCI).

However much national pride those figures might inspire, we feminists do not hesitate to denounce the Mexican state as a rapist macho man, using it as a rallying cry in our gender struggles. That is perhaps one of the most frequently used slogans in the March 8 marches. And at the same time, at an official event, I wouldn’t hesitate for a second to salute my flag with pride.

Perhaps, more than certainties, this article raised more questions for our readership. It was probably meant to be that way. And that’s the wonder of the social sciences: They don’t aim to provide straight answers, but rather to expand the conversation to raise more interesting questions — no matter how uncomfortable or painful they may be.

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: Corruption, bribes and who Mexicans trust the least
World.content:
In 2025, 15.6% of people who carried out a bureaucratic procedure (trámite), made a payment to a government office, requested a public service or had any other kind of contact with authorities experienced an “act of corruption,” according to the results of the latest National Survey of Governmental Quality and Impact (ENCIG).

The national statistics agency INEGI conducted the survey at 46,000 homes in late 2025 and the results were published in May.

In this “Mexico in Numbers” article, we look at where in Mexico people are most and least likely to encounter corruption when interacting with municipal, state and federal authorities. One of the main ways people experience corruption in Mexico is by being asked to pay a bribe.

We also present survey results on:

The situations in which corruption directly affecting citizens is most prevalent.

The institutions that are considered the most and least corrupt.

Where is corruption most and least prevalent?

The state where people most commonly experience corruption is Hidalgo. Around 21.5% of residents from that state who came into contact with authorities last year experienced an act of corruption, according to the ENCIG results.

The states with the next highest percentages of people who were victims of an act of corruption last year were:

Oaxaca: 20.3%

Sinaloa: 19.8%

Chihuahua: 18.4%

Sonora: 18.3%

The states with the lowest percentages of people who were victims of an act of corruption last year were:

Colima: 7%

Nayarit: 8.9%

Zacatecas: 9.4%

Querétaro: 9.5%

Tamaulipas: 10.8%

In what situations is corruption most prevalent?

According to the ENCIG results, the five most common situations in which acts of corruption occurred last year were:

When people came into contact with public security authorities, such as police: 63.5% of respondents who experienced corruption said it occurred in this context. When people were applying for property-related permits: 32% When people were making “other payments,” submitting bureaucratic paperwork (trámites) or submitting “requests”: 29.3% When people were submitting trámites to open a business: 23.5%. When people were submitting trámites to the Federal Attorney General’s Office or a State Attorney General’s Office: 22.3%

Of the five most common situations in which acts of corruption occurred last year, the only one whose incidence declined compared to 2023 was No. 4.

Which institutions are seen as most and least corrupt?

ENCIG respondents were also asked their opinions about the frequency with which various institutions engage in corruption.

Police forces are seen as the most corrupt institution. (Note: The survey didn’t differentiate between municipal police forces and state police forces.)

Almost nine in 10 respondents — 86.5% — believe that police engage in corruption “very frequently” or “frequently.”

According to survey respondents, the next most corrupt institutions are:

Political parties: 83.9% of respondents believe they engage in corruption “very frequently” or “frequently.”

Prosecutor’s Offices: 75.3%

State governments: 74.1%

Houses of Congress: 73%.

According to survey respondents, the least corrupt institutions in Mexico are:

Public schools: 31.8% of respondents believe they engage in corruption “very frequently” or “frequently.”

Public autonomous organizations: 36.9%

Civil society organizations: 41.2%

Religious institutions: 43%

The Army and Navy: 46.1%

INEGI also asked respondents their opinions about the frequency with which families, neighbors and work colleagues engage in corruption. The results were as follows:

Families: 18.7% of respondents believe they engage in corruption “very frequently” or “frequently.”

Neighbors: 19.1%

Work colleagues: 21.8%

The full Europe Intelligence Dossier — the editor’s leader, the deep dive, the country health check and the people who matter — is updated daily by the Rio Times Intelligence Desk. Open the dossier

Friday’s psychogram, from Hamburg to Hastings: the morning after, and the invoice passed around the table. Thursday’s rate rise in Berlin was hours old, yet the continent was already doing what it does with a central bank: reading the decision for class meaning. A German household reads a new inflation forecast as next winter’s heating bill. A British statistician reads it as cover for patience. A French exporter reads the 1.16 euro as a discount taken off the invoice. Everyone, from Lisbon to Tallinn, understands that “no pre-commitment” is a sentence markets will parse until December.

Read in English, German, French, Italian, Spanish and Polish, across the continent’s largest outlets and our own Europe desk.

Germany: The Bill Arrives By Memory

No country wakes the morning after a European rate decision with more homework than Germany, because no country carries the memory this one does. The ECB’s projections, published with Thursday’s Berlin meeting, carry inflation averaging 3.0 per cent this year and 2.5 per cent next — above target throughout, with 2027 and 2028 both revised upward. And at the press conference the gas question arrived ready-made, put to the president by a journalist: the adverse scenario that priced gas at 60 euros a megawatt-hour in June now confronts an actual price around 82.

Germany does not hear that as energy-market trivia; it hears 2022. The country has stored what a gas bill can do to a government’s standing, and the new forecast reaches past next winter into the one after. Berlin’s coalition inherits the discomfort, and German industry — the economy’s spine — reads a deposit rate of 2.50 per cent as a verdict that the squeeze is worth it, delivered by people whose factories pay the invoice. The German mood is the continent’s in concentrate: stoicism underwritten by a memory that will not fade as fast as the invoices did.

Britain: Relief, Hedged Twice

The Office for National Statistics delivered Friday’s one hard number: UK gross domestic product rose 0.4 per cent month-on-month in July, accelerating from 0.3 per cent in June and no growth in May. One month is not a recovery, and the figures are revisable; but a 0.4 is a 0.4, and for a country that has spent the summer arguing about whether it grows at all, the decimal point is political currency.

The British reaction is the most nationally characteristic in Europe: relief, hedged twice, optimism expressed in the subjunctive. For the Bank of England the print buys time rather than direction — a committee weighing a cooling labour market against fading demand can now afford patience. Britain’s psychogram this week is a small pleasure in watching the continental dilemma from across the water: London argues about how fast to cut, while Frankfurt argues about how high to hold, and each finds the other’s problem faintly reassuring.

The Exporters’ Euro: Strength That Spends Like Debt

Around 1.16 to the dollar, the single currency is doing Europe’s psychogram work. A euro at that level flatters the importer and taxes the exporter, and Europe is, in aggregate, the world’s exporter: German machinery, French aerospace, Italian luxury all quote in dollars and earn in euros. Each of them watched the currency climb while Berlin tightened, and each did the arithmetic both ways — cheaper energy inputs, dearer order books — and liked neither total.

There is a second reading underneath the first, and it is less comfortable. A strong euro is what a currency looks like when foreign capital decides your central bank means what it says; it is also what it looks like when the dollar stumbles on its own politics. Europe did not choose this strength so much as inherit it, and inherited strength spends like borrowed money. The continent’s export lobby knows the difference between owning a currency and renting one’s reputation, and on Friday it could feel which it was doing.

The War Premium Arrives By Sea

Underneath the monetary arithmetic runs the older one, and it arrives by tanker. Wire agencies describe the strait of Hormuz as effectively shut to traffic, and Brent crude traded around US$107.60 a barrel in early Asian dealing on Friday, up more than 6 per cent in days, after the fall of the Yemeni port of Mokha moved the fighting eighty kilometres closer to the Bab al-Mandab strait. Europe, which imports the better part of its hydrocarbons by sea, pays the premium in freight, insurance and futures curves before any politician issues a statement.

This is the line that connects Thursday’s Berlin decision to Friday’s household dread: the ECB’s gas scenarios are not modelling curiosities but tanker routes. The continent’s inflation fight is being set at sea, by pilots, insurers and admirals — none of whom take minutes in Frankfurt. Europe’s mood about this is resigned rather than panicked; it has learned, in three hard years, to treat energy insecurity as weather.

Frankfurt’s Long Afternoon

The day’s remaining appointments are parsing exercises. Lagarde speaks at 18:00 and chief economist Philip Lane at 21:00, and every word will be weighed against Berlin’s operative phrase: “no pre-commitment”. Markets heard it as a door left ajar; doves heard it as a bank refusing to be cornered; and the sentence was engineered, as such sentences are, to be heard both ways.

What the afternoon cannot change is the forecast: inflation above target through 2027, energy’s adverse line redrawn by a war at sea, and a continent told the truth slowly — the price of normality went up, and the instalments run for years. The psychogram of the long afternoon is Europe’s oldest financial habit: the reading of tea leaves as a collective sport, practised most passionately by those who no longer believe the leaves can save them.

What This Means From Latin America

A euro at 1.16 and a European bank in no hurry to cut redraw the transatlantic weather. Europe buys the hemisphere’s copper, coffee, lithium and soy, and a strong euro makes every one of those invoices cheaper in European hands — supportive for exporters, deflationary for the rural districts that vote on prices. Meanwhile a central bank holding firm keeps global money tight, and tight money is the climate in which the hemisphere’s dollar debts and budget deficits pay full fare.

The strategic reading is simpler: Europe’s energy anxiety is Latin America’s standing invitation. A continent that learned to fear gas dependence in 2022 is still searching for reliable suppliers of everything electrons can replace, and the hemisphere holds the copper, the lithium and — in Brazil and Guyana — the hydrocarbons to be that supplier. Friday’s Frankfurt arithmetic is, read from this side of the Atlantic, a procurement list, and it has been open for three years.

What We Are Watching

Lagarde at 18:00 — whether Berlin’s “no pre-commitment” hardens into guidance or softens into choreography, and which verbs survive the translation.

The Bigger Picture Friday’s Europe is an invoice being passed around the table. The central bank issued it on Thursday in Berlin — inflation above target through 2027, energy’s line redrawn by a war at sea, no promises attached. Friday found every country reading its own line item: Germany the gas memory, Britain a modest growth surprise, the exporters the currency, and the whole continent the premium arriving by tanker. Nobody at the table disputes the total; the argument, which will run for months, is about who tips. The psychogram is stoicism with an expiry date. Europe has stopped expecting cheap energy, stopped expecting a weak currency, and stopped expecting its central bank to protect it from either. What replaces those expectations is the continent’s oldest habit: adjustment, itemised, borne with a patience that is half virtue and half fatigue. The morning after a hard decision is when Europe discovers what it actually decided — and on Friday, from Hamburg to Hastings, the arithmetic was arriving faster than the reassurance.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the ECB decide in Berlin, and what does Friday change?

On Thursday the bank raised its deposit rate to 2.50 per cent and published new projections showing inflation averaging 3.0 per cent this year and 2.5 per cent next — above target throughout, with 2027 and 2028 revised upward. Friday is the first full day of interpretation: President Lagarde speaks at 18:00 and chief economist Philip Lane at 21:00, and markets are testing whether Berlin’s “no pre-commitment” language leaves the door open for another rise or closes it.

What did the UK GDP figure show?

The Office for National Statistics reported month-on-month growth of 0.4 per cent for July 2026, accelerating from 0.3 per cent in June and no growth in May. A single month is not a trend and the figures are revisable, but the print weakens the stagnation narrative and gives the Bank of England room to stay patient on rate cuts.

Why does the gas scenario matter so much?

Because Europe imports most of its energy by sea, and the sea route is at war. At Thursday’s press conference the gas question was put directly to President Lagarde: the adverse scenario that priced gas at 60 euros a megawatt-hour in June now confronts an actual price around 82, a spread driven by a war at sea that wire agencies describe as leaving the strait of Hormuz effectively shut. If tanker disruption persists, the 82-euro line becomes the operative one — feeding directly into the inflation forecast Berlin just published.

Who gains and who loses from a euro at 1.16?

Importers gain: energy, commodities and dollar-priced inputs cost fewer euros. Exporters lose: German machinery, French aerospace and Italian luxury all quote in dollars and earn in euros, so each sale converts into less home currency. The level also signals that global capital rates the ECB’s resolve — welcome for credibility, costly for the order book.

Sources: European Central Bank (projections and account of the Berlin decision), UK Office for National Statistics, Gulf News and wire agencies (energy markets) · 10–11 Sep 2026.

Friday’s psychogram, from Shenzhen to Taipei: a continent discovering what its bottleneck is worth. Asia built the world’s artificial-intelligence machine and assumed that building it was the same as controlling it. This week the machine taught the continent otherwise: one small, unglamorous component — memory — now decides the pace of everyone’s ambition, and each capital is reacting to that discovery in its own national accent. Beijing hears proof that self-reliance is worth any price. Seoul hears leverage it has not held in years. Taipei hears a record month and, in the same breath, a warning.

Read in English, Mandarin, Japanese, Korean, Bahasa and Hindi, across the region’s largest outlets and our own Asia desk.

China: Defiance, Priced By The Card

The number of the week in Beijing is 250,000 — yuan, the indicated price of Huawei’s Ascend 950DT accelerator card, about US$37,000 at the prevailing rate of roughly 6.7 yuan to the dollar. Reuters reports the mark-up runs 20 to 50 per cent over quotes from just two months earlier, driven by a worldwide shortage of high-bandwidth memory, the stacked DRAM that every serious AI server requires and that SK Hynix and Samsung in Korea ration to whoever orders furthest ahead.

For any other country a 50-per-cent price rise would be a procurement problem; for China it reads as a strategic memo. The official narrative has long held that American export controls would only accelerate indigenous capability, and Friday’s sticker price is the first time that argument arrives with a receipt attached — expensive, yes, but available, which is the property Beijing values above all others. The defiance is genuine, and so is the arithmetic underneath it: a nation paying a scarcity premium to itself is still paying a scarcity premium.

Korea’s Leverage, And Its Discomfort

The same shortage that taxes Beijing empowers Seoul, and the Korean reaction is the week’s most interesting psychogram. SK Hynix and Samsung hold the memory bottleneck the entire AI world must pass through, a position of leverage Washington’s export rules never designed and cannot easily command. Korea has spent its modern history as an indispensable intermediary — vital to everyone’s supply chain, master of none of it — and a component shortage is the first lever it has held that depends on Korean factories rather than American permission.

Yet the mood in Seoul is caution dressed as opportunity, and the caution is earned. Leverage held by a middle power invites two responses in sequence: first dependency from customers, then determined replacement by them. Korea has watched this film in shipbuilding and displays, and it knows that bottlenecks, like monopolies, are rented rather than owned. The quiet hope in Seoul is to convert the memory shortage into durable alliances — before the customers it is currently pricing learn to do without it.

The Pass-Through Reaches America’s Clouds

Bloomberg’s reporting, carried across the trade press, says Nvidia’s contract manufacturers have notified major data-centre operators — Microsoft, Google and Oracle among them — that prices for servers carrying its AI chips will rise by more than 15 per cent in many configurations, effective with shipments early next year. The mechanism is worth pausing on: an export-control regime built to slow China’s AI capacity is now, through a memory squeeze, raising the price of America’s own build-out.

For Asia the significance is psychological rather than financial. The clouds of the United States — the buyers at the top of the whole chain — are being asked to fund the AI era at scarcity prices, in contracts signed quarters before delivery. The region reads that as the week’s quietest admission: in the technology war, everyone pays, and the invoice travels in all directions at once.

DeepSeek’s Quiet Upset: A Debate About Character

Under the hardware noise, the software league moved in a way that mainland observers read as a national-character argument. The South China Morning Post reports that DeepSeek’s new V4.1 Flash edged past Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 on independent benchmark runs — 90.6 to 88.3 on the Terminal-Bench 2.1 suite — reversing an ordering the market had treated as settled.

The two labs embody rival theories of Chinese capability, and the rivalry is cultural before it is commercial. Moonshot bets the way a great power is expected to bet: massive capital, vast infrastructure, scale as destiny. DeepSeek bets on mathematics and thrift, the old argument that cleverness can substitute for wealth — an argument with deep roots in a country that remembers being poor and outnumbered. Friday’s benchmark is one data point, but it lands in a week when the physical layer of AI grew scarcer and dearer, and a win for the frugal school reads, in Beijing, as permission to hope that brains can still beat money.

Malaysia: The Patience Strategy

Compute has started migrating toward electricity, and this week the migration acquired an address. Reuters reports that OpenAI signed a multi-year deal with Firmus, the Nvidia-backed Australian AI-infrastructure developer, becoming anchor customer for two Malaysian AI factories that will run Vera Rubin-generation processors; with OpenAI aboard, Firmus says its total contracted capacity across all customers now exceeds 900 megawatts. The peninsula’s southern tip already serves Singapore’s overflow; the deal makes it a primary address in its own right.

For Kuala Lumpur the psychogram is strategic patience, the region’s most underrated asset. While the great powers contest chips and models, Malaysia has quietly positioned itself to own what both consume: power, land and permits. It is a gambit with a long history on the peninsula — let the impatient exhaust themselves, then inherit the position they vacate. Southeast Asia owns neither the memory nor the models, and on Friday it looked closer than either superpower to owning the plugs.

Taiwan: Pride That Curdles Into Dependence

Foxconn reported August revenue of NT$921.8 billion — about US$29.1 billion at roughly 31.7 Taiwan dollars to the US dollar — the largest month in the company’s history, with management guiding that the third quarter should beat market expectations. Taiwan’s assembler, not its foundry, is printing the biggest month the island’s industry has ever recorded, and the pride is genuine: Hon Hai’s payroll now absorbs a measurable share of the world’s AI hardware cycle.

But pride is only half the island’s reaction, and the other half is the truer psychogram. A record built on assembling other people’s designs, for other people’s models, in a component market controlled by Korea, is dependence that has learned to celebrate itself. Taiwan knows better than any economy in Asia how quickly indispensable can become precarious; the memory squeeze that powers Foxconn’s August is the same squeeze that could ration its September. The mood in Taipei is the week’s in miniature: exhilaration, armoured in anxiety.

What This Means From Latin America

Asia’s bottleneck week reads in Latin America as a parable about position. The hemisphere sits on the copper, lithium and electrons that the AI era consumes, yet buys the era’s hardware at retail — and Nvidia’s more-than-15-per-cent pass-through will arrive, eventually, in every integrator’s quote from Bogotá to Buenos Aires. The region supplies the body and rents the brain.

The Asian counterexamples are instructive. Malaysia’s patience — converting land, power and permits into leverage while others fight over chips — maps directly onto the hemisphere’s energy advantages: Brazilian hydro, Chilean solar, Argentine gas, all waiting for the same conversion. And Korea’s uncomfortable discovery, that a bottleneck is rented rather than owned, is the hemisphere’s oldest lesson about commodity wealth, offered back from the other side of the world. Foxconn’s record month proves the demand is real; the open question, on both continents, is whose grid and whose ground it ultimately feeds.

What We Are Watching

Memory allocation — whether SK Hynix and Samsung expand HBM output fast enough to cool the 20-to-50-per-cent premium before year-end, or let scarcity do their pricing.

— whether SK Hynix and Samsung expand HBM output fast enough to cool the 20-to-50-per-cent premium before year-end, or let scarcity do their pricing. The Ascend price — whether Huawei’s 950DT holds above 250,000 yuan as domestic memory supply catches up, or marks the top of the squeeze.

— whether Huawei’s 950DT holds above 250,000 yuan as domestic memory supply catches up, or marks the top of the squeeze. Benchmark rematches — whether Moonshot answers V4.1 Flash before the mainland’s model league reorders funding across the sector.

— whether Moonshot answers V4.1 Flash before the mainland’s model league reorders funding across the sector. Johor’s build-out — how fast Firmus converts its OpenAI anchor deal into live Malaysian capacity, and whether Singapore responds with capacity of its own.

— how fast Firmus converts its OpenAI anchor deal into live Malaysian capacity, and whether Singapore responds with capacity of its own. Foxconn’s September — whether the record August becomes a run rate or a peak, and what the AI-server mix does to margins.

The Bigger Picture Asia’s Friday is a parable of the technology age told in national accents. The continent that fabricates the world’s intelligence is short of the one component intelligence cannot be shipped without; the models argue over character while the hardware prices scarcity; and the strategic asset that matters most turns out to be neither the chip nor the model but the megawatt — which is why an Australian firm and an American AI lab signed the week’s most consequential deal on Malaysian soil. The psychogram is ambition armoured in anxiety. China pays 250,000 yuan for a card it cannot yet make cheaply and calls it independence. Korea holds a lever it knows is rented. Taiwan celebrates a record that doubles as a dependency. Every capital in Asia knows the bottleneck will be broken eventually — and every capital is racing to be holding it when it is. Scarcity, as this week demonstrated, is the most political substance on the continent: whoever controls the narrow point controls the mood of everyone downstream.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are AI chip prices rising in China?

Because high-bandwidth memory, the stacked DRAM every AI accelerator needs, is in shortage. Reuters reports the constraint has lifted Chinese AI-chip prices by 20 to 50 per cent; Huawei’s Ascend 950DT is now indicated above 250,000 yuan (about US$37,000 at the prevailing rate of roughly 6.7 yuan to the dollar), while Bloomberg reports that AI-server prices for Microsoft, Google and Oracle will rise by more than 15 per cent in many configurations from shipments early next year.

What did DeepSeek V4.1 Flash beat?

Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, on independent benchmark runs reported by the South China Morning Post — 90.6 to 88.3 on the Terminal-Bench 2.1 suite. The result reverses the recent ordering of mainland AI labs and strengthens the efficiency-first school of Chinese model development at a moment when the hardware layer is scarce and expensive.

What are OpenAI and Firmus building in Malaysia?

OpenAI signed a multi-year capacity deal with Firmus, the Nvidia-backed Australian AI-infrastructure firm, becoming anchor customer for two Malaysian AI factories running Vera Rubin-generation processors; Firmus says its total contracted capacity across all customers now tops 900 megawatts, reported by Reuters. The deal extends Singapore’s spillover southward and positions Malaysia as a primary AI-hosting address in its own right — evidence that electricity, not chips, is now the binding constraint on compute geography.

Why does Foxconn’s August matter beyond Taiwan?

Because the contract manufacturer is a proxy for the entire AI hardware cycle. August revenue of NT$921.8 billion (about US$29.1 billion at roughly 31.7 Taiwan dollars to the US dollar) is the largest month in Foxconn’s history, confirming that AI-server demand is still accelerating through the industry’s biggest assembler — and that the memory squeeze is the one thing standing between that demand and even larger numbers.

Sources: Reuters (HBM squeeze, Firmus-OpenAI, Foxconn), Bloomberg (server pricing, via trade press), South China Morning Post (DeepSeek benchmark) · 5–11 Sep 2026.

Friday’s psychogram, continent-wide: what a nation buys when its myth goes on sale. Lagos is days from finding out whether Nigerians will pay to own a piece of the one miracle their country agrees on and argues about in the same breath. Harare watched its president’s money men purchase the time the constitution no longer withholds. Pretoria is discovering what remains of a political identity once the assumption under it has died, and Ituri keeps the kind of accounts that no offer document can settle.

Read in English, French, Arabic, Portuguese and Swahili, across the continent’s largest outlets and our own Africa desk.

Nigeria: The Miracle, Priced By The Share

Every country has one story it tells about itself until the story becomes furniture. Nigeria’s is that it pumps the crude and imports the fuel, a nation refuelling on its own absurdity, and the Dangote refinery at Lekki was built to end the telling of that story. On Monday the signing ceremonies were held in Lagos; on 14 September the public offer opens, 4.1 billion shares at ₦525 apiece, ₦2.15 trillion in all — about US$1.63 billion at roughly 1,320 naira to the dollar — with a US$400 million underwriting pledge from Nigerian banks and a listing planned for later this year.

What is being sold is therefore not a security but a role. For the first time the family empire is asking the street to own a slice of it, and the street — traders, clerks, pension funds, the diaspora — will have to decide whether the refinery is theirs because it is Nigeria’s, or his because nothing that size is ever anyone else’s. Africa Confidential names Vetiva Capital as lead manager, and the book is built for retail buyers — the rare offer where the customer and the subject are the same nation.

The refinery matters to the mood because it is the one place the absurdity visibly ended. Expansion from 650,000 to 1.4 million barrels a day would make it among the largest anywhere, a fact Nigerians cite with a pride that mixes, in the same sentence, with the old resentment. Africa Confidential’s warning is the shadow across the pride: the listing, it cautions, may expose how much of the empire’s success rests on political favour. Every subscriber now gets to read that answer and decide whether it matters — which is itself the most honest referendum Nigeria has held in years.

Zimbabwe: Time, Purchased Over The People’s Heads

Zimbabwe’s constitution was already amended in July — that is the quiet horror. The Act lengthens presidential and parliamentary terms from five to seven years, extends President Emmerson Mnangagwa’s own mandate from 2028 to 2030, and moves the election of presidents to parliament. Africa Confidential’s reporting this week concerns what comes after the ink: the president’s money men buying time, and buying off resistance, for an order the law has already delivered.

The national mood this produces has a name older than the republic: déjà vu. A liberation movement has once again conflated its survival with the nation’s, and a public that has watched this film in two currencies responds with the weary literacy of repeat viewers. They know the money passed around Harare is not an economic programme but a subscription fee for silence, and they price their own futures accordingly, in a currency that remembers what politicians ask it to forget.

South Africa: After The Default Setting

For thirty years South African politics had a default setting, and on 4 November the country votes on whether to keep pretending it does. Africa Confidential’s assessment of the municipal elections is blunt: the African National Congress’s hegemony is fracturing, and no successor hegemon waits in the structure — not the Democratic Alliance in its Cape Town comfort, not the uMkhonto weSizwe project built around Jacob Zuma’s grievances, not the Economic Freedom Fighters’ permanent audition.

What dies on 4 November is not a party but a habit of assumption, and habits of assumption are what people build identities inside. The rand, at R16.19 to the dollar in AfrAsia’s morning wrap, carries the ambivalence: a country confident in its institutions and unconvinced by everyone staffing them. After November every metro will be governed by arithmetic done out loud, and South Africa will find out whether it experiences that as democratic maturity or as the end of the only political story it has ever known how to tell about itself.

Madagascar: Relevance, Rented By The Hour

Small countries in a cold diplomatic season have one asset larger nations lack: they can be useful to everyone and threatening to no one. Africa Confidential flags Siteny Thierry Randrianasoloniaiko — the opposition figure who now presides over Madagascar’s national assembly — as the key intermediary between the island’s new authorities and Moscow, offering Antananarivo as the channel for capitals that no longer speak to each other directly.

The mood it creates in Antananarivo is the island’s oldest anxiety in modern dress: that its politics becomes a corridor for other people’s traffic. Madagascar has been a passage for slaves, for spices, for navies; now it is a passage for messages. The pride of being needed is real, and so is the knowledge, learned across centuries, of what a passage is worth to its owner versus to those who merely are one.

Egypt: The Gavel And The Camera

A Cairo court sentenced television presenter Sarah Khalifa to death this week, alongside eleven other defendants, in a case built on more than 750 kilograms of seized narcotics; her lawyer says they will appeal. The verdict arrives in a media climate tightened over years by security litigation, and lands on a profession that reads each sentence as a message addressed to it.

Whatever the legal merits, the psychogram is the familiar Egyptian bargain between visibility and safety. A presenter’s face is among the most public assets in the country, and Friday’s verdict reminds everyone who owns the air that public faces are held on private sufferance. The fear this produces is not chaos but choreography: rooms full of professionals calculating, in real time, the exact cost of the next true sentence.

Libya And Niger: Fire At The Refinery, Fantasy In Niamey

North of the Sahara, two governments managed anxiety by pointing it at objects. In Libya, authorities announced five arrests — including foreigners — after drone attacks hit the Zawiya refinery complex and power infrastructure; every litre of damage returns within the week as a fuel queue, and the queue as a militia’s recruitment arithmetic. In Niger, the ruling council accused France of orchestrating the mutiny its own forces say they suppressed in late August, a charge Paris called pure fantasy.

Neither story is really about its stated subject. Tripoli’s arrests say a state that cannot protect a refinery can at least perform the hunt; Niamey’s accusation says a government that survived its own garrison needs a foreign hand to blame before anyone asks why the garrison moved. The shared mood is a region governing by pointer: look there, not here. It works, for a while, because anxiety prefers any object to none.

DR Congo: The Arithmetic Of Grief

Thursday’s brief carried the hard count — 6,757 confirmed cases and 3,267 deaths in the US Centers for Disease Control’s 7 September tally, with no licensed vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain. Friday’s update is not a new number but a new bottleneck, and it is human: OkayAfrica’s reporting from Ituri describes burial teams working at their limit, paid around US$20 a day and facing attacks while doing the most dangerous job in the entire response.

Epidemiologists call safe burial the last line of defence; in Ituri it is also the least funded, and the psychogram of the outbreak lives in that gap. A response that cannot pay its undertakers is telling you what it is willing to lose, and the answer, read through the wage slip, is the poor. Every unsafe funeral becomes a new cluster, which is how grief itself becomes a transmission vector and the arithmetic of death stops needing the virus’s help.

What This Means From Latin America

The Dangote offer is a mirror held up to Latin America’s state champions, and the reflection is uncomfortable. Pemex and Petroecuador were national answers that became national dependencies; Lagos is attempting the reverse sequence, building the miracle first and selling it to the public second. Whether the model travels depends on something no prospectus discloses: a state willing to let one private project outcompete it, which is precisely what the hemisphere’s oil nationalism never managed to permit.

The deeper echo is the Zimbabwe lesson, which Latin America also knows by heart: constitutional time is the last asset a tired ruling class buys, and the currency always pays for the purchase. Africa’s Friday is, in the end, the hemisphere’s oldest story told on a new day: myth, miracle and mandate going on sale together, with the buyer always asked to fund the seller’s version of both.

What We Are Watching

The subscription book — whether the Dangote offer fills on domestic demand alone or needs the underwriting banks to step in.

— whether the Dangote offer fills on domestic demand alone or needs the underwriting banks to step in. Harare’s quiet market — whether the money men’s payments consolidate the new constitutional order or meet resistance the treasury cannot buy off.

— whether the money men’s payments consolidate the new constitutional order or meet resistance the treasury cannot buy off. Pretoria’s metros — whether any party reaches 4 November able to govern Johannesburg without a three-way coalition.

— whether any party reaches 4 November able to govern Johannesburg without a three-way coalition. The Khalifa appeal — whether Egypt’s courts commute or confirm a sentence international broadcasters already frame as a press-freedom test.

— whether Egypt’s courts commute or confirm a sentence international broadcasters already frame as a press-freedom test. Zawiya’s repairs — how long the refinery stays offline and what the fuel queue in Tripoli looks like by the end of the month.

— how long the refinery stays offline and what the fuel queue in Tripoli looks like by the end of the month. Ituri’s undertakers — whether burial-team pay and protection improve before exhaustion turns into resignations.

The Bigger Picture Friday’s continent asked one question in four dialects: what is continuity worth? Lagos is pricing it at ₦2.15 trillion — US$1.63 billion — and inviting the public to pay in person. Harare already paid in constitutional language and is now settling the bill in cash. Pretoria discovered the item cannot be bought at all any more, only assembled coalition by coalition. And Ituri, beyond pricing entirely, keeps counting what continuity costs when it fails: 6,757 cases, 3,267 deaths, and a burial team working for US$20 a day. The psychogram underneath is ambition colliding with audit. Africa’s great family empires are discovering that monuments must eventually open their books; its liberation parties are discovering that time can be amended but not purchased; its newest epidemic is discovering that the last link in the chain is a human being with a shovel and a wage. The mood is neither hope nor fear but disclosure — a week when the continent’s ledgers, unusually, were opened at the same moment they were being settled.

Frequently Asked Questions

What exactly is Dangote selling, and when?

Dangote Petroleum Refinery & Petrochemicals will list 4.1 billion shares at ₦525 each on the Nigerian Exchange, an offer Reuters values at ₦2.15 trillion — about US$1.63 billion at roughly 1,320 naira to the dollar. The subscription window runs from 14 September to 13 October 2026, with the listing planned for later this year and a US$400 million underwriting commitment from Nigerian banks.

What is Zimbabwe’s CAB3 amendment?

The Constitution of Zimbabwe Amendment (No. 3) Act, signed into law in July 2026, lengthens presidential and parliamentary terms from five to seven years, extends President Emmerson Mnangagwa’s current mandate from 2028 to 2030, and moves the election of presidents to parliament. Africa Confidential reports his financial backers are now buying time and acquiescence around the new order — treating a settled constitutional question as a financing problem.

Why does the Congo Ebola outbreak hinge on burial teams?

Because the Bundibugyo strain has no licensed vaccine, prevention depends on stopping transmission at every contact point — and the deadliest contact point is the funeral. OkayAfrica reports Ituri’s burial teams are at their limit, paid around US$20 a day and facing attacks; each unsafe burial becomes a new cluster. The CDC’s 7 September tally carried in Thursday’s brief recorded 6,757 cases and 3,267 deaths.

Why do South Africa’s November municipal elections matter nationally?

Municipal polls are where South Africa’s post-1994 assumption — that the ANC is politics’ default setting — faces its cleanest test. Africa Confidential argues the party’s hegemony is fracturing with no successor hegemon in sight, meaning the 4 November vote will produce coalition arithmetic in the metros that national politics has so far managed to avoid.

For expats in Central America, this is the most significant rock tour the isthmus sees this year — the music of Latin America’s most important rock band, staged as a tribute at arena scale.

A Regional Sweep in November

The ‘Ecos’ production has drawn its most ambitious Central American map yet: six shows across five countries in two weeks — Tegucigalpa on November 4, San Salvador on November 7 and 8, Alajuela on November 11, Managua on November 14 and Panama City on November 18.

It is the fullest treatment the isthmus has received from any production carrying the Soda Stereo name — and the demand has matched, with El Salvador earning a second night by sellout.

What ‘Ecos’ Is

‘Ecos’ is the production that carries Soda Stereo’s catalog back to the stage — a tribute built around the band’s surviving members and a cast of guest vocalists, performing the songs that defined rock en español.

The show approaches the material with the scale it deserves: full production, the catalog’s essential arrangements, and a staging designed to honor rather than imitate.

Why Soda Stereo Still Fills Arenas

Soda Stereo remains the measuring stick for Latin American rock — the band that proved the region could produce a world-class rock act on its own terms, in Spanish, without apology.

Three decades on, the catalog — ‘De música ligera’, ‘Persiana americana’, ‘Cuando pase el temblor’, ‘En la ciudad de la furia’ — belongs to three generations at once, which is exactly who shows up to these nights.

The Route, City by City

The leg opens at Tegucigalpa’s Polideportivo UNAH on November 4, then doubles in San Salvador — November 7 and 8 at the Gimnasio Nacional Adolfo Pineda — before crossing to Costa Rica’s Parque Viva in Alajuela on the 11th.

Managua’s Polideportivo Alexis Argüello hosts on November 14, and the run closes at Panama City’s Arena Roberto Durán on November 18 — a Tuesday-to-Wednesday arc across the entire isthmus.

Central America’s Rock Hunger

The region has historically been underserved by major rock productions — routing costs and venue limits pushed most tours to Mexico or South America — which is why a five-country leg of this profile lands as an event rather than a tour.

Promoters have been correcting the map: Parque Viva’s rise as a regional hub and the refurbishing of the national venues on this route have made the isthmus viable for arena-scale rock again.

What Expats Should Know

Tickets are handled per country by the local official sellers — buy only through the channels each venue announces, since cross-border demand for this leg has made resale fraud a real risk.

For regional travelers: the routing makes a two-country trip easy — San Salvador’s double night into Costa Rica’s Parque Viva weekend is the popular combination, with short hops on Copa or Avianca between the capitals.

The Guest-Vocalist Format

The ‘Ecos’ approach keeps the catalog alive without freezing it: guest vocalists rotate through the set, each bringing their own relationship to the songs — a format that has kept the production fresh across three years of touring.

For audiences, the surprise is part of the ticket: local and regional guests typically appear at each stop, making every city’s show slightly different from the last.

A Region Worth the Detour

For expats based in Mexico or South America, the leg doubles as a reason to see Central America itself: five compact capitals, short flights, and November weather at the tail of the rains.

The San Salvador double-header into Costa Rica’s Parque Viva weekend is the natural itinerary — two shows, two countries, under four hours of total flight time.

Barranquilla Gets the New Tour

The album closes its arc with two dedications to Evaluna: ‘For Eva’, a title playing on ‘forever’, mixes pop with orchestral bolero, while ‘Luna’ builds a bright, luminous pop around images of the universe.

It is the couple’s most personal chapter on record — a family album in the literal sense, from two of Latin pop’s most public partners.

Camilo’s Family Audience

The University of Salsa, Twice in One Night

El Gran Combo de Puerto Rico returns to Lima on September 18 with a format that measures the demand: two full shows at the Gran Teatro Nacional — 6:00 and 8:45 p.m. — because one night was never going to hold this audience.

Peru is salsa’s second homeland outside the Caribbean, and Lima’s relationship with El Gran Combo runs across six decades of radio, weddings, and street parties that made the orchestra’s catalog local property.

Six Decades of El Gran Combo

Founded in 1962 in San Juan, El Gran Combo became the institution its nickname promises — ‘La Universidad de la Salsa’ — the orchestra that trained generations of singers and set the genre’s standard for swing, precision and joy.

The songbook is the soundtrack of Latin life: ‘Me liberé’, ‘Brujería’, ‘Un verano en Nueva York’, ‘Timbalero’, ‘Azuquita pa’l café’ and ‘La fiesta de Pilito’ — every one of them a communal memory in Lima.

A Tribute Carried Onstage

The current tour carries a special weight: the orchestra performs in tribute to its founder, Rafael Ithier, the pianist and arranger whose vision shaped the group’s sound from the first rehearsal.

Expect the classics framed by that homage — a night that works simultaneously as dance party, history lesson and thank-you note from the institution to its architect.

The Gran Teatro Nacional

Lima’s Gran Teatro Nacional, in San Borja next to the National Library, is the country’s premier concert hall — a modern, acoustically serious room that hosts everything from symphonies to salsa’s biggest nights.

The venue’s location makes logistics simple: the Metropolitano busway stops nearby, and the district’s restaurants fill early on show nights — book dinner before the 6:00 p.m. crowd arrives.

Tickets via Teleticket

Both shows are ticketed through Teleticket, online and at the theater’s box office; the presale waves of June are past, and remaining seats are in general sale while they last.

Choose your show by rhythm: the 6:00 p.m. function suits families and early diners, the 8:45 p.m. show runs later and looser — the dancers’ choice.

What Expats Should Know

Lima’s salsa culture is participatory: nobody sits still at a Gran Combo night, and the theater’s aisles famously fill with dancers — comfortable shoes are a better plan than formal ones.

For newcomers to the genre, this is the best possible first concert: the orchestra that wrote the textbook, in the country’s best room, with an audience that will happily teach you the steps.

Peru’s Salsa Exception

Salsa in Peru is not nostalgia — it is the country’s most durable popular music, sustained by radio, family parties and a circuit of orchestras that has never thinned. The Caribbean’s greatest band plays, effectively, to family.

That is why the double function happened: Lima is one of the few cities outside San Juan where El Gran Combo can sell a concert hall twice in one night on announcement alone.

The Puerto Rico–Peru Connection

The musical line between San Juan and Lima is old and two-way: Puerto Rican orchestras have headlined Peruvian summers for sixty years, and Peruvian salsa musicians have recorded on the island.

A Gran Combo night in Lima is that history made audible — the Caribbean and the Pacific meeting in a theater full of dancers who treat the distance as a technicality.

Lima has always been Calamaro country: the city embraced Los Rodríguez in the nineties and has filled every venue he has played since, from theaters to the big seaside rooms.

Four Decades of Songbook

Few catalogs in Spanish-language rock run deeper: Los Abuelos de la Nada’s new-wave classics, Los Rodríguez’s ‘Sin documentos’ era, and a solo career that produced ‘Flaca’, ‘Paloma’, ‘Crímenes perfectos’, ‘Te quiero igual’ and ‘Estadio Azteca’.

A Calamaro setlist is an argument about what to leave out — expect the hits, a handful of deep cuts and at least one extended jam that reminds you the band can play.

The ‘Como cantor’ Tour

The current run is framed around the singer as singer — the crooner dimension of an artist who has always moved between rock, tango, bolero and ballad without asking permission.

Reviews from the tour describe a relaxed, generous show: long sets, a band of veterans, and a frontman clearly enjoying the road more than the myth suggests he should.

Costa 21: Lima’s Seaside Stage

Costa 21, in San Miguel on the Costa Verde, is the venue Lima built for exactly these nights — an open-air concert space facing the Pacific that has hosted the city’s biggest international shows of the decade.

September on the Costa Verde means cool evenings and the season’s mist off the ocean: bring a jacket, whatever the afternoon sun suggests.

Calamaro’s Lima crowd spans forty years of fandom — expect teenagers next to grandparents, and a sing-along culture that treats ‘Flaca’ as a national anthem by adoption.

The venue is easiest by rideshare; the post-show exit along the Costa Verde moves slowly, so a short walk toward San Miguel before requesting your ride saves twenty minutes of surge pricing.

Why the Region Claims Him

Calamaro is Argentine, but Latin America long ago naturalized him: the Los Rodríguez years made him half-Spanish, the Bolero recordings made him everybody’s crooner, and Lima treats him as a local.

That explains the particular warmth of his Peruvian shows — audiences here do not discover the songs, they remember them, and the exchange between stage and floor runs on shared history.

If You Only Know the Hits

The deep-cut moments are where the show reveals itself: the tango phrasing he absorbed in Buenos Aires, the bolero discipline of his Cuban period, the rock attack of the early solo records.

Arrive with the big five songs memorized and leave with five more — the Calamaro catalog rewards exactly that kind of homework, and the Lima crowd will happily test you on all of them from the first chorus.

World.title: Costa Rica Nears 49,000 Short-Term Rentals as Tourist Numbers Lag
World.content:
Costa Rica now has nearly 49,000 active short-term rental listings, more than double the number in 2019, while international arrivals have yet to return to pre-pandemic levels, according to a new study by the Center for Tourism Studies (CET). The report, prepared by CET director Víctor Umaña and released Wednesday, counts 48,985 active listings across 243 markets on platforms including Airbnb, Vrbo and Booking.com.

The CET estimates those listings generated about $813.5 million in revenue in the 12 months ending in June 2026. The average nightly rate stood at $204, with average occupancy of 43.7% and annual revenue of $16,606 per listing, according to the study. Entire homes account for 83.3% of listings in the sample analyzed, and 66.4% are tied to hosts who manage more than one listing.

The CET describes the market as professionalized, noting that short-term rentals are no longer mainly occasional exchanges between private individuals. The typical property has 2.3 bedrooms and supply has grown far faster than demand. The CET estimates that short-term rental inventory rose from roughly 22,500 listings in 2019 to 48,985 by June 2026, while traditional lodging tracked by the Costa Rica Tourism Board (ICT) grew 13.3%, from 50,264 to 56,950 rooms between 2019 and 2025.

Over a similar period, international arrivals fell 6.2%, from 3.14 million in 2019 to 2.94 million in 2025. The study calculates that the number of international visitors per available lodging unit dropped from about 43 in 2019 to 28 in 2025-2026. The CET says demand is becoming the main constraint on the market. In the 213 markets with year-on-year data, inventory was essentially flat at minus 0.2%, while revenue per listing rose 8.7%, growth the study attributes more to pricing and occupancy than to new supply.

The destination data show wide gaps in earnings. Cabo Velas, which covers Flamingo and Conchal, leads with average annual revenue of $28,800 per listing, followed by Tamarindo at $28,640 and Nosara at $26,100. Nosara also posts the highest average nightly rate, at $384, and the highest occupancy, at 53%. Jacó, with 3,786 listings, has the lowest occupancy among the main destinations, at 40%.

The Greater Metropolitan Area (GMA) has the largest single inventory, with 4,025 listings and 50% occupancy. It also has the lowest earnings, with an average nightly rate of $61 and $7,200 in annual revenue per listing, reflecting smaller units and shorter stays.

Destination Active listings Avg. nightly rate Avg. occupancy Annual revenue per listing Greater Metropolitan Area 4,025 $61 50% $7,200 Jacó 3,786 $306 40% $23,371 Cahuita / Southern Caribbean 3,779 $126 46% $13,400 Tamarindo 3,598 $336 47% $28,640 Cóbano / Santa Teresa-Montezuma 2,860 $274 50% $21,300 Sardinal / Playas del Coco 2,537 $214 48% $16,500 Bahía Ballena / Uvita 2,184 $217 46% $17,500 Quepos / Manuel Antonio 1,902 $259 47% $25,806 Cabo Velas / Flamingo-Conchal 1,678 $346 48% $28,800 Nosara 1,537 $384 53% $26,100 La Fortuna 1,397 $151 44% $14,900

Source: Center for Tourism Studies (CET), based on AirDNA data for the 12 months ending June 2026.

Nationally, the CET calculates a density of 9.4 short-term rentals per 1,000 residents. That places Costa Rica slightly above Barcelona, at 9.0, and above every large city in the comparison, including Rio de Janeiro, New York and Mexico City, though well below Mallorca, Hawaii and Crete.

The study places Costa Rica in the most permissive of four regulatory categories, alongside Belize, Rio de Janeiro and Cape Town. Hosts must register under Law 9742, but there are no national limits on nights rented, no zoning restrictions and no tax specific to short-term rental lodging, according to the CET comparison.

On housing, the report says short-term rentals can push up land values and residential rents in tourist destinations with limited housing supply, adding pressure on workers employed in tourism. It also notes that many coastal villas and condominiums were built specifically for visitors, so restricting them would not necessarily return units to the long-term housing market.

The CET ends by saying that effective policy would need to distinguish between homes converted into short-term rentals and properties developed for tourism from the outset. The study describes its analysis as descriptive and cautions that its market figures are third-party estimates built from public platform data, with methodologies that differ.

World.title: Convicted police officer Dexter Diego apologizes to 14-year-old victim for unlawful sex with her; faces separate trial for allegedly raping 10-year-old girl
World.content:
Convicted police officer Dexter Diego apologizes to 14-year-old victim for unlawful sex with her; faces separate trial for allegedly raping 10-year-old girl

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Convicted police officer Dexter Diego expressed remorse in the High Court this week as Justice Nigel Pilgrim heard mitigation ahead of his sentencing for four counts of unlawful sexual intercourse involving a minor.

Diego, 29, pleaded guilty on July 27 to the four counts involving a girl who was 13 years old when the sexual relationship began. His trial had been scheduled to begin that day, but he entered guilty pleas before Justice Pilgrim. Public reports say the court subsequently ordered a prison report, social inquiry report and victim impact statement ahead of sentencing.

Addressing the court during Wednesday’s mitigation hearing, an emotional Diego apologized to the victim, her family, the court, the Belize Police Department and his own family.

“I am fully aware of my decisions that I have made. I know that they were wrong,” Diego told the court, adding that he regretted the pain his actions had caused.

His sister also testified as a character witness, describing her brother as a helpful and respectable person who provided for his stepmother. She told the court that the case has taken a heavy toll on their family and asked Justice Pilgrim to show leniency when imposing sentence.

The court also heard an emotional victim impact statement from the girl, who said Diego had gained her trust by acting as a confidant before pressuring her into a sexual relationship. She told the court that the experience left her ashamed and embarrassed, forced her to relocate and affected her life.

Diego is also before the courts in a separate case involving another minor. On May 4, 2026, the interdicted police officer was arraigned in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on four counts of rape of a child. Prosecutors allege that three of the offences occurred in December 2024, when the girl was 10 years old, while a fourth allegedly occurred in 2025, when she was 11. Diego was remanded to the Belize Central Prison because the Magistrate’s Court could not grant bail on the charges.

The new charges were brought while Diego was already before the courts in connection with the case for which he has now pleaded guilty. The four rape charges remain pending allegations, and Diego has not been convicted in that separate matter.

World.title: Belize and Guyana strengthen cooperation through public sector knowledge exchange
World.content:
Belize and Guyana strengthen cooperation through public sector knowledge exchange

By Zoila Palma: A delegation from the Government of Belize conducted a three-day Knowledge Exchange visit to the Cooperative Republic of Guyana from September 8 to 10, 2026, aimed at strengthening capacity in public-sector management, digital transformation, procurement and project cycle management.

The exchange, coordinated by the High Commission of Belize in Guyana, provided Belizean officials with an opportunity to engage their Guyanese counterparts, examine institutional practices and learn about digital tools and systems being used to improve government service delivery, project implementation and oversight.

The Belize delegation included officials from the Ministry of Finance, Investment, Economic Transformation, Civil Aviation and E-Governance. Discussions focused on project monitoring and oversight, public-sector investment programme planning, procurement reforms, e-Procurement, digital identification and digital government services.

Officials also examined Guyana’s National Digital Management Authority and its experience with E-ID and digital transformation. Presentations highlighted digital systems and innovations supporting service delivery in areas including health, public safety and law enforcement, and agriculture.

Chief Executive Officer for Economic Transformation Carlos Pol said the exchange provides Belize with an opportunity to identify practical approaches that could support the country’s development priorities. “Knowledge sharing among countries in the region allows us to learn from practical experiences, including both successes and challenges. This exchange will help Belize identify approaches that can strengthen project management, procurement, digital transformation, and overall public-sector effectiveness.”

CEO for E-Governance Jose Urbina highlighted the importance of digital innovation in modernizing government services. “Digital transformation is no longer simply about introducing technology; it is about rethinking how Government operates and how citizens access public services,” he said.
