The visit is expected to lead to continued technical cooperation, including support for Belize’s digitalization efforts, healthcare workforce capacity-building, PSIP management and oversight, and e-Procurement. The Government of Belize thanked the Government of Guyana, the High Commission of Belize in Guyana and the Inter-American Development Bank for facilitating the exchange.

World.title: International News: Guatemalan Riot police responds to road blockages as fuel price protests continue
World.content:
International News: Guatemalan Riot police responds to road blockages as fuel price protests continue

By Zoila Palma: Today, road blockades continued across Guatemala as protesters demonstrated against rising fuel prices, disrupting traffic on major highways and sections of Guatemala City.

The demonstrations have affected thousands of commuters and disrupted the movement of essential goods, including food, medicine and fuel., Prensa Libre reports.

Blockades have been reported along several of the country’s main highways, as well as on the Periférico Ring Road near the entrance to the Bethania neighborhood and the Atlantic Highway at key entrances and exits to the capital.

Some blockades, including those in Cuyotenango, Suchitepéquez, and Río Hondo, Zacapa, have lasted more than 24 hours.

Minister of the Interior Marco Antonio Villeda has ordered protesters to clear the roads within 30 minutes, warning that those who refuse could be arrested and brought before the courts.

In addition, Guatemalan officials announced a joint operation involving the National Civil Police and the Army to clear blocked routes, following a Constitutional Court ruling ordering the removal of the blockades.

The business sector has called for immediate action, citing significant economic losses caused by the disruptions.

World.title: International News: Latin America faces growing drone threat as criminal groups take to the skies
World.content:
International News: Latin America faces growing drone threat as criminal groups take to the skies

By Zoila Palma: Drones are rapidly becoming a powerful tool for organized crime across Latin America, with criminal groups increasingly using the technology for surveillance, smuggling, coordination and attacks, while governments struggle to keep pace.

A report by the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) recorded around 670 armed-drone events since 2018, with more than 72% occurring between January 2025 and August 21, 2026.

The threat has become particularly visible in Mexico, Colombia and Brazil, CNN reports.

In Brazil, a 2025 police operation in Rio de Janeiro saw a bomb dropped from a drone during a massive raid against the Comando Vermelho criminal organization.

Mexican cartels have also used drones to monitor security forces, territorial rivals and border areas, while attaching explosives to some devices.

In Colombia, armed groups have increasingly incorporated drones into attacks and surveillance, with ACLED identifying the country as the epicenter of armed-drone activity in the region.

Experts say criminal groups are moving beyond experimental drone use toward organized and repeatable operations.

Governments across the region are responding with counter-drone technology, intelligence operations and increased surveillance, but experts warn that criminal innovation is advancing faster than many governments can adapt.

World.title: Keon Mossiah brings Gold to Belize, makes history as First IMMAF Champion
World.content:
Keon Mossiah brings Gold to Belize, makes history as First IMMAF Champion

By Zoila Palma: Belizean mixed martial artist Keon Mossiah, who proudly hails from Santa Elena, Cayo, has made history becoming the first Belizean to win a gold medal at the International Mixed Martial Arts Federation (IMMAF) Pan American Championships.

Mossiah secured the historic victory at the 2026 IMMAF Pan American Championships in Monterrey, Mexico, where he represented Belize against talented fighters from across the Americas.

His gold medal marks a major milestone for Belizean amateur mixed martial arts and adds to the country’s growing success at international IMMAF competitions.

Mossiah’s achievement also highlights the continued development of mixed martial arts in Belize and the work of the Belize Mixed Martial Arts Federation, which has been creating opportunities for local athletes to compete at the international level.

Mossiah now returns home with a historic distinction as Belize’s first IMMAF champion, bringing gold and national pride back to Belize.

World.title: Santa Elena’s Keon Mossiah makes history as Belize’s First IMMAF Pan Am Champion
World.content:
Santa Elena’s Keon Mossiah makes history as Belize’s First IMMAF Pan Am Champion

By Zoila Palma: Belizean mixed martial artist Keon Mossiah who proudly hails from Santa Elena, Cayo has made history, becoming the first Belizean to win a gold medal at the International Mixed Martial Arts Federation (IMMAF) Pan American Championships.

Mossiah secured the historic victory in Monterrey, Mexico, earning Belize’s first-ever IMMAF Pan Ams gold medal and putting the Belizean flag on top of the podium.

Following his victory, the Belize national anthem was played during the medal ceremony as Mossiah proudly represented his country on the international stage.

His achievement has sparked congratulations from supporters and Belizeans celebrating the historic milestone.

Congratulations, Keon Mossiah!

Your gold-medal performance has made history and brought pride to Belize.

World.title: Multiple Guatemalan vessels near Sarstoon during Belize Territorial Volunteers visit
World.content:
Multiple Guatemalan vessels near Sarstoon during Belize Territorial Volunteers visit

By Zoila Palma: Reports indicate that almost 15 Guatemalan vessels were reportedly seen near Sarstoon Island as the Belize Territorial Volunteers carried out their annual September 10 visit.

The Belize Territorial Volunteers traveled to the area with an escort of two Belize Defence Force (BDF) boats and accompaniment from the Belize Coast Guard.

However, following a security assessment, the group agreed to proceed only as far as the BDF Forward Operating Base (FOB).

World.title: Prime Minister tours Westlake Facility as temporary generation capacity nears operation
World.content:
Prime Minister tours Westlake Facility as temporary generation capacity nears operation

By Zoila Palma: Today, Prime Minister John Briceño toured the Belize Electricity Limited (BEL) Westlake Facility, where temporary generation capacity is being installed to strengthen Belize’s electricity supply and reduce the risk of further disruptions to the national grid.

BEL said the temporary generation capacity is currently being installed at the Westlake Facility and is expected to begin operations by mid-September 2026.

The additional capacity is being procured for an initial six-month period as the company works to improve reliability and resilience across the national electricity system.

During his visit, Prime Minister Briceño said the tour provided an opportunity to get a firsthand understanding of the facility’s operations and current generation capacity. “Today, I visited the Westlake facility for a firsthand look at its operations and generation capacity. Understanding what is working on the ground is important as we continue strengthening Belize’s energy supply and planning for greater reliability and resilience,” he said.

The temporary generation is expected to provide additional support to the national grid during a period when Belize continues to focus on strengthening electricity infrastructure and ensuring a more stable and reliable supply for consumers.

World.title: Market Bag: Peppers hit $700, lettuce now $1,500 as food prices continue to soar
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Food prices continue to rise at the Coronation Market in downtown Kingston as farmers struggle with the effects of a worsening drought, pushing up the cost of several essential produce items.

Among the more expensive items this week are lettuce, which is selling for $1,500 per pound, and Scotch bonnet peppers and sweet peppers, both priced at $700. Other items seeing steep increases include carrots at $500 per pound; Irish potatoes and pumpkin at $400 each; onions at $350; and sweet potatoes at $350.

With the rising costs, ISSA-certified nutritionist Orandy Smith is encouraging Jamaicans to “work with what is working with you” when preparing meals and making food choices.

Speaking on the latest episode of Market Bag with host Carlysia Ramdeen, Smith said some ingredients remain essential in his household, regardless of price.

“Because my food must be flavourful, regardless of what the cost for seasoning, I’m going to buy them…I must do my onion, I must do my tomato, I must do my escallion, I must do my thyme, I must do my garlic, I must do all of my seasonings. So all of them are non-negotiable,” he said.

Catch the latest episode of Market Bag on all Jamaica Observer digital platforms.

World.title: Jamaica finish second in mixed 4x100m at Ultimate Championships
World.content:
Jamaica's Ackeem Blake take the start in mixed's relay 4x100m final during the World Athletics Ultimate Championship at the Gyula Zsivotzky National Athletics Centre, in Budapest on September 11, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

Jamaica finished second in the mixed 4x100m relay final on Friday’s opening day of the inaugural Ultimate Championships at the National Athletics Center in Budapest, Hungary,

The team of Ackeem Blake, Tina Clayton, Kadrian Goldson and Jonielle Smith clocked 39.72 seconds to finish a step behind the USA team that set a national record 39.64 seconds to win the event. Great Britain was third in 40.26 seconds.

In the only individual track final contested by a Jamaican, Megan Simmonds was fifth in the 100m hurdles with a season’s best 12.42 seconds (0.1m/s). American world record holder Masai Russell completed an unbeaten season, winning with 12.22 seconds, just overtaking the field at the end with Nigeria’s Tobi Amusan placing second with 12.34 seconds and Nadine Visser of the Bahamas third with 12.39 seconds.

Lamara Distin only cleared one height in the women’s high jump, finishing joint sixth with 1.86m as Yaroslava Mahuchikh won with 1.99m, ahead of two Australians – Nicola Olyslagers-1.96m and Eleanor Patterson-1.91m.

Meanwhile, Nickisha Pryce qualified for Saturday’s final of the women’s 400m after she was third in her semi-final, running 49.72 seconds, after leading through the first 200m.

World leader and Diamond League winner Marileidy Paulino of the Dominican Republic won with 49.58 seconds ahead of Salwa Eid Nasa of Bahrain who clocked 49.67 seconds.

Cuba’s Roxana Gomez was fourth in 50.34 seconds to get the other qualifying spot.

Stacey-Ann Williams was sixth in her semi-final, clocking 50.43 seconds from lane nine.

Also on Friday, Ackera Nugent failed to complete her 100m hurdle semi-finals after she fell at the ninth hurdle, while two-time world champion winner Danielle Williams just missed qualifying after she placed fifth in 12.72 seconds (-0.2m/s). National champion Demisha Roswell was eighth in 13.04 seconds.

Orlando Bennett was also fifth in his 110m hurdles semi-final, running 13.29 seconds (0.7m/s), while Demario Prince was seventh in 13.58 seconds after hitting a hurdle near the end of the race. Tyler Mason was seventh in his semi-final in 13.46 seconds (0.6m/s).

-Paul A Reid

World.title: Stalled by squatters
World.content:
FALMOUTH, Trelawny — Squatters have taken over hundreds of acres of privately owned land across this parish, with approximately 58 acres of a 147.48-acre property at Flamingo Beach already illegally occupied, threatening to derail a major development for which a plan has been submitted to the Trelawny Municipal Corporation (TMC).

Falmouth Mayor C Junior Gager, who on Thursday raised the alarm during the corporation’s regular monthly meeting, said the growing problem has resulted in the TMC being inundated with complaints from frustrated landowners.

“We have had a number of landowners coming to the corporation to report instances where individuals have occupied and begun developing their properties without the owners’ permission,” Gager said.

He warned that the scale of the illegal occupation is undermining the development of the parish he described as having significant potential for growth.

Gager said the situation at Flamingo Beach was particularly concerning.

“There is a submitted plan here for that property that will help to build Trelawny, but we cannot proceed because there is this problem of squatting,” he bemoaned.

“Approximately 58 acres of [well-known attorney] Gordon Brown’s property has been illegally occupied,” Gager added.

Efforts to get a comment from Brown were unsuccessful as, up to press time he did not return the phone call as promised.

Meanwhile, according to the mayor, at another property in Flamingo Beach, 11 acres of a 57.6-acre parcel have also been informally settled.

Explaining the extent of the problem, he pointed to Cooper’s Pen in Trelawny — which recently made news headlines following the early-morning demolition of about 20 structures — where approximately 12 acres of the property have been informally occupied.

Gager also referenced significant squatting on sections of 344.5 acres of land in an area called Tilston; Hague, where one acre has been informally settled; and Hague Cave Island, where four acres of the property have similarly been occupied.

Gager, who is also chairman of the TMC, said squatters are relying on claims of adverse possession which, for privately owned land, is based on undisturbed occupation of at least 12 years.

“Once they get a little cut on it they try to say that they have been there for over 12 years, when in fact they weren’t there,” he said.

“We find that the law-abiding citizen who pays their taxes, buy their land for maybe later on in their years when things get bad and they want to protect their future, they are now met with a problem that they might have to… find extra money to take it to the Supreme Court level,” the mayor added.

Gager pushed back against criticism of the TMC and the Government over the squatting crisis, insisting that the authorities have been taking steps within their remit.

“We must do all that we can and, as the municipality, I must note that we have been serving our notices on those that occupy the lands,” he said, adding that notices have also been served on landowners to facilitate court action.

He said the TMC is frequently contacted by property owners seeking help, but its ability to resolve disputes is ultimately limited when matters enter the judicial system.

“All we can do sometimes is have a discussion and try to guide them into the right process where they are going,” said Gager.

Pointing to the substantial structures being erected in some of the settlements, he questioned whether everyone occupying the properties could legitimately be regarded as people without the means to legitimately acquire property.

The mayor said he has seen two- and three-storey houses, split-level structures and buildings apparently configured to accommodate renters and commercial activity.

“I can see houses that are really arranged for business, so that renters can accommodate. How can we be so lawless?” he asked.

Gager urged politicians, members of the police force, social workers, and ordinary citizens not to facilitate or encourage illegal occupation, warning that continued squatting could tarnish Trelawny’s development prospects.

“This cannot continue in a growing parish. The future of this parish is great; let us not mar the beauty of this parish by encouraging squatting,” he urged.

World.title: $6.8-m payout for unjust redundancy
World.content:
The Industrial Disputes Tribunal.

THE Industrial Disputes Tribunal (IDT) has ordered Spectrum Insurance Brokers to pay a former employee $6.8 million after it found that his dismissal by way of redundancy in 2019 was “unjustifiable”.

In a ruling handed down on Tuesday the IDT rejected the company’s arguments that it was facing financial challenges at the time it decided to make the position of Claims Manager Laurel Smith redundant.

Initially, lawyers representing the company had argued that the IDT lacked the jurisdiction to hear matters regarding redundancies after the Ministry of Labour sent the dispute for its hearing in 2021.

Lawyers representing Spectrum took the matter to the Supreme Court seeking to challenge the authority of the IDT, but in a 2023 ruling the court said there was no legal basis for it to grant a stay of the judicial review proceedings.

When the matter finally started before the IDT in January 2025 the company argued that Smith’s post was made redundant as it was experiencing financial difficulties in 2019 and it was agreed that his position of claims manager would be absorbed into the operations manager position for the purpose of greater efficiency.

The company, however, admitted that Smith’s post was the only one made redundant and argued that he was offered a new post of recovery officer but he did not express an interest in that job.

It was also confirmed that there was no issue with Smith’s performance and no disciplinary matter pending against him.

Witnesses who testified on Smith’s behalf pointed out that he was a good manager and claimed that “he would be ranked among the best in the industry”.

In his testimony Smith claimed to have had a problem with how a senior manager — who was employed by the company five years after him — spoke to the staff and, after he tackled her about this, his department was faced with significant attacks, until it was indicated that his post would be made redundant.

According to Smith, he was embarrassed and traumatised by the redundancy, which affected him financially with his house being put on the market for sale.

In its ruling the IDT said despite the company’s claims of facing increasing financial challenges, the records show that its operating profit moved from approximately $17.3 million in 2018 to approximately $20.2 million in 2019, with its total revenue climbing to $19.3 million compared to a budgeted 16.5 million.

“Based on the evidence before us, we are able to make specific findings of fact that the company’s case suffered from a number of infirmities and fallacies. When weighted against the provisions… governing redundancy, their contentions, (which are more asserted that demonstrated) that this was a genuine redundancy, could not pass muster,” said the IDT panel chaired by Donald Roberts.

“The redundancy exercise fell afoul of the requirements… as the process did not satisfy the standards of fairness and the company did not show that it engaged in meaningful consultation, that it made reasonable attempts to avoid redundancy, and that it assisted Mr Smith in finding alternative employment,” the IDT added as it made the award to Smith.

World.title: Skatta upbeat as Coolie Dance rhythm takes flight, again
World.content:
BURRELL... I’m always happy whenever a new interest comes to fruition and a great song is released with the sample.

THE success of the Coolie dance rhythm sampled hit Bby WOW by Karol G, featuring Judeline and rusowsky, has once again propelled the enigmatic Cordell “Skatta” Burrell-produced beat into the spotlight.

Bby WOW is the biggest song globally at present, topping both Billboard’s Global 200 and Global 200 Excluding US charts. It is also #1 on Billboard’s Hot Latin Songs, and Hot Latin Rhythm Songs charts.

Outside of the United States, the song has so far hit #1 in Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Peru and in Spain.

Created in early 2004, the initial Coolie Dance rhythm featured more than 70 songs. Among the hits at the time were songs by dancehall acts Guinness by Jagwa, Yuh Gaawn by Bounty Killer, Geenie Dance by Elephant Man, Head Gaawn by Elephant Man, Do it To Me Baby by Ce’Cile, Gal Dem Way by TOK,

Tell Me Why by Frisco Kid, Please Mr Please by Vybz Kartel and Feel Alright by Sean Paul.

Mr Vegas’ Pull Up and Jook Gal (Wine Wine) by Elephant Man, Kiprich, Twista and YoungBloodz were Billboard chart-hitters, so too Culo by Pitbull and Nina Sky’s Move Your Body, both of which hit the Billboard Hot 100 charts in late 2004, and most recently After Hours by R&B singer Kehlani.

In an interview with the Jamaica Observer on Thursday, Burrell who is also a former judge on the television reality series Magnum Kings and Queens of Dancehall, spoke about the renewed interest in the beat which he created 22 years ago.

“I’m always happy whenever a new interest comes to fruition and a great song is released with the sample,” said Burrell. “It reminds me that the riddim is timeless and has the ability to connect with generations of music lovers. I think the continued interest from international acts in sampling the rhythm has a lot to do with the original approach I made when I sat down to create it. I took a more artistic approach than musical, meaning mostly drums and percussions slightly aggressive but still groovy enough to make you feel the movement between each sound. Less sometimes means more so not crowded. My dancehall influences along with the Indian samples all together made it not only appealing to my culture but straight across the globe.”

According to Burrell, the latest sampling of the beat was brought to his attention by his publishing company.

“My publishing company was contacted after the song’s release, and we did what we could and ensured that we covered all the necessary areas that suited all parties. I think they did a great job on the production because the first thing that stood out was the beautiful synth melodies and vocal samples that played alongside the lead vocals and even though its in Spanish, the sound is captivating enough and is still enjoyed and appreciated,” said Burrell.

Unlike most of his projects, the beat for the Coolie Dance rhythm was not created in a recording studio. Burrell shared that he envisioned the production would have been a hit.

“The rhythm itself was not created in a studio. I was in New York at the time and was by a friend’s house. I purchased a sample CD at a place called Samash music somewhere in Queens I think and was eager to sit with it and get creative. The first opportunity I got was in my friend’s living room. I plugged in my drum machine and put my headphones on and got to work. The process was about an hour because from listening to the samples in the car, I knew exactly how I wanted to interpret and build around it. I knew it was different and had extreme potential so when I had an offer of purchase from another producer, I made the decision not to sell it and instead use it for my own label and the minute I played it for Bounty Killer, he also gave me the nod that it was a hit,” Burrell recalled.

Though not 100 per cent sure, Burrell recalled that budding artiste at the time Jagwa may have recorded the first song on the Coolie Dance rhythm.

Prior to venturing into music production, Burrell tried his hand at becoming a recording artiste, but that didn’t work out.

“I got into music while attending The United Pentecostal Church on Grant’s Pen Road where at a very young age, I used to sit at the front bench and mimic Clevie the drummer as he played. I eventually got the opportunity to play the drums after some time and that’s where my passion grew. From beating the desk at Calabar High school classrooms to building beats and recording demos in my friend Benzly Hype’s home studio on Hillary Avenue. I was rejected as an artiste at Celestial Sound because my voice wasn’t good enough, so I decided to learn the 56 Channel Amek Hendricks Mixing Console at the first digital studio owned by Steven Ventura,” he shared.

“He gave me the opportunity to be a fly on the wall to watch and learn until I started recording and mixing. Iley Dread, however, gave me the biggest support by giving me his label, Kings Of Kings, to run for almost two years and that’s where I homed in on my passion and worked with many artistes, musicians and producers. Norris Man gave me my very first hit song and Ce’Cile and I did our very first dancehall juggling that propelled me to the mainstream lanes from which I was able to navigate my success,” the producer reminisced.

World.title: INVESTORS SNAP UP JAMAICA BOND
World.content:
NEARLY 10 months after Hurricane Melissa inflicted an estimated US$8.8 billion in damage across Jamaica, international investors have turned out strongly for the Government’s latest US$1-billion bond, allowing the country to borrow at a lower rate than initially indicated.

The bond was heavily oversubscribed after Jamaica returned to the international capital markets last week to raise funds for both debt management and general budgetary needs.

Before the offer was formally launched, investors were initially being guided to an interest rate of about 6.50 per cent. Strong demand subsequently allowed the Government to offer the bond at 6.25 per cent, according to market sources.

In simple terms, investors wanted more of the bond than Jamaica was seeking to sell, giving the Government room to offer a lower return and still attract sufficient buyers.

The strong reception is particularly notable given Jamaica’s return to the market less than a year after Hurricane Melissa caused widespread damage and disrupted economic activity.

Of the US$1 billion being raised, approximately US$600 million was earmarked to help repurchase portions of three older Government of Jamaica global bonds, while the remaining US$400 million, or about $63 billion, was intended for general budgetary purposes.

The transaction forms part of the Government’s wider liability management strategy, under which it is seeking to replace portions of older, more expensive debt with new borrowing while pushing some repayments further into the future.

At the same time that the new bond was being marketed, the Government invited holders of its 6.75 per cent notes due in 2028, 8.50 per cent notes due in 2036, and 8.00 per cent notes due in 2039 to sell some of those securities back to Jamaica.

By the time that tender offer closed on September 9, investors had submitted approximately US$476.62 million in bonds for repurchase.

After adjusting for the amortisation of the 2028 notes, the amount represented approximately US$392.23 million.

The Government is expected to determine how much of those tendered notes it will accept, with settlement scheduled for September 17. The official tender documents confirm that completion of the buyback is tied to the closing of the new international bond transaction.

“Jamaica intends to apply a portion of the net proceeds of its new notes offering announced on Wednesday, September 2, 2026 to purchase the Old Notes accepted pursuant to the Invitation at the applicable Total Purchase Price,” the Government said in its release.

The repurchase is expected to lower the Government’s annual interest bill by approximately US$3.5 million while moving part of its external debt obligations further into the future.

Beyond the savings, however, the reception to the new bond provides another test of how international investors now view Jamaica’s creditworthiness.

That assessment has changed significantly over the past decade.

When Jamaica raised US$2.05 billion on the international market in July 2015, its April 2028 bond carried an interest rate of 6.75 per cent while its July 2045 bond carried a rate of 7.875 per cent.

At the time, Jamaica was rated B by S&P Global, B– by Fitch Ratings, and Caa2 by Moody’s.

Today, the country carries a BB rating from S&P Global with a stable outlook, BB– from Fitch with a stable outlook, and Ba3 from Moody’s with a stable outlook.

The improvement has accompanied a steep reduction in public debt, with Jamaica’s debt-to-gross domestic product (GDP) ratio falling from approximately 116 per cent in 2015 to about 68 per cent today.

The ratings have also been maintained despite the economic damage caused by Hurricane Melissa.

Investor demand for the latest bond therefore provides another indication that international markets continue to place weight on Jamaica’s fiscal management and debt reduction record, even as the country faces significant reconstruction costs.

The comparison is even more striking against the backdrop of rising US interest rates.

The yield on the benchmark 10-year United States Treasury has recently moved close to five per cent amid a global bond sell-off. On Wednesday it was trading at approximately 4.8 per cent.

At a 6.25 per cent rate, Jamaica would, therefore, be borrowing at roughly 1.4 percentage points above the yield available on US Government debt.

That margin, known in the market as the spread, represents the additional return investors demand for taking the greater risk associated with lending to Jamaica instead of the United States.

The narrower that gap, generally, the more favourably investors are assessing Jamaica’s risk.

A comparison with Trinidad and Tobago provides some regional context.

Trinidad and Tobago, which carries stronger credit ratings than Jamaica, issued a 10-year US$1-billion bond earlier this year at 6.50 per cent and later raised another US$800 million through a 12-year bond at 6.20 per cent.

When Trinidad issued the January bond, its borrowing rate was roughly 2.27 percentage points above the US 10-year Treasury yield prevailing at the time.

Jamaica’s latest transaction, despite its lower sovereign credit rating, appears to have been priced at a smaller premium above US Treasuries.

That does not mean Jamaica is viewed as less risky than Trinidad across the board, since bond pricing is also affected by market conditions, maturity, and investor demand at the time of issuance.

It nevertheless points to strong appetite for Jamaican debt during the latest transaction.

The new unsecured bond is expected to mature in 2037, giving it an 11-year tenure.

Citigroup Global Markets Inc and Scotia Capital (USA) Inc acted as deal managers and joint lead underwriters. Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton LLP and Patterson Mair Hamilton advised the managers, while the Government was advised by Paul Hastings LLP and the Attorney General’s Chambers.

World.title: IT WILL BE GREAT!
World.content:
Oblique Seville celebrates winning the men’s 100m final during the World Athletics Diamond League athletics meeting in Belgium on September 4, 2026. He is set to compete in the Ultimate Championships in Hungary. (Photo: AFP)

Despite several of Jamaica’s top athletes set to compete, retired Jamaican-born Olympic and world champion Donovan Bailey admits the World Athletics Ultimate Championships could lose some of its appeal with several of the sport’s biggest stars, including American Noah Lyles, set to miss the event.

The inaugural three-day invitational meet, which gets underway on Friday in Budapest, will feature the world’s top 16 athletes in individual track events and the top eight competitors in field events. Gold medallists from the 2024 Paris Olympics, 2025 Tokyo World Championships and this year’s Diamond League final winners earned automatic qualification while the remaining entrants were determined by the World Athletics Ranking for the period from last September to the start of this September.

However, reigning Olympic Games 100m champion and 200m world champion Lyles will be absent due to injury.

American star 400m and 400m hurdles star Sydney McLaughlin Levrone, America’s Olympic long jump champion Tara Davis-Woodhall, Kenyan middle-distance star Faith Kipyegon, Kenya’s 800m world champion Lilian Odira, and reigning Olympic and World Champion in the 5000m Faith Kipyegon will also be missing from the championships for different reasons.

Former world record holder Bailey, who won 100m gold for Canada at the 1996 Olympics and the 1995 World Championships, says World Athletics will miss the star power but believes it will still be a great event.

“I think that anytime that you’re having major championships and this is the ultimate championship [in] it’s first year, the big stars that are missing, it does dampen it a little bit,” he said on CBC Sports. “I think that in any sport, you want to have the greatest people of that time, appealing to the fans, catering to the crowd and breaking world records and winning stuff.”

“But I also think that there are some incredible stars that are established now and there are some really, really talented young athletes that’s going to establish themselves. I’m looking forward to it, I’m sorry for the athletes that are injured or season’s done or whatever but there’s going to be some great competition.”

With the Ultimate Championships being the first of its kind, it’s not yet viewed as a major championship on the level of the Olympics and World Championships.

However, Bailey believes it gives athletes another opportunity to compete for additional prize money as well as securing bragging rights.

“I think that championships matter, consistency matters, delivering messages matter, being confident, being injury-free matters,” he said. “We look at the Commonwealth Games or PanAm Games, some sort of regional championships — to me, the Ultimate Championships now is like a regional championships. If you win, you win and you’re going to get paid. Does it matter? Yes, it matters for the person that wins.”

“Also, it matters for everyone that competes there because they’re going to have money. If you win, it’s incredible because it’s a title and what this does next year going into, uh, 2027 [with the] World Championships and when you’re on a Diamond League starting line, the Ultimate Championship champion is another title that gets added and maybe you can demand a little bit more cash.”

Each competitor at the Ultimate Championships is guaranteed at least US$2,000 with the winner set to earn US$150,000.

Reigning 100m world and Diamond League champion Seville heads the list of 27 Jamaicans set to compete at the event.

Jamaica’s long-serving technical leader Maurice Wilson and former Olympic and world champion Michael Frater will be Jamaica’s two-man delegation in charge of the relay teams.

Men: Oblique Seville, Ackeem Blake, Christopher Taylor, Navasky Anderson, Orlando Bennett, Romaine Beckford, Bryan Levell, Tyler Mason, Demario Prince.

Women: Tina Clayton, Ackera Nugent, Danielle Williams, Lamara Distin, Nickisha Pryce, Brianna Lyston, Rushell Clayton, Shiann Salmon, Jonielle Smith, Ashanti Moore, Ackelia Smith, Demisha Roswell, Megan Simmonds, Sanique Walker, Jodean Williams, Lavanya Williams.

World.title: Ottey cleaves through dexterity competition
World.content:
Cleve Ottey bested all others by a two-second margin in what was an exciting run to the finish.

Cleve Ottey was the winner at the third round of the Point 2 Point Time Attack dexterity series, held on Saturday, August 22, at Overton Plaza, Montego Bay.

“It feels good to win. It’s been a while since I’ve had to put down such a spectacular drive, but it was great,” Ottey told the Jamaica Observer’s weekly Auto magazine.

And spectacular it was as Ottey held off rivals during the two-lap championship runs, after trading close times all event from said opposition. His Toyota Starlet took blows from familiar names like Maurice Whittingham, Christopher Addison, and Zachary Isaacs. He even had to fend off front-wheel drive charges from Kai Chuck-Dixon and Daren Givans, but in the end Ottey managed to pull out a two-second lead to seal the deal at the end of the night.

“I just settled down, kept my composure, and tried to point and shoot the car. That’s how I got the time,” said Ottey.

Running in reverse order for the championship runs, it was Givans who first did the unthinkable, posting both the fastest front-wheel drive run of the section and the fastest time until then. Once done, the massive crowd was on the edge of their seats to see if the 1:15.307 time could be beaten. It took the might of Whittingham to best the simple Corolla, with an anti-lag snorting 1:13.894. Isaacs, who had been the fastest in the main event by a 10th of a second over Ottey, lowered it even further after a 1:11.919 run. Both men would finish third and second, respectively, as Ottey continued the two-second margin trend, winning overall after completing a 1:09.916.

Givans would head back to Kingston with a class win for front-wheel drive and the respect of the Montegonian fans. Chuck-Dixon claimed the front-wheel drive with limited slip differential class in his Honda Civic. The rear-wheel drive with limited slip differential class went to Isaacs, a small consolation prize for almost winning the event.

“It was a magnificent event for all involved. The runs were superb. The drivers were excellent,” Stephen Mahoney, event organiser, said.

The series heads for conclusion in October.

World.title: ‘Abuse of power’: Von der Leyen rapped after backing space mega deal
World.content:
“Endorsing a merger at a conference covered by the media, without any substantive review, is an abuse of power and misconduct,” the French MEP wrote on X.

Von der Leyen was referring to Project Bromo, a joint venture between satellite makers Airbus, Leonardo and Thales to compete, at least in part, with the Starlink satellite-internet service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which recently went public in the U.S. and is valued around $2 trillion.

“These are the types of industrial champions we need if Europe is to lead in the space economy of tomorrow,” von der Leyen said.

Her words would have been music to the ears of the summit host, French President Emmanuel Macron, who has publicly backed the project together with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

But they raised red flags with the antitrust community in Brussels, where the project has yet to be formally notified or assessed by the EU executive’s competition department led by Executive Vice President Teresa Ribera.

“What is the point of Competition Commissioner Teresa Ribera and the Directorate General for Competition if it is the president of the Commission who unilaterally decides a case?” Yon-Courtin asked.

World.title: Sweden’s NATO missions are at risk if the left wins election, warns PM Kristersson
World.content:
Until recently, Sunday’s upcoming vote seemed like it would be a comfortable victory for Andersson’s Social Democrats and their political allies in smaller parties on the left. But their poll lead shrank dramatically in the past two weeks to as low as 2.6%, within the statistical margin of error.

Far-right friends

Kristersson’s center-right coalition has been governing for the past four years with the support of the far-right Sweden Democrats. He defended his decision to cooperate with a party opponents claim is too extreme despite its internal efforts to clean up its past neo-Nazi links.

“I have full respect for the fact that there are eight parties in the Swedish parliament,” said Kristersson. “None of these parties are even close to a majority of their own. If you cannot unite parties on specific topics and ambitions, then you will simply not get anything done at all.”

Social Democrat Magdalena Andersson, the first woman to serve as Swedish PM, leads the polls. | Tim Ross/POLITICO

Under leader Jimmie Åkesson, the Sweden Democrats are in second place behind Andersson’s Social Democrats in the polls. Åkesson has said he’s eyeing up the chance of becoming prime minister at the next vote, due in 2030.

If Kristersson returns as prime minister after Sunday’s election, he has said he’s ready to give Sweden Democrat politicians roles as ministers in his government for the first time. It would be a major change for Sweden — and the left-wing bloc has campaigned against it.

Kristersson suggested that being part of a team would limit the opportunities for any individual ministers to go rogue with extremist policies.

“In Sweden, we have a collective decision-making process in government,” he said. “I would never say that one minister is not important, but every minister is part of a team that jointly makes all the decisions — so there is very little room for people to play in a role of their own.

“And since I will be the person that is forming that government, and the person that will appoint every one of them, I can guarantee you that it will only be very skilled and experienced and people with good judgment that would be part of my government.”

World.title: UK MPs reject bill legalizing assisted dying bill despite previous support
World.content:
The bill, introduced by backbench Labour MP Lauren Edwards, would have legalized assisted dying for adults aged 18 or over who are judged by two doctors as expected to die within six months.

It will now make no further progress and follows members of the Scottish Parliament rejecting similar legislation in March and a previous vote by MPs against assisted dying in 2015.

Assisted dying is currently illegal in the U.K. and assisting someone to end their life is punishable by up to 14 years in prison in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.

The vote was a matter of conscience, meaning parties did not whip their MPs who could vote as they wished.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was not an MP when Leadbeater's bill was previously debated, deliberately abstained to avoid swaying the views of MPs.

Nonetheless, Burnham argued soon after becoming PM that fixing palliative and social care should come before legalizing assisted dying.

“It is very challenging to introduce that wider debate in a context of people not receiving that care and having the peace of mind about that care,” he said in July.

Isabel Loubser contributed to this report.

World.title: Iran-backed Houthis seize Red Sea port, putting another key trade route at risk
World.content:
At its narrowest, the strait is only about 30 kilometers wide. Yemen’s internationally recognized President Rashad al-Alimi warned Thursday it “must not be allowed to become another Strait of Hormuz.”

The Iranian-supported rebel advance raises the prospect of simultaneous disruption at two of global trade’s most vital chokepoints, potentially compounding shipping delays, supply shortages and inflationary pressure worldwide.

Tehran on Friday voiced support for Yemen’s "independence, national sovereignty and territorial integrity," while blaming the country’s crisis on blockade and foreign military intervention. The Iranian foreign ministry's statement, published on official state-run news agency IRNA, did not address the Houthi advance or Bab al-Mandeb.

The Houthis’ military capabilities have also drawn fresh scrutiny. A weapons cell based in Northern Yemen, a large part of which is controlled by the Houthis, used Anthropic’s Claude AI to develop guidance, navigation and control software for rockets and ballistic missiles, the tech giant reported in a memo published Thursday.

Western concerns are growing over the ramifications of the Iran war spreading further across the region.

Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot warned Friday in a post on X that “Bab al-Mandab is not a bargaining chip.”

World.title: US excludes French groups from MAGA-aligned grant program
World.content:
The grant program was formally advertised in the summer after U.S. State Department officials held talks with MAGA-aligned think tanks and advocacy groups about funding opportunities earlier this year. That led French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot to warn against what he described as potential “foreign interference in [European] electoral processes.”

The country is beefing up its arsenal to fight online disinformation and foreign interference ahead of the 2027 presidential campaign, with a law set to be considered by the Senate in October.

A spokesperson for the State Department said the program “does not and will not fund political parties, in Europe or elsewhere” and added that the allocation of grants “was still in active deliberation.”

The U.S. administration, most prominently Vice President JD Vance, has repeatedly framed the EU’s hate speech laws and election safety measures as attempts to curtail free speech and civil rights.

Its high-profile support for Hungary’s autocratic former leader Viktor Orbán and its pledge to support like-minded “patriotic European parties” in its National Security Strategy have raised fears of election interference ahead of several key elections in Europe.

The spokesperson for the State Department said the strategy objectives included “collaborating with European partners to jointly support European revitalization and civilizational self-confidence.”

Nicolas Conquer, the founder of the MAGA-aligned French think tank Western Arc, has applied for the funding. He said he had yet to receive a formal response to his application.

World.title: EU should sanction Israeli settlements like Russian-occupied Crimea, Kallas says
World.content:
“Especially today, on the eve of the Jewish New Year, it is hard to believe that [she] would draw a direct parallel between The Western wall and the Jewish Quarter in Jerusalem and the situation in Crimea, regardless of her personal worldview,” the mission said.

The EU foreign policy chief has long backed a push from several member countries to pressure the European Commission to ban trade with territories illegally occupied by Israel — an issue that divides capitals and has become a flashpoint in the rift between Kallas and the Commission’s president, Ursula von der Leyen.

Kallas’ backing has so far failed to force the Commission’s hand. In July, only a minority of EU foreign ministers called on the Commission to bring specific measures for member countries to vote on. While a handful of countries including the Netherlands, Belgium and Sweden have pushed for bloc-wide restrictions, the Czech Republic has vowed to oppose any new sanctions — withholding the unanimity required among EU capitals.

But the debate was reignited Tuesday when eight EU countries, including France, Spain and Ireland, joined the U.K. and Canada in a pledge to impose trade sanctions on Israeli settlements.

“All EU Member States agree that Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law,” Kallas said after the announcement. “The Israeli Government’s settlement expansions in the West Bank are undermining the prospects for a viable two-State solution.”

Kallas’ positions have previously drawn the ire of Israeli officials. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar vowed to “sever all contact” with the EU’s top diplomat in June, after reports that she had compared Israel’s treatment of Palestinians to apartheid-era South Africa.

World.title: ‘The Europe she fought for will miss her’: Politicians pay tribute to Emma Bonino
World.content:
A veteran of Italy’s fight for civil and women’s rights, Bonino played a key role in the campaigns that led to the legalization of divorce and abortion in the country during the 1970s.

In 2017, she co-founded the liberal More Europe party, which paid tribute to her on Friday. “Activist, parliamentarian, minister, European commissioner. Always radically free,” party leader Riccardo Magi wrote on X. “Her life was a long struggle against everything that denies freedoms.”

Carlo Calenda, leader of the liberal Italian Action party, said: “The last great protagonist of the civil battles that led to the modernization of this country,” adding that “a piece of Italian and European political history is passing away.”

Bonino’s endeavors extended beyond Italy. She served as a European commissioner in the 1990s, notably overseeing an increase in humanitarian aid to countries and regions affected by some of the most devastating conflicts of the decade, including the Balkans, Rwanda and Afghanistan.

“Emma Bonino has never waited for the world to be ready. She has always chosen to move forward, showing the way to others,” wrote European Parliament President Roberta Metsola. “The Europe she fought for will miss her.”

World.title: Hamas planned Berlin-Vienna attacks for Oct. 7 anniversary, indictment shows
World.content:
Federal prosecutors said last year that they had arrested men linked to the Palestinian militant group who were suspected of planning attacks on Israeli and Jewish targets in Germany. The indictment, which has not been made public, reveals that Vienna was also an intended target — and that the attacks in the two capitals were to be coordinated. The principal targets included Israeli diplomats, Jewish community centers and pro-Israel demonstrations.

Seven men have been charged in connection with the plot and remain in pretrial detention, according to the indictment. One of the accused was working as a confidential informant for Germany’s domestic intelligence agency. The files show that the informant continued reporting to his intelligence handler while allegedly failing to disclose the full extent of his own involvement in obtaining ammunition for the group.

The indictment portrays the plot as part of a broader shift in Hamas’ operations in Europe. Intelligence assessments cited in the filing say plans existed even before the Oct. 7, 2023 attack to establish and train operational cells on the continent, using Turkey as a base and directing attacks remotely from abroad.

The prosecutors alleged the weapons operation was also coordinated from Lebanon, where a Hamas operative allegedly oversaw one of the procurement channels linking members of the network across Europe.

According to the indictment, the objective was to move beyond the fundraising, propaganda and logistical activity that had long characterized Hamas’ presence in Europe and develop the capability to carry out attacks against Israeli and Jewish targets in the West.

The plot began to unravel on Oct. 1, 2025, just six days before the planned attacks, when German authorities arrested three suspects in Berlin during the handover of a cache of weapons that prosecutors say had been assembled for the operation.

World.title: Houthis seize key Yemeni island in Bab el-Mandeb, taking control of the strait
World.content:
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis took control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait on Friday, after capturing an island located in the middle of the crucial Red Sea waterway, a local government official and eyewitnesses said.

 

"Boats carrying armed Houthi fighters reached Mayyun Island after government forces withdrew from it yesterday," the official said, referring to a rocky volcanic island also known as Perim that divides the narrowest part of the strait into two shipping lanes.

"The Houthis have completed their takeover of the Bab el-Mandeb area and Mayyun Island, which is located in the middle of the strait," he added, speaking on condition of anonymity.

An eyewitness said gunmen were "deploying along the Bab el-Mandeb shore and are driving around in military vehicles."

Further reports emerged on Friday that the group also seized the town of Dhubab and the coastal village of Murad, meaning that all of Yemen's Red Sea coast was now under Houthi control in an 18-hour blitz.

Government military sources said that the Houthis have besieged government troops on the Hanish islands, following earlier reports that the Zuqar island — the largest of the three major islands in the Red Sea archipelago further north from Bab el-Mandeb — was already captured.

They said they were unsure about the status of their soldiers, who number more than 2,000, but believe the Houthis have ordered them to surrender.

A senior military official said that the besieged forces have appealed to authorities for "rescue, food and water, and the lifting of the siege, which would require air support".

On Thursday, Houthis captured the strategic port city of Mokha from government forces in a blitz offensive that also saw them taking control of Zuqar Island in the southern Red Sea "after rocket attacks and a ground assault carried out using boats transporting fighters," according to military sources.

By Thursday evening, multiple videos appeared online of Houthi fighters' apparent celebrations in Mokha and their seizure of considerable weapons and equipment left behind by government forces. Euronews could not verify the authenticity of the footage.

Another crisis on the horizon

The Houthis, who controlled about one-third of Yemen's territory prior to the offensive, have previously targeted shipping in the narrow waterway which links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal.

Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb account for more than one quarter of seaborne crude oil and petroleum trade. Nearly one-third of the world's container traffic passes through the Red Sea alone.

The Houthis have also reportedly consulted with Tehran on imposing a safe passage toll through the strait over the summer, in an apparent plot to further strain global economies.

Yemen's internationally recognised government has repeatedly warned of Houthi plans for taking control of the waterway, whose name in Arabic means "Gate of Tears".

Yet a member of the Houthis' politburo on Friday sought to allay global fears for international shipping, stating the group posed "no danger" to Red Sea cargo routes.

"Freedom of navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab are safe and orderly," Hazem al-Assad told the Al-Araby al-Jadeed news outlet. "There is no cause for international concern, as they face no danger from the Yemeni side."

FILE: Yemeni fishermen pass by a commercial ship at the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, 5 April 2026 AP Photo

The Houthis corrected this statement to say Saudi Arabia remains an exception.

"Maritime navigation is safe for all companies except Saudi ships, which have already been banned," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Friday evening.

According to Senior Director at the Soufan Center Caroline Rose, the Houthi takeover of Perim Island and Yemen's coastline creates in a chokehold which fill force shipping operators to reconsider costlier alternatives, while also impacting the key infrastructure the region relies on, such as the Suez Canal.

"Instead of going through the Red Sea, Suez, then Europe, they now have to explore a much more onerous path through Asia, the Cape of Good Hope, the Atlantic, then to Europe," Rose told Euronews.

"This adds weeks, greater insurance requirements given the proliferation of drones and overall risk, cost, and personnel needs to the journey, something that will undoubtedly increase prices."

Houthis marching on

Formally known as Ansar Allah, the Houthis came to power in late 2014 after storming Sana'a and seizing the presidential palace and key military sites, forcing Yemen's government into exile.

The group is part of Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.

The group triggered a return to hostilities in Yemen's civil war in July, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace.

Riyadh retaliated by striking the airport, triggering the Houthis to declare a blockade on the kingdom targeting its oil trade in July.

FILE: A Yemeni fighter backed by the Saudi-led coalition fires his weapon during clashes with Houthi rebels on the Kassara frontline near Marib, 20 June 2021 AP Photo

The Houthis engaged in a large-scale offensive last week against government forces backed by Saudi Arabia, while also launching attacks on Saudi territory that left dozens wounded, leading Riyadh to respond with daily strikes on Houthi-held parts of Yemen.

Saudi Arabia, which earlier this week said it had always offered “opportunities for negotiation,” also said it has the right to defend itself.

Houthi attacks on oil infrastructure and Saudi tankers have further contributed to a spike in oil prices, which surpassed $100 a barrel on Thursday.

A friend in need

Last month, Saudi Arabia signed a NATO-style mutual defence agreement with Turkey and nuclear-armed Pakistan in Mecca, but it seems unlikely either of the two would get involved.

On Tuesday, Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said Pakistan would "honour" the pact "in case there is a need".

Just one day later, the Pakistan foreign ministry said that the Mecca pact was a "defensive alliance focused on deterrence".

"There is no such thing under discussion right now. When the time comes, we will act under the agreement," spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan told the press at the weekly media briefing.

In July, US President Donald Trump said Washington would respond against the Houthis if they attempted to block maritime traffic in the Red Sea, after weeks of US strikes from March 2025 — early in Trump's second term — hit a range of military and industrial targets.

However, Washington is reportedly reluctant to enter the fray at this time as it remains bogged down in its own war with Iran since February.

According to US outlets, Trump rejected a request from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for strikes on Houthi positions as they approached Mokha on Thursday. Riyadh and the White House are yet to comment on these reports.

FILE: US President Donald Trump welcomes Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to the White House, 18 November 2025 AP Photo

Meanwhile in Brussels, the EU's External Action Service strongly condemned Houthi attacks earlier this week, calling for the group to "end all attacks inside and outside Yemen, including attacks against commercial shipping in the Red Sea" and respect UN resolutions.

Brussels had not publicly commented on the Houthis' seizure of Perim Island and the Bab al-Mandeb shoreline at the time of publication.

Operation Aspides, the 27-member bloc's defensive naval mission stationed in Djibouti has been tasked with protecting freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, but its current mandate does not cover offensive action against Houthi positions on land or on islands.

It is not clear at this time whether the group's lightning takeover of Bab el-Mandeb will expedite talks about expanding its mandate which EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told Euronews in mid-July were already under way.

"What is tricky about the Houthis is that they have proven resilient with on-and-off-again maritime campaigns and coalitions directed at degrading their offensive capabilities," Rose said.

"Neither the US nor the EU have revived former efforts to consolidate a concerted campaign around the Houthis’ recent expansion, though it’s possible in the next few months as the US seeks leverage with Iran," she added.

Tehran salutes 'resounding victory'

Tehran chimed in on Friday, calling for an end to Saudi Arabia's blockade of Yemen and the immediate resumption of talks, in its first public statement since the Houthi Red Sea offensive.

In a statement carried by the state-run IRNA news agency, Iran's foreign ministry said Yemen’s sovereignty must be respected, and its problems cannot be resolved through a blockade or military alliances.

Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iranian Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, congratulated the Houthis on their "resounding victory" on Friday.

Meanwhile, reports have claimed that Iran's elite paramilitary IRGC has deployed dozens of advisors to aid the Houthis in their operations. Euronews could not independently verify the claims at this time.

Supporters celebrate at a rally to celebrate the group's capture of the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, in Houthi-controlled Sana'a, 11 September 2026 AP Photo

A potential disruption to Bab el-Mandeb would work in Tehran's favour, as its blockade of Hormuz has put significant pressure on the world's energy markets, sparking a crisis that could worsen even further as the northern hemisphere approaches winter.

"The Houthi offensive to capture territory near the Bab al Mandeb advances Iranian objectives under the current regional campaign that Iran is waging against the United States and its allies," Washington-based think tank Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said in its latest analysis on Friday.

"Iran has recently pursued the following lines of effort under this regional campaign: targeting US naval forces, attacking US forces across the region, (and) disrupting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz," it added.

"The Houthis and Iran may currently share a common objective in Houthi control over the Red Sea coastline, but the nature of their relationship means that the Houthis will independently determine their level of involvement in supporting other Iranian objectives."

The leader of Yemen's internationally recognised governing council on Thursday urged Arab and other nations to help it defend the country's coasts.

"The protection of Yemen's coasts and the restoration of state control over its territory, ports and waters is a joint Yemeni, Egyptian, Arab and international interest," Rashad al-Alimi, who heads Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, said during a meeting with Egypt's ambassador.

The Houthi offensive has cost more than 500 lives and has displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.

World.title: French blockade looms over Commission’s plan to fast-track trade deals in English
World.content:
France will push back against a European Commission plan to fast-track ratification of trade agreements by circulating only English-language versions during talks with EU governments and lawmakers, skipping translation into the bloc’s 24 official languages, according to several sources.

 

The slow ratification of the contentious EU–Mercosur trade deal has frustrated the Commission, which wants to accelerate negotiations and bring deals into force more quickly as it seeks new markets amid rising geopolitical tensions.

Translating the agreements into every official EU language can take months due to the legal scrubbing required before the ratification process begins.

The EU executive has confirmed to Euronews that trade chief Maroš Šefčovič told EU trade ministers in February that the trade deal with India concluded on 27 January could serve as a test case for using English as the main language during ratification.

“We lost almost €300 billion by not having the Mercosur agreement in place since 2021, if it comes to the GDP, and more than €200 billion in export opportunities,” Šefčovič told journalists after meeting ministers on 20 February, adding that once negotiations end it can take up to 2.5 years before businesses can operate in partner countries.

“In today's world, we cannot simply lose the time,” he said.

Šefčovič said the Commission would ensure the agreements are translated into all 24 official EU languages once published in the Official Journal, i.e. after ratification. He added the proposal was backed by at least seven member states at the meeting, though not all countries had time to speak.

French sources who spoke to Euronews were insistent that Paris would vigorously oppose the move to English-only agreements if necessary.

“As a matter of principle, we defend the use of all the languages of the Union, and in particular French, which is one of the EU’s working languages,” one official told Euronews.

'Transparency, precision and understanding'

Language policy in the bloc’s institutions remains politically sensitive for countries such as France, whose language has declined sharply over the past decades as English massively dominates daily work in the European Union institutions – despite French, German and English being the three official working languages.

“Switching entirely to English raises a legal and democratic issue, and the Commission is well aware of it,” another French official told Euronews.

On its website, the European Commission says linguistic diversity is essential and that the EU promotes multilingualism in its institutional work.

The bloc once even had a commissioner dedicated to multilingualism, though the portfolio was gradually merged with others and eventually disappeared.

"I have the impression that in some cases the Commission seizes the opportunity to push the idea that English has a superior status, and that the other official languages are translation languages that can come later," Michele Gazzola, expert in language policy, said.

He added that relying only on English during ratification could pose problems for members of the European Parliament, and even more so if national parliaments are involved.

“It’s a matter of transparency, precision and understanding."

World.title: France joins Slovakia in asking to delist Russian oligarch Usmanov
World.content:
The French government has joined Slovakia in seeking the delisting of Russian-Uzbek businessman Alisher Usmanov, causing “huge frustration” among other EU countries, four EU diplomats told Euronews.

 

Slovakia has long pushed for Usmanov and another Russian oligarch, Mikhail Fridman, to be removed from the EU's sanctions list targeting individuals close to Vladimir Putin's regime and the military-industrial complex sustaining the war in Ukraine.

But Bratislava is no longer alone. Paris has also called for Usmanov, who has been under EU sanctions since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, to be delisted.

Usmanov is an Uzbek-born Russian billionaire who built his fortune through investments in metals, mining, telecommunications and technology and is considered close to the Kremlin.

Usmanov denies this.

The French move has caused “huge frustration” among other member states, particularly against the backdrop of escalating hybrid threats in Europe, including the latest case of an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport in Germany.

“It raised a lot of questions about the motivation — seems mostly economic reasons at play here. Not a lot of understanding on the side of other member states,” an EU diplomat told Euronews, speaking on condition of anonymity given the sensitivity of the talks.

The EU sanctions regime currently targets more than 3,000 individuals and entities linked to Russia's military-industrial complex and its contribution to the invasion of Ukraine. The regime is due for renewal on 15 September, with member states under pressure to reach an agreement by then.

Individual listings have so far been renewed every six months, but a 12-month renewal is now on the table. Sectoral sanctions already shifted from six-month to 12-month renewal cycles in July.

In several meetings of EU ambassadors, Slovakia has opposed the renewal, pushing for both oligarchs to be delisted and the six-month timeframe to remain in place.

The Slovak demands are not new. Bratislava has repeatedly called for the delisting of the two high-profile Russian oligarchs, including when the sanctions were last extended in March.

EU sanctions require unanimous approval for renewal, meaning a single country can veto an extension. Slovakia's opposition has already caused frustration among member states, but France's new position is likely to complicate the talks further.

Paris presented Usmanov's delisting as a political compromise, betting that Slovakia would not abandon its two delisting demands as it did last time.

EU ambassadors are due to meet again on Monday to discuss the renewal and will be under pressure to reach a political agreement before the 15 September deadline.

A French official said Paris supported the renewal of sanctions, but declined to comment on the discussions, citing confidentiality.

World.title: UK police ban face coverings at planned anti-migrant protest
World.content:
Police in southern England have banned face coverings at an anti-immigration rally as well as in a counter-protest planned in Portsmouth on Saturday, amid concerns over potential unrest.

 

The demonstration, organised by protesters calling themselves “patriots”, is expected to begin at around noon.

Hampshire Police, which has responsibility for Portsmouth, said the mask ban was to "reduce opportunities for violence, intimidation and criminality".

It said the move followed "recent incidents of violence and intimidation by a minority of those who have been intent on disrupting peaceful protest".

A separate order will allow police to require people to remove masks or other items covering their identity.

Assistant Chief Constable Paul Bartolomeo, quoted by the BBC, said: "It is important to stress that this power will apply to any groups that attend the protest and will be enforced equally and impartially.

"Let me be clear, these powers are not being implemented to prevent protest, but they are being used to help prevent crime and disorder, while making communities feel safer."

The demonstrations come less than a week after clashes between protesters and police in Portsmouth. Masked protesters attempted to prevent a group of asylum seekers who had crossed the English Channel in a small boat from leaving the area.

Police said official vehicles were damaged and several officers were injured during the unrest, which the government condemned as “thuggish”.

A day earlier, hundreds of masked protesters gathered in Dover and briefly blocked access to the Channel port during a demonstration against migrant crossings.

The unrest in Portsmouth and Dover was condemned by political leaders.

Police were given powers last year to ban face coverings used to conceal identities at protests.

World.title: US commemorates 25th anniversary of devastating 9/11 attacks as their legacy endures
World.content:
The United States on Friday marked the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks with a solemn ceremony in New York.

 

The anniversary was marked by commemorations across the country, including wreath-laying ceremonies, moments of silence, vigils and readings of victims’ names, as well as volunteer initiatives.

On 11 September 2001, hijackers from al-Qaeda, an Islamist extremist group, seized four commercial jets and crashed them into New York’s World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, killing nearly 3,000 people.

US President Donald Trump attended a ceremony at the Pentagon rather than in New York, drawing criticism from some victims’ relatives and linked the post-9/11 “war on terror” to the current war in Iran.

"Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago. We will never, ever forget. That's why we fight today," Trump said.

President Donald Trump, left, and first lady Melania Trump arrive at an observance ceremony on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, Friday, 11Sept., 2026, Pentagon. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)

9/11’s legacy: Security vs freedom

The 11 September attacks left a lasting impact on many aspects of life in the United States and continue to shape the debate over the balance between security and freedom.

The attacks transformed US air travel, led to the creation of the Department of Homeland Security and prompted new federal surveillance and intelligence-gathering powers, as well as new banking regulations.

People listen to the U.S. national anthem at the memorial on the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Friday, 11 Sept., 2026, in New York. AP Photo

They also fostered a culture of individual vigilance, summed up by the slogan “if you see something, say something”, while a wave of patriotism encouraged some Americans to join the military, fire departments and police forces.

New York mayor attends 9/11 ceremony amid criticism

The September 11 attacks fuelled mistrust, prejudice and hate crimes against Muslims in the United States. Twenty-five years later, Muslim Americans have a growing role in public life, with Zohran Mamdani serving as New York City’s first Muslim mayor.

Mamdani attended Friday’s Ground Zero ceremony despite a campaign urging him to stay away, backed by former Mayor Rudy Giuliani and the right-wing New York Post newspaper.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani meets with people after a memorial on the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Friday, 11 Sept., 2026, in New York Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

A petition was signed by more than 100,000 people. It accuses Mamdani of links to individuals seen as dismissive of US institutions or extremist ideologies.

Mamdani was recently praised for releasing documents revealing what city officials knew about toxic air in Lower Manhattan after 9/11, which has been linked to cancers affecting thousands of New Yorkers.

World.title: French father jailed for threatening to behead his son’s teacher
World.content:
A French court has sentenced a man to six months in prison after he threatened to “cut off the head” of a teacher at his son’s school last week.

 

The defendant confronted his son’s teacher in the school car park in the southwestern town of Le Fauga last week, after the nine-year-old was moved to another class because of his behaviour.

He threatened to decapitate the 58-year-old teacher before entering the school, where he repeated the threats in front of the headteacher.

Remarks of 'great violence'

The court sentenced the defendant to six months in prison, to be served immediately, a harsher sentence than the six months under electronic monitoring sought by the public prosecutor.

The presiding judge, Fabrice Rives, condemned the “extremely worrying remarks” and described them as being of “great violence”, explicitly referring to the murder of Samuel Paty.

In that case, Paty, a history and geography teacher, was beheaded in 2020 by an 18-year-old radical Islamist of Chechen origin after showing his class caricatures of the Prophet Mohammed.

At the hearing, the defendant apologised, saying he had “not realised the seriousness” of his words.

Describing himself as “very, very protective” of his children, he said he was not a violent person and did not know what had come over him that day.

Teacher 'traumatised'

The teacher is currently on sick leave and unsure whether she will return to the classroom, according to her lawyer, Jocelyn Momasso-Momasso.

He said she was “traumatised”, adding that she had told him: “I didn’t 

At the hearing, the defendant said he had already agreed to move two of his three children who attended the school to another establishment.

World.title: Russia sends sanctioned ships to Mediterranean as NATO tracks 'Syrian Express' convoy
World.content:
Russia's navy has returned to the Mediterranean for the first time in two months, ending what military sources described as the first interruption to its Mediterranean presence since 2013 — with ships reportedly detected switching off their tracking transponders before passing through the Strait of Gibraltar.

 

Speaking on condition of anonymity, a senior European military source said the "Syrian Express" ships had arrived at the Syrian port of Tartus on Monday.

The informal name "Syrian Express" refers to Moscow's maritime logistics network that transfers military supplies, weapons, and equipment between Russian ports and Tartus.

It has been running intermittently since Russia's military intervention in Syria in 2015, frequently involving sanctioned vessels that have also been associated with Russia's broader shadow fleet, which Moscow uses to circumvent Western sanctions.

The latest Russian convoy included the sanctioned cargo vessel Sparta, the sanctioned tanker General Skobelev, and the replenishment ship Akademik Pashin, all escorted by the destroyer Admiral Levchenko.

Tight European surveillance

Despite its return to the Mediterranean, Russia's navy remains under tight European surveillance.

The ships in question were closely tracked by the Italian Carabinieri frigate as they sailed through the central Mediterranean after they were spotted at Gibraltar.

Euronews obtained exclusive photos of the Italian frigate alongside the Russian ships.

Euronews obtained exclusive photos of the Italian Carabiniere frigate, alongside the Syrian express ships Military source

Tracking data from the specialised website MarineTraffic indicates that the vessels switched off their automatic identification system (AIS) transponders — which automatically broadcast ships' identity, position, speed, and course — before passing through the Strait of Gibraltar.

Britain deployed three ships — HMS Duncan, HMS St Albans and HMS Severn — to monitor the convoy as it sailed through the English Channel.

The military source told Euronews that in recent months, Syrian express ships have begun cutting off AIS transponders even "more frequently" than in the past, with this practice almost becoming "systematic".

Russia retains post-al-Assad presence in Syria

Tartus is Russia's only naval base outside the former Soviet Union and its sole resupply and maintenance point in the Mediterranean.

The Soviet Union established the facility in 1971 under a lease agreement with Damascus, using it to sustain its Mediterranean fleet during the Cold War.

Russia intervened militarily in Syria in September 2015, entering the country's civil war on the side of Bashar al-Assad at a moment when his forces were losing ground to opposition groups.

Moscow initially said its strikes were targeting the so-called Islamic State terrorist group, but international organisations documented that the majority of Russian air strikes hit opposition-held civilian areas, with the Airwars monitoring group assessing that those strikes resulted in the deaths of more than 14,000 Syrian civilians.

The nine-year campaign in Syria was the Kremlin's most significant military participation in a war outside the former Soviet Union before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

When the al-Assad regime finally collapsed in December 2024, Russian warships evacuated from Tartus within days — a precautionary move to avoid being seized or denied departure.

In August, Damascus announced it had reached a deal with Moscow to retain Russia's future presence in the two military bases it has in the country.

On 9 August, Syria’s state news agency SANA quoted the Foreign Ministry as saying the Hmeimim airbase and Tartus naval base would become “joint training and capacity-building centres” under new arrangements aimed at preserving "mutual interests".

The senior European military source outlined several factors which are hindering Moscow's ability to maintain its presence in the Mediterranean including Russia's ageing navy, European sanctions against its shadow fleet, as well as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones targeting its Black Sea fleet.

European and Ukrainian pressure on the shadow fleet is also pushing Russia to deploy military escorts for its oil tankers.

World.title: UK lawmakers reject assisted dying bill for England and Wales
World.content:
UK lawmakers on Friday rejected legislation that would have allowed terminally ill adults in England and Wales to choose to end their lives.

 

Following an impassioned four-hour debate in the House of Commons, the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill was rejected by 286 votes to 270.

The outcome marked a notable reversal from last year, when an almost identical bill passed with a majority of 23 votes.

The bill would have allowed adults in England and Wales with fewer than six months to live to apply for an assisted death, subject to the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.

The vote brings an end to a two-year debate in Parliament over assisted dying, during which the House of Commons had backed the measure on two previous occasions.
