The delegation was provided with detailed information about the construction work being carried out at the mosque and the status of the project's implementation.

On September 11, a two-day visit by representatives of the diplomatic corps accredited in Azerbaijan to Karabakh and East Zangezur began, accompanied by the Assistant to the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan and Head of the Foreign Policy Affairs Department of the Presidential Administration, Hikmet Hajiyev.

The visit is attended by a delegation of 150 people representing 58 countries and 9 international organizations.

World.title: The tactics at 'Trump-a-palooza' reveal risks for Republicans
World.content:
The first thing I saw when I walked into "Trump-a-palooza" was Joe Biden.

The stadium screens were projecting his headshot, his eyes shooting red laser beams like a killer robot.

The use of the old meme came to represent two things about this week's Republican convention in Texas.

The first thing: even more than the event was about Trump, it was about Democrats.

On day one, at least, Biden and Kamala Harris kept flashing up on the screens as though we'd time-travelled to 2024.

And the second thing: the Republican messaging hasn't shifted a whole lot since Biden and Harris were in office.

It was a Republican convention, but Kamala Harris and Joe Biden kept showing up. (Reuters: Jessica Koscielniak)

This event featured the same scares as the 2024 convention: transgender athletes want to take over your daughters' sports leagues. Pro-vaccine doctors want to steal your power to decide what's best for your kids. Criminal illegal aliens might murder you during the night.

The most notable change to the talking points was how the adjectives had been amplified.

The "radical left lunatics" are now "crazy communists". Democrats are pursuing a "Bolshevik revolution" and want to "remake America in the image of every socialist hellscape of the last century".

Arguably, Trump's mistruths, as they are sometimes politely described, have been notched up too.

Separating real facts from "alternative facts" can get tricky when Trump speaks, but not always. There is something surreal about watching a speaker deliver a lengthy insistence that a venue is full while there are hundreds of unfilled seats around you.

"The highest rafter, no empty seats," Trump said, while actually pointing to entire sections of empty seats in the stadium's highest rafter.

Three topics proved taboo, except when Trump spoke

The headline from Trump's keynote address was an offer of free cash — a "Trump dividend", rather than a bribe, payable if voters vote the right way.

But his lengthy speech otherwise contained a lot of recycled material.

He told a familiar story about where "tariffs" fits on his list of favourite words. He recited a well-worn tale about being bullied by reporters over the price of eggs. And he reminded the crowd, no fewer than half a dozen times, that Iran must not have nuclear weapon.

Anyone who had listened to enough Trump rallies had heard it all before.

But it was notable that Trump chose to spend so much time on these three issues. Tariffs, affordability and Iran had largely been absent from the previous speeches.

They all rate highly among the list of factors contributing to Trump's poor approval rating, so other speakers largely steered clear of them.

The convention aims to motivate the party base before the November midterms. (Reuters: Callaghan O'Hare)

One of Trump's most politically interesting choices was to speak dismissively about cost-of-living issues, and re-prosecute his old argument that the "affordability crisis" is "fake", but, in any case, he has solved it.

"Food prices and almost every other item are rapidly going down," he said.

"And by the way, oil will be going down as soon as we win the war with Iran, which is taking place right now."

Polls consistently show voters are not buying this message. In one recent poll, 69 per cent of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of inflation and living costs, while just 17 per cent approved.

A telling conversation in a Texas park

So what was the point of the midterms convention spectacle?

What's the president's strategy when he insists that the affordability crisis is not a thing?

Why tell Americans, who keep complaining to pollsters they are struggling with rising prices, that "tariffs" remains a favourite word?

And for that matter, why speak at such length about the stadium being full? All that was ever guaranteed to do was spawn viral videos showing rows of empty seats and a man on stage insisting a lie is a truth.

The MAGA diehards in the arena were hyped. But away from it all, is there any chance that a parade-of-speeches event like this can move the midterms needle?

"Trump-a-palooza" took place in Texas, a critical state for the upcoming midterm elections. (Reuters: Callaghan O'Hare)

One of the most interesting people I met in Dallas was a Trump supporter who did not attend the convention. He was a long-time local named Daniel, who I chatted with in a city park.

"Personally, I love Trump," Daniel said. "He's the best president we've ever had. He's brought our economy back up. That's about all I've got to say about the good guy."

But when I asked if there was anything he didn't like, it turned out he did have more to say.

"He's so hard on a lot of the good, good Spanish [speaking] people in Texas," he said.

"A lot of them don't have papers, but they're part of Texas now."

Daniel revealed himself as one of those Trump voters who felt his mass deportation campaign had gone too far. His views were a long way from the narrative about "criminal illegal aliens" being pushed at the convention.

"It kind of brings a tear to my eye," Daniel continued.

"I can understand him doing his job and deporting the bad ones, but a lot of them are here just to provide for their family, you know. It really hurts."

Risks for Republicans

On issues ranging from immigration and Iran, and especially when it comes to living costs, some Trump supporters are seeing problems with their president.

The party is aware of this risk, and how Trump's "pretend I'm on the ballot" strategy could backfire in the midterms.

Trump's 'Mini-Mamdani' crackdown Democratic socialism is on the rise in the US, and it is sparking a sharp campaign from Republicans.

Vice-President JD Vance pleaded with those voters in his keynote address.

"Do not throw the baby out with the bathwater," he said. "Don't give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy here or there."

While the party's messaging may not have changed a lot since 2024, circumstances have.

Trump's approval rating is at dire lows. But he has deliberately tied his party's fortunes to his own popularity, and he demonstrated his campaign strategy is not shifting.

The Republicans face a real risk of losing control of Congress in November's midterm elections.

Away from the stadium, those Americans who actually paid attention to "Trump-a-palooza" will likely be left wondering if it can improve the party's prospects at all.

World.title: Growing pains in Rockingham before AUKUS subs even arrive
World.content:
The arrival of the first AUKUS nuclear submarine and associated personnel is 385 days away and the council is wondering how it will cope with the influx of service people, their families and increased demand on already strained infrastructure.

Even before the arrival of the first Submarine Rotational Force personnel, the area near HMAS Stirling is experiencing strong population growth, Rockingham Mayor Lorna Buchan told 102.5 ABC Perth.

"We're growing by 14 people a day, which is over 5,000 people a year coming to Rockingham without any defence personnel arriving," Ms Buchan said.

"We have to think about the numbers involved within the rotational force coming from the US.

"There will be approximately 1,200 serving personnel arriving over the next four years, and approximately 50 per cent of them will have families."

An average of 14 people a day are moving to the area. (ABC News: Jasmine Hughes)

A report commissioned by the City of Rockingham in 2023 showed roads around Cape Peron were already at capacity, and people had already begun using "rat runs" to get through the traffic.

The area lacks any kind of industrial hub, exacerbating the traffic problem because 70 per cent of the population leave the area to work and study.

Call for greater funding

Ms Buchan said it also meant the city was largely reliant on residential rates income, because the defence facilities within the city were not required to pay rates.

With greater population comes greater demand for council services such as swimming pools and sporting facilities, as well as pressure on services like health care and child care, and increased demand for housing.

Both Ms Buchan and Warwick Carter, the director of Perth South West Metropolitan Alliance, representing six local councils in Perth's southern corridor, would like to see the federal government set up a dedicated fund to support communities that host defence facilities.

Warwick Carter says the region is preparing for activity equivalent to 10 Olympic Games. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

Mr Carter said the influx of defence personnel and workers in defence industries would in turn stimulate the creation of many more jobs, both boosting the economy, and creating pressures on the community.

"We want to keep the quality of life we have down here," he said.

"Can we make sure baristas can still afford to live here? Can we make sure there's enough childcare centres? Can we make sure there's enough retail? Because that's where the growth pressures will be felt.

"We've put a proposal to the federal government saying we should have a fund.

"We've suggested a pilot project of $50 million, not just for our region, but for any defence community in Australia, so places like Wagga, Townsville, they could apply for it as well to put in infrastructure that helps create more resilient communities."

In addition to AUKUS, Mr Carter said there were a number of other projects coming to the region which would both boost the economy and strain existing infrastructure.



"We're tracking about $70 billion worth of government-backed investment coming into the region over the coming decades.

“To put that in context, the Olympic Games in Brisbane is $7 billion, so it's 10 Olympic Games' worth of activity coming to our region."

Amber-Jade Sanderson, who is both WA minister for manufacturing, skills and TAFE and minister assisting the minister for defence industries, said the state government had already provided support and would provide more in the future.

Amber-Jade Sanderson says local schools and the hospital are being upgraded. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

"There's significant support already going into the community and we're always looking at how we can support more," Ms Sanderson said.

"They've been provided around $20 million worth of funding from the state government for sporting facilities, including their aquatic centre and the basketball centre.

"We're upgrading local schools. We're providing a new mental health emergency centre for Rockingham Hospital. We're starting the work around that redevelopment of Rockingham Hospital."

Local training hopes

The other need local leaders identify as urgent is for more training to be available locally for all the skilled jobs that will be created in defence and associated industries.

Ms Buchan said the Rockingham campus of Murdoch University, which has not hosted students since 2014, should be reopened, as well as a skills centre in Rockingham.

"We need that [campus] pulled out of mothballs. That will need significant investment from the state government to help that happen," she said.

AUKUS is set to transform Rockingham from a quiet beachside outer suburb into a much busier place. (ABC News: Rhiannon Shine)

Ms Sanderson said she was looking at a range of ways to train the workforce the state would need in the future.

"We'll be releasing the Workforce Development Plan later this year, which is an industry-based plan for the resources sector, defence, creative skills and industry, manufacturing, clean energy," she said.

"We need every industry to lean in and invest in apprentices, invest in training, support school leavers with school-based traineeships and apprentices and make sure that they're getting opportunities.

"I agree with the mayor that we do need the skills centre here."

Ms Sanderson said despite the challenges, local communities should welcome the investment that AUKUS would bring.

"This is a beautiful place to live and work and that's why so many people are coming to this area," she said.

"It's not necessarily because of the AUKUS program or the naval shipbuilding, but to inject that amount of investment in the local economy should be welcomed by the local government and local businesses.

"We're going to give them opportunities that just would not have been presented if this had not been happening."

World.title: Rio Tinto's exit from remote NT town looms large over by-election
World.content:
Rio Tinto's impending withdrawal from the Gove Peninsula is looming large over a remote by-election in the Northern Territory.

Production at the mining giant's north-east Arnhem Land bauxite mine will stop in 2029 — a second blow for Nhulunbuy after its alumina refinery shut in 2014.

Yiŋiya Guyula resigned from NT parliament last month, triggering a by-election. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

The town's future without its largest employer is the focus of today's Mulka by-election, triggered by the resignation of 10-year independent MLA Yiŋiya Guyula.

Yiŋiya Guyula resigns, labelling CLP policies 'dehumanising' The independent member for Mulka, Yiŋiya Guyula, has resigned from NT parliament effective immediately.

Mr Guyula quit suddenly last month, citing an inability to work with a Country Liberal Party (CLP) government he claimed was "not willing to listen or form partnerships with Aboriginal communities".

Only a Labor and independent candidate are seeking to replace Mr Guyula, with the CLP choosing not to run in a seat the party has not held since 1980.

Mulka is a former safe seat for Labor, until former deputy leader Lynne Walker lost to Mr Guyula by eight votes in 2016.

Yiwarr McGrath, a former NT Young Australian of the Year and trailblazing nurse, was preselected by the party last month and said the region had been forgotten.

Yiwarr McGrath is the Labor contender for the seat of Mulka. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"The CLP government has neglected this part of the world — how do we have ongoing sustainability around housing, healthcare," he said.

"I've been listening — I'm going to bring those issues to the table so [the government] is aware of what's going on post-mining.

" I'm from Mulka, I am Yolŋu, I grew up here, I know the issues here — I've been through poverty — I'll bring real experience and embed practicality. "

Although it is not running a candidate, Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro has said the CLP is committed to the future of Nhulunbuy, which is also losing its major supermarket, Woolworths, next year.

At the Garma Festival in July, Mrs Finocchiaro announced the town's lease would be handed to the Rirratjingu clan after Rio Tinto's exit, and also called for greater fuel security in the region.

Andrew Blamey is running as an independent, saying the two-party system is not working. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Independent candidate Andrew Blamey said he was running in the by-election after coming to the view that politics in the NT was "broken".

"The two-party system is failing us," he said.

" Independent voices in the parliament are very important to get people's views spoken about. "

A Territorian for almost 20 years and a Nhulunbuy resident for three, Mr Blamey said while in government, Labor had dropped the ball on the town's transition.

"I think it's important to remember that Rio Tinto announced they were leaving the area in 2019," he said.

Yirrkala residents have already begun voting in the by-election for the remote seat of Mulka. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"Labor were in power for [eight] years until 2024.

"I feel we need to move away from the blame game and a lot of voters are saying that to me as well.

"They want real answers and outcomes."

Long-standing issues remain

Just south of Nhulunbuy in Yirrkala, Laynhapuy Homelands Aboriginal Corporation vice-chair Barayuwa Munuŋgurr said overcrowded homes remained a key issue in the region's Aboriginal communities.

Barayuwa Munuŋgurr says overcrowding is an issue in remote communities. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"We need more houses, to get the wellness and wellbeing of our people, the same, because I feel that health comes first, with housing," he said.

"We have issues with diabetes, kidney failures, it's due to overcrowding and not enough housing."

Yirrkala resident Charles Yunupiŋu said he was living with his family in a home where he shared one room between five people.

"It is really frustrating for everyone, it's difficult for everyone to sleep," he said.

Charles Yunupiŋu says north-east Arnhem Land needs more skills training for young people. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Mr Yunupiŋu said the region also needed more skills training for young people.

"We need people to jump on work — most people just walk around and do nothing, you know, it's a bit sad too actually," he said.

"We need to help people to build their future for the next generation."

World.title: Country Women's Association celebrates 90 years in outback town
World.content:
An outback branch of the Country Women's Association (CWA) is celebrating 90 years of service in one of Australia's most remote towns.

The Tennant Creek branch in the Northern Territory was founded in 1936 during a gold rush in the area, when local men outnumbered women ten to one.

It is the longest continuously active branch in the NT, and it still serves the town's population of about 3,000 people, nearly 1,000 kilometres south of Darwin in the Barkly region.

Founded in 1922, the CWA has more than 1,000 branches across Australia and aims to improve the lives of women and children through community service and supporting cultural and welfare projects.

Celebrations for the 90th anniversary will include an afternoon tea and a fashion parade. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

Women vastly outnumbered

When CWA Tennant Creek formed, women made up 45 of the 600 residents, and after two years of informal catch-ups over cups of tea, the branch was officially launched.

President and life member Roddy Calvert said the CWA gave women and kids in the town a chance to find connection in the outback.

"I think it was for the companionship in those earlier days because a lot of these men … they were out on the field and often they just had their mine lease away from the town," she said.

" There just wasn't telephones and all that back in those days at all, so they just leaned on each other. "

Roddy Calvert is a CWA NT life member and has been a Tennant Creek resident for over 45 years. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

Service to the community

The Tennant Creek branch fundraises for various causes in the Barkly region, including supporting women's shelters in local Aboriginal communities and community groups.

The group also provided support during national emergencies, including to stationed soldiers in World War II and evacuees after Cyclone Tracy destroyed Darwin in the 70s.

CWA Tennant Creek volunteers supporting visiting soldiers during World War II, less than a decade after the branch formed. (Supplied: CWA Tennant Creek)

For many volunteers, the community spirit in the CWA was instilled in them from childhood.

Volunteer Helen Kempe regularly travels more than 1,000km from Mount Riddock cattle station to Tennant Creek to ensure her family's long association with the organisation continues.

"Both my grandmother and my mother were CWA members, so I know what it's all about," Ms Kempe said.

" So I think it's a great honour to be a member and I'm glad I joined. "

Helen Kempe joined the branch while living in Tennant Creek and continues to volunteer despite living more than 550 kilometres from the town. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

Looking towards a century

While excitement about the milestone is high, membership has fallen to fewer than 20 people in recent years, with fewer young people involved compared to the past.

However, branch member Alba Brockie said the CWA will always have a place in remote areas like Tennant Creek.

"The things that CWA have always fought for around isolated people, isolated children, women and children's health, those issues remain important," she said.

World.title: Teen charged over mistaken identity murder of Sydney tradie
World.content:
Police have charged a teenager who allegedly provided drone surveillance during a mistaken identity underworld attack last week.

The 18-year-old was arrested in West Hoxton on Friday by the Raptor Squad and has been charged with murder over the death of Joshua Macdonald.

Police allege officers seized a drone linked to the man that showed his involvement in the killing of the much-loved Western Sydney tradesman.

Mr Macdonald, 40, was gunned down outside a home in Merrylands West in broad daylight on September 2.

Joshua Macdonald, pictured with his aunt Darlene, was 40 years old. (Supplied)

Police sources have since told the ABC the intended target was a member of the notorious Alameddine crime family.

The gang's senior members remain in Lebanon, but police believe a recent surge in violence is linked to a feud between them and the "Coconut Cartel".

The cartel operates a crime network in Western Sydney from overseas and takes its name from a historical slur against Pasifika people.

Boosted powers to target Sydney's gangsters, but police face a new problem They are the extraordinary powers the premier has promised to expand in a bid to combat gangland violence, but they face a major test in this era of organised crime.

Mr Macdonald's death marked the seventh mistaken identity fatality linked to the conflict over the past 18 months.

His death led to renewed focus on legislation targeting Sydney's underworld.

The 18-year-old was refused bail and is due to front a Sydney bail court on Saturday.

During the operation on Friday, a 19-year-old was also arrested and charged with participating in a criminal group and driving with a suspended licence.

He was granted bail in Liverpool Local Court and is expected to face court again later this month.

World.title: After nearly 50 years, this master craftsman is hanging up his tools
World.content:
The craftsmen of Tasmania's heritage construction trade have had a busy month inside a 146-year-old church in Campbell Town.

A solid plasterer, a stained glass worker, and a heritage building specialist have all been working together to help restore the former Brickhill Memorial Church.

Gavin Merrington, 64, expects it will be his last major restoration project.

After almost 50 years spent repairing stained glass in buildings around Tasmania, he's preparing to hang up the tools — for the big jobs at least.

The 146-year-old Brickhill Memorial Church has just undergone weeks of restoration work with heritage tradespeople. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Original stained glass restored

The Campbell Town project, in Tasmania's midlands, hasn't been a small task.

The church's original High Street-facing main window had never been replaced, and after almost 150 years, the soft lead holding the glass together was well and truly breaking down.

"The putty under the lead starts to wash out and then the water gets in and they just degenerate," Mr Merrington said.

" You could see a few broken [pieces] but when you pull them out they start to separate, and there was heaps broken. "

Gavin Merrington's career in lead-lighting was kickstarted after he responded to an ad in a newspaper, aged 16. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Mr Merrington was able to track down the exact type of glass used in the original windows.

Intricate pieces were then hand-painted and fired in a kiln, with the process repeated many times until the desired colour and effect were reached.

That was done for "maybe 90 pieces", he said.

Based out of his studio in South Hobart, the work on the main windows at Brickhill took ten weeks.

Vivid colours in the newly reinstalled main window at the Brickhill Memorial Church. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

The glass was then carefully transported to Campbell Town, placed in a wooden crate and secured with screws before being levered up 5 metres off the ground to where it needed to be fitted.

"If you touch it on the scaffold you're likely to break something, and they're very heavy too, so it's a matter of being careful and having lots of hands on the windows to get them up," he said.

Leadlighting around the world

It was a newspaper ad that inspired Mr Merrington to pick up the trade of leadlighting at the age of 16.

He has spent much of his career working on church windows, a passion that has taken him around the world.

After being awarded a Churchill Fellowship in 2014, Mr Merrington travelled to Europe to learn from global experts in glazing and glass preservation — skills he brought back home to Tasmania.

Intricate pieces of glass were handpainted and fired in a kiln, as part of the restoration of the church's windows. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

"Coming back it was just sort of reiterated, we're on the right path and we're looking good as far as the skills that are being disseminated around Australia," he said.

"Australia is quite up with world trends as far as conservation."

Mr Merrington lists Launceston's Holy Trinity Church and Hobart churches St Mary's Cathedral and All Saints as some of his favourite projects he has worked on.

Heritage trades 'quite a community'

Campbell Town builder Peter Evans's family has been in the Northern Midlands region for five generations. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Heritage building specialist Peter Evans, who has also been working on the Brickhill project, first met Mr Merrington 20 years ago on a different church restoration.

He said that was typical of Tasmania's heritage trades, with many of the people working on these buildings having known each other for decades.

"It's quite a community; we all rely heavily on each other," he said.

" All the people I work with, a lot of our relationships go back 35 to 38 years. "

The heritage trade community is a small one, with workers often seeing each other at the same jobs around the state. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

A fifth-generation Campbell Town local, Mr Evans said the region was dotted with Victorian farmhouses and churches that kept him and his team of six busy.

"[There was] such a flurry of buildings in the 1830s, so this area here through to I suppose, Hobart, but particularly the Midlands," he said.

" It's good to be able to take our part in preserving these buildings and we'll hand over to the next generation, mainly just keeping them watertight and sound. "

Tasmania's heritage trade specialists rely heavily on each other. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

An unlikely owner

Ohio-born Matt Collins always wanted to buy a church.

After moving to Australia in 2017, he set his sights on Brickhill.

Built in 1880 with money left by former convict-turned-merchant Joseph Brickhill, the church was deconsecrated in 1964.

Since then, it has been a wool museum, a co-working space and now operates as short-stay accommodation.

US-born Matt Collins says, when you buy a heritage property, you have a "duty" to maintain it. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

"I think there is a duty and responsibility when you own or steward a building like this one to preserve it because it has such a rich history, relevance and significance to the local community," Mr Collins said.

"I'm really, really honoured that I've had Gavin and his team come and work on this building, with all the years of experience and knowledge that they have."

Heritage construction specialist Peter Evans chats to hard plasterer Mark Woodley during the restoration. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

The work on the main windows at Brickhill took ten weeks. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Future of heritage crafts

After Brickhill, Mr Merrington is stepping back from major restoration work.

But he is not walking away from the craft entirely.

He will continue working on smaller jobs and consultancy work.

Mr Merrington said he was confident his heritage trade was in safe hands.

"I've got an employee who will keep going after me hopefully, and he's got all the skills so that's really good," he said.

Mr Merrington said while it was a "shame so many churches are being sold", having people like Matt committed to restoring them was "better than it could have ever been expected", even compared to remaining in the church's hands.

He said after almost 50 years of travelling around the state, he was looking forward to his break.

"A few holidays, spend some time with the wife and the grandkids, that kind of thing."

World.title: Darwin soccer club helps migrants find community and a place to call home
World.content:
When Kaung Zayar-Thaw kicked a soccer ball for the first time at age 13, he was displaced in Thailand.

His father, Zaw Zaw Htoo, had been a member of Myanmar's parliament with the National League for Democracy and in 2021, the military junta seized their home in a military coup.

The family was forced to make the dangerous journey into Thailand, hiding in a forest for several days in fear of being caught and deported.

Zaw Zaw Htoo in front of the shelter where the family lived after fleeing Myanmar in 2021. (Picture: Supplied)

Soon after arriving in Thailand, Kaung said he spotted some people kicking a ball around and was intrigued.

From there, the so-called "world game" went on to play a role in helping him cope with adversity.

"Football is the only thing that helped me get through stuff," he says.

Kaung Zayar-Thaw says playing soccer helps him to cope with life's challenges. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

When he arrived in the Top End in 2024, Kaung joined the Darwin Olympic Sporting Club, where his teammates helped him practise his English as well as soccer.

Now 15, Kaung plays as a defender for Darwin Olympic, and he says football has become much more than a sport.

"Football is the only way out of things when I'm under stress from all the pressure from the schoolwork and stuff," he says.

The team train together and discuss football strategies at Darwin's Malak Oval. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"It's fun, and it just teaches me how to … communicate with my teammates.

" My teammates help me. I just feel [like I] belong, [and] I really like being a part of this Olympic team. "

A club shaped by migration

The Darwin Olympic Sporting Club was founded in 1967 by Greek migrants to the city as a place for their community to come together through soccer.

Almost 60 years later, the club has grown into a multicultural community representing more than 30 nationalities.

Yianni Prouzos says soccer brings together people from all over the world. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Club president Yianni Prouzos believes the club's home base in Darwin's multicultural northern suburbs has made it a natural meeting place for migrant communities.

"Football is the world's most common language," Yianni says.

"You come here, you don't have to speak the same language — you just have to know how to kick the ball and pass the ball."

Yianni, who moved to Australia as a child, says migrants now contribute to the club well beyond the playing pitch.

For these Darwinites, their soccer club is about so much more than sport. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"We've got a lot of our migrants that come and help us," he said.

"Every person has different experiences, has different cultures … so what do they bring? Knowledge."

A family starting again

After a period of uncertainty, Kaung's mother, Kyi Kyi Nwe, says the family has felt safe since arriving in Darwin, but that adjusting to their new home has been challenging.

Kaung Zayar-Thaw and his mother Kyi Kyi Nwe now call Darwin home. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"The difficulty we faced is that people speak a different language, culture, and the food is really difficult for us," she said.

But football has given the family a reason to get involved in the community.

"When we are seen in the community engaging with others in activities, it makes us feel that we're involved in the community and part of the community as well," Kyi says.

According to Charles Darwin University senior lecturer Devaki Monani, Darwin's small and diverse population can make those connections easier to build.

Devaki Monani says Darwin is a multicultural city and sport is critical to connecting new migrants with their communities. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"You can actually really get a multicultural experience and … you're not excluded," she said.

"Sport has great potential in connecting communities and breaking down those language and political barriers.

"In a place like Darwin, sporting activities are critical for families to engage with other families, whether migrants or not."

Soccer brings sense of belonging

Football Northern Territory chief executive Jaime Monteith says for many migrants, their first preference when it comes to sport is soccer.

He says the game can give people a sense of belonging while also opening doors to volunteering, coaching and refereeing.

Jaime Monteith says soccer can open doors to involvement for a wide range of people. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"What it does is it breaks down barriers, breaks down the ability for new arrivals, migrants, to find a home or a sense of belonging," Jaime says.

For Kaung's family, those connections are helping to turn Darwin from somewhere they arrived into somewhere they can call home.

Kyi Kyi Nwe, Kaung Zayar-Thaw and Zaw Zaw Htoo are all part of Darwin's soccer community. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"We are trying our best to look after each other and be welcoming and make this place our home," Kyi Kyi Nwe said.

World.title: Aussie athletics star shocked at massive pay packet for coming second
World.content:
Nicola Olyslagers has had the best bad night of her career after missing out on becoming a new 'Ultimate' athletics high jump champion, only to learn to her surprise that she had still leapt to the biggest payday of her life.

Australia's world champion only managed to clear 1.95m on the first night of World Athletics' inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest this morning (AEST).

She struggled with her approach on a difficult surface on a cold night as Ukraine's Olympic champ Yaroslava Mahuchikh beat her to the title with a 1.99m leap.

Olyslagers' runner-up spot earned her $US75,000 ($105,000) — $5,000 more than she pocketed for winning the world title last year — as part of the record $US10 million ($14 million) prize pot for the streamlined new event that World Athletics hopes will attract a host of new fans.

Only when speaking to reporters afterwards did Olyslagers realise just what she would be taking home.

Nicola Olyslagers clears the bar on her way to second in the high jump. (Getty Images: Christel Saneh/World Athletics)

"What? Really? I genuinely thought it was just first prize got the 150k and second was like 10,000," she said.

"You are the bearer of good news. That's fantastic."

Olyslagers, wrapped in a scarf and still shivering 40 minutes after her event, said she struggled with her approach on a firm-surface run-up but, with more than half the field exiting early, she realised that after two fails at 1.95 a clearance would be enough for second place.

She duly sailed over at the final attempt, punching the air in delight.

"That's the happiest I've ever been after a 1.95. I think I celebrated as if I'd won the whole competition and it was a really good jump," she said.

"It just showed tonight that all of us were a little bit tired but I mean, that 95 jump, I'm still living off that."

Olyslagers' domestic rival Eleanor Patterson also looked uncomfortable all evening but took joint third with a modest clearance of 1.91 a week after she'd jumped 10cm higher to win the Diamond League crown.

"It's the lowest I've jumped all year. Really, really frustrating," Commonwealth champ Patterson said.

"After the best season of my life I really wanted to enjoy it but I didn't really."

Marschall fourth as Duplantis stars again

Meanwhile, triple Commonwealth pole vault champion Kurtis Marschall managed only fourth with a best of 5.95m as Swedish superstar Armand Duplantis again revelled in being the star attraction, having seen the event open with a theme song he had both co-written and performed.

With the title secure after a faultless run to 6.20m, the spellbound full house of 20,000 willed him to clear a world record 6.32, but he narrowly failed in what would have been a remarkable 16th world best in six years.

Earlier, Australia's Ky Robinson gave it a real go in the 5,000m, leading at the bell, but got swallowed up in the run for home as Norway's Jakob Ingebrigtsen roared back to his best with a superbly-judged victory charge.

Sarah Billings ran well in her 800m semi-final to qualify for tomorrow's final when there will be four more Australians in action.

Abbey Caldwell and Jess Hull will go in the women's 1,500m, Mackenzie Little in the javelin and Oceania record holder Lachlan Kennedy in the men's 100m.

World.title: Academy alumni take to big stage together in Roosters finals tilt
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Academy alumni take to big stage together in Roosters finals tilt Chris Barrett September 12, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In the block of units they called home as teenagers, Siua Wong, Robert Toia, Salesi Foketi and Benaiah Ioelu usually just ate with each other. But now and then, there was a high-powered guest list at the Sydney Roosters academy housing in Kingsford. Benaiah Ioelu, Robert Toia, Salesi Foketi and Siua Wong have come through the ranks together. James Brickwood “At least once a month not only Nick [Politis] but the whole board would come over for dinner,” said back-rower Wong. “It was pretty cool having that relationship. A lot of us young boys moving from outside of Sydney coming in, hearing about the board, you feel a bit nervous. But for them to be so down to earth and express a lot of humility to get to know some of the young boys was something that I really loved.



“I think that’s one of the big values of this club, being a family club, and it definitely showed through that.” Several years after those evenings hosting club chairman Politis, and fellow directors such as Mark Bouris and Luke Ricketson, the quartet is in the big time as the Roosters’ semi-finals campaign gets going. Wong was the first graduate of the academy and made his NRL debut in 2023. Getty Images Wong, 23, Toia, 22, and Foketi, 20 are in the starting side for Sunday’s clash against minor premiers Penrith at CommBank Stadium. Ioelu, 22, is a reserve. Their appearance together at the pointy end of the season is validation of the Roosters’ decision to establish an academy in 2021 after visiting the facilities of Spanish football giants Barcelona FC.



Determined to produce more of their own, the eastern suburbs club can also count homegrown Roosters Hugo Savala, Victor Radley and Billy Smith in the line-up against the Panthers. The graduates emerged from a carefully designed program engineered by Politis and Roosters coach Trent Robinson and led by three-time premiership winners and one-club servants Mitchell Aubusson and Jake Friend. Foketi has made his mark on the edge for the Roosters in his second season in the top grade. Getty Images The grand plan is for the entire Roosters squad to eventually be comprised of players from their development system. “The dream is to one day have 17 players playing on the paddock that have come through our academy. So to have all those boys play on the weekend is great,” said Friend, a defence guru with the Roosters who was the academy’s inaugural head coach.



“We don’t have a big junior base obviously but with the guys we get, we want to breed long-term NRL players.” The former dummy-half said with potentially three teams joining the NRL over the next three seasons, it was even more important for clubs to grow their own and retain them. Toia makes a break against North Queensland in round 22. Getty Images Underpinning the Roosters’ approach is an attention to detail aimed at forging a lasting association with the tri-colours. From dinners with the board in the academy units, to nutrition advice from champion fullback Anthony Minichiello and one-on-one video sessions with Friend and Aubusson, now the Roosters rugby league director, the first batch of academy alumni learned from the best. “You look at the soccer academies, they’re a business in a sense. You develop a player and you get a transfer fee,” Friend said.



Related Article NRL 2026 ‘I love the Sharks’: From boyhood fan to Cronulla’s billionaire backer “You don’t get that in rugby league. They do have an ability to leave. But we’ve seen some guys probably have the opportunity to leave and stay. I think that’s got to do with the Roosters academy. We want to keep as many of them as we can.” Wong, who was scouted by the Roosters in Auckland at the age of 14 and has been a mainstay in Robinson’s side for the past two seasons, said on the eve of the finals his time in the academy was one of the best experiences of his life. “Nick, Aubbo and Jake Friend set up a great environment for us boys to develop and I think it’s shown through the footy players that we’ve been able to become,” he said. “It really instilled in me what it is to be a Rooster, and what that means on the field and off the field, and I feel like that’s so important for young players coming through.”



It also left a lasting mark on Toia, who has since become a Queensland State of Origin centre. “When we moved out was when we realised how great we had it,” he said. “Being there, you could tell how much the Roosters care.”

World.title: BBL sell-off plans will be on the right side of history
World.content:
SportCricketBig Bash Opinion BBL sell-off plans will be on the right side of history

Colin Smith September 12, 2026 — 9:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cricket NSW’s negative commentary on Big Bash League clubs privatisation plans suggests it will threaten the system, risks long-lasting impacts at all levels and endangers a model that is “the envy of the world.” While it is concerning rhetoric, it is also, on the evidence, not supported by facts and backs the wrong side of history. Cricket Australia chair Mike Baird defended the privitisation move for the Twenty20 franchises. George Chan Strip away the emotion, and Cricket Australia’s case for external investment in the clubs is straightforward and offers an exciting path that ensures global leadership in growing TV audiences (and hence media rights) and attendances. Critically, it also reinforces Test cricket. BBL and TV audiences have grown significantly following CA’s decision in 2023–24 to cut the BBL to 44 games.



However, fielding Australia’s centrally contracted stars in the league is a challenge. The salary pool intended to keep Australia’s best players at home has been increased from $1.9 million to more than $3 million per squad. That’s just to remain competitive with emerging leagues in South Africa and the United Arab Emirates — competitions that didn’t exist five years ago and can potentially outbid the BBL for Australian players. It helps to be clear about what “cricket” now includes because the debate is too often framed as T20 eroding the “real” game. The success of the Indian Premier League has given cricket financial security. AP It isn’t. Even the Board of Control for Cricket in India — an organisation with every incentive to focus on T20 — calls Test cricket “the bedrock of our game” and backs it with a financial incentive scheme for players who prioritise red-ball cricket. Modern cricket is a dual-format sport: Tests supply history and depth, and T20 provides the commercial engine that funds the lot. Since the Indian Premier League’s 2008 launch, T20 has grown.



Sixteen leagues operate worldwide, 87 nations entered qualification for the 2026 T20 World Cup cycle, and cricket (T20) will return to the Olympics in 2028 at Los Angeles after a 128-year absence. Not coincidentally, India is a favoured bidder for the 2036 Olympics. No comparably short, spectator-friendly format in any other sport has built anything like it. But none has become a standalone financial engine for its parent sport the way T20 funds cricket. A huge crowd celebrated 2014 IPL champions Kolkata Knight Riders in Kolkata, India. Getty That’s the opportunity NSW is arguing Australian cricket should avoid. The IPL is worth roughly $18.5 billion, built almost entirely on media rights.



Another perspective Investigation

Australian soccer How A-League’s biggest investor got a $140m get out of jail free card It sits within the world’s top 10 sports leagues by value and holds the sixth-highest sports broadcast rights value globally. IPL club owners have gone shopping abroad - Reliance, GMR, RPSG, Sun Group - because there’s only one Mumbai Indians licence at home. South Africa sold its entire domestic T20 competition to those same IPL groups in 2022 and has recorded broadcast growth of up to 47 per cent locally and 257 per cent in Indian media reach. England sold 49 per cent stakes in each of its eight franchises in The Hundred league for more than £500 million, keeping counties in majority control and ring-fencing 10 per cent for the grassroots. None of these boards let in outside capital out of desperation. They let it in because they could see where T20’s value was heading and who controlled the playbook to get there.



In all cases, these countries own their T20 leagues, with investors and shareholders in the clubs. NSW’s counter-argument is that its model works — the Sixers and Thunder are “successful and healthy,” profits are reinvested, and participation among 5-to-12-year-olds is up 80 per cent. All true, but this sidesteps the question of whether a wholly state-owned model can fund an escalating global talent-salary war for the next decade. In Australia, there are four sports leagues that are “must-haves” and “must-broadcast” - the NRL, AFL, Australian Open tennis and cricket (Test and BBL). There are genuine governance lessons here. The A-Leagues took private equity money in 2021 while individual clubs slid towards insolvency. But the lesson isn’t “don’t sell” — it’s “don’t sell vaguely”.



Editor's pick Australian cricket Sell off the BBL, or sell out to sports betting: Cricket’s huge call Money without a mechanism to enforce disciplined use just buys time, not a turnaround. The ECB’s Hundred sale is that template because it embeds discipline: tiered distribution, a grassroots share, and spending guardrails for the counties. None of this makes privatisation risk-free, or Cricket Australia’s process above reproach — NSW’s complaint is that four conditions agreed by all state chairs in June went unmet before the CA Board pressed ahead. But a complaint about process isn’t a case against the substance, and on the substance the global evidence is clear: leagues combining private capital for the BBL clubs only with disciplined guardrails are growing broadcast value and building the star power that keeps players and crowds in the BBL, not lost overseas. Cricket Australia chair Mike Baird and CEO Todd Greenberg address the media pack in Sydney this week. Getty Images



Importantly, investing in the BBL clubs ensures that the exciting growth and professionalisation of women’s BBL continue – as is happening with WPL in India. Cricket NSW built the two most successful clubs in the competition’s history. It should be shaping this conversation from a position of strength, rather than resisting it. With the likely sale of the Melbourne Renegades to external investors, NSW will be the sole owner of two clubs in the BBL. Furthermore, there is no example globally across leading sports leagues of a single owner of two clubs in the same league. Colin Smith of Global Media and Sports has spent two decades advising the world’s biggest sports and media rights holders and broadcasters on sports media rights, including cricket media rights and design models for the BBL.

World.title: ‘It’s the Wild West’: How a shaken Sydney is grappling with the gang war
World.content:
NationalNSWSydney's ganglands ‘It’s the Wild West’: How a shaken Sydney is grappling with the gang war Mostafa Rachwani September 12, 2026 — 9:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ahmad Hraichie has buried many gangsters in his time as a Muslim undertaker. He’s buried small time runners, heads of crime families and everyone in between. He knows death and its sudden movements well. But even he is shaken by the escalating gangland violence in western Sydney. Muslim undertaker Ahmad Hraichie says the community is “frustrated” at inaction on gang violence. Sitthixay Ditthavong “There were rules before: you don’t shoot innocent people, you don’t shoot kids or women, you don’t shoot at funerals,” he says. “It’s wild now, there are no rules.” “Yeah, it’s gangsters, but gangsters once had ethics and morals and integrity. They’d help an old lady on the street.



“Now it’s brazen, it’s lawless, like the Wild West.” Hraichie is speaking at the Muslim morgue under Lakemba Mosque where Louis Meehan was washed and prepared for burial on Saturday, as per the strict Islamic protocols on death. A body must be washed, wrapped in a white shroud, prayed over and buried as soon as possible, part of a broader Islamic belief in death being a transition from life to the afterlife. Delays are seen as holding the soul back from moving to the next phase of existence. Meehan was shot dead behind his boxing gym in the Punchbowl Community Centre car park on Wednesday night, as community members and school students watched on.



He died under a hail of gunfire from an assailant who fled in a silver Lexus. Police believe the attack is linked to organised crime in western Sydney. Meehan had posted photos online wearing merchandise linked to the Alameddine crime gang, which is locked in a murderous war with rival gang the Coconut Cartel. Meehan’s killing was the third in a little over a week. University student Marco Tapia, 23, was shot dead in his bed in Glen Alpine on Tuesday last week. The next day, Joshua Macdonald, 40, was shot in the doorway of a Merrylands West home. Two men were arrested on Friday in connection with that shooting, including an alleged drone operator. In the two years to June, 19 people died amid escalating violence, a Herald analysis found, including 100 shootings and 52 firebombings. The violence has coalesced into a haze that hangs over western Sydney, a dread looming over a region that has known violence before but not like this. “It’s getting worse, and it is driven by many factors, including the intoxicating draw of social media and the internet,” Hraichie says. “It’s brazen now. People are doing it in the middle of the day, and part of that is the internet.



“The world has become so fast and people are struggling. And to these kids, it’s all about the lifestyle, the haircuts, the cars, the money. It’s all about living in this moment, right now, no future. “It’s an alien world,” he says, shaking his head. Like many in western Sydney, Hraichie has seen different eras of gang violence break out. There were the gangland wars of the 1980s, the postcode wars of the late 2010s, the feud between the Hamzy and Alameddine families. Muslim undertaker Ahmad Hraichie says gang violence is a “cancer”. Sitthixay Ditthavong With a regional robustness charged by generations of migrants from wartorn backgrounds who won’t be shaken by much, the violence remained for a while as cultural background noise, shrugged at and ignored.



But it has since spilled out into community spaces, into daylight, and into the cultural consciousness with brazen acts. As more innocent people die than ever before, Hraichie says frustration is growing at a lack of action from authorities. “There isn’t fear, there’s frustration,” he says. “I don’t think fear is part of the equation or vocabulary for these parts. But people are frustrated: why haven’t these guys been stopped?” That sense of frustration hardly abated when acting Assistant Police Commissioner Grant Taylor said on Thursday that gangland shootings were “part and parcel of life in a big metropolis”. “It always looks like crime is out of control but, when you look at it, we’re on track,” Taylor said.



“We always have about eight organised crime murders a year. We’ve had six, and then last night made seven. It’s always going to be part and parcel of life in a big metropolis; this is no different.” The comments were swiftly shot down by Premier Chris Minns, who said the violence was shocking and the community “shouldn’t have to put up with” it. Related Article Exclusive

NSW State Parliament Gangland violence threatens Labor’s grip on outer Sydney “I’d hate it for anyone to believe that we’re accepting of the status quo, or we believe that it’s normal, or that it’s acceptable, or that we just have to turn a blind eye,” Minns said. “I don’t think any premier or any political leader can ever make the claim or promise that murder will stop in a big state like NSW, but we can promise arrests, and we can promise longer jail time for the people who are involved.”



Criminologist Dr Vincent Hurley, who spent 23 years as a NSW Police detective, said that if the violence was not curbed soon, it could start to have lasting cultural consequences. “The names that they adopt almost set in train this narrative that tarnishes the rest of the community,” he said. Related Article Editorial

Crime Authorities must get their acts together on organised-crime killings The Herald's View Editorial “I think the frustration is that it seems to be every day, all day, and that’s probably not the case. And I think they find it frustrating because people stereotype them. It wears them down over time, and people can’t break away from their surname, from their culture.” Hurley warned that without urgent intervention, communities could become insular and pull away from the rest of Sydney, culturally and economically.



“They’re going to bunker down and become very protective of themselves, and it’ll be us versus them, even if they’re not involved in any type of crime,” he said. “Just by the mere fact of stereotyping, it’s going to have a massive effect on kids at school, who then want to go out and get a job; they probably won’t leave that geographic area. These areas will become siloed. “Ultimately, I really feel sorry for the community members of these cultural groups because they have no control over the narrative.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Tom Lynagh is Australian rugby’s biggest enigma. Can he be a saviour, too?
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Opinion Tom Lynagh is Australian rugby’s biggest enigma. Can he be a saviour, too? Iain Payten Senior Sports Reporter September 12, 2026 — 7:52am

September 12, 2026 — 7:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There won’t be a huge audience for the opening game of Super Rugby AUS early on Saturday afternoon, when Queensland host the Western Force at Ballymore. But those rugby-hungry types who do tune into Stan Sport will be watching intently – and none more so than Wallabies coach Les Kiss, who has problems to resolve before naming an updated squad on Monday for Tests against the Springboks and the All Blacks. Loading He’ll be assessing whether Jock Campbell is worth recalling to replace Tom Wright, and he’ll keep tabs on Zac Lomax’s return from injury, in the fascinating position of No.13 for the Force. But mostly Kiss will be on his couch studying the men duelling in the No.10 jerseys: Tom Lynagh and Harry McLaughlin-Phillips.



Some fingers may be crossed. The Wallabies need another five-eighth to join the squad after Carter Gordon broke his leg in Mendoza. Carter Gordon (R) broke his leg Test against the Pumas in Mendoza. Getty Images Ben Donaldson and Declan Meredith are in the squad, but both have failed to claim the No.10 jersey this year, so filling Gordon’s vacancy isn’t necessarily just for a third-cab-off-the-rank player. It could be for the top job, if the right man stands up. Setting aside the experienced options of James O’Connor and Bernard Foley – who haven’t trained in a team environment for a few months – and Japan-based Noah Lolesio, who is not available in October under regulation 9, the here-and-now candidates boil down to Lynagh, McLaughlin-Phillips and Tane Edmed.



The latter played 10 Tests last year but is now down the pecking order behind Meredith, Donaldson and McLaughlin-Phillips, who was also called into the Wallabies squad last month ahead of him. But McLaughlin-Phillips, a running No.10, is a developing youngster you’d select as a third cab. Lynagh is not, and if he can prove his fitness, the Reds playmaker has the class to not only return to the Wallabies but to become the assertive game controller the side badly needs. Tom Lynagh has had a nightmare run of injuries with the Wallabies and Reds. Getty Images But all of that comes with a very big if. Hence, the crossed fingers. Lynagh has played just 17 minutes this year, after suffering a string of soft-tissue injuries dating back to this time last year, when he tore a hamstring playing for the Wallabies against Argentina.



Lynagh was not considered for the spring tour so that he could have an off-season to get stronger and more physically resilient. It didn’t have the desired effect. Lynagh suffered repeated tears of the soleus (lower calf) muscle throughout the Super Rugby season. Wallabies five-eighth Tom Lynagh pictured in Coogee last year. Dion Georgopoulos The long absence, combined with a lack of public information about Lynagh’s status, saw the odd conspiracy theory pop up, including that he didn’t even want to play rugby. They were all wrong – Lynagh re-signing with Queensland in May was proof of his desire – but as Reds coach, Kiss played the long-game and put Lynagh on a go-slow conditioning plan to build sufficient resilience in his body to get through full games, and full seasons. Lynagh put on five kilograms of muscle, but again, it didn’t fix the problems.



As the months dragged on, Lynagh suffered multiple setbacks with the injured calf, each time re-setting the comeback clock. Brilliant and brittle in equal parts, Lynagh is now Australian rugby’s biggest enigma. Though he is extremely tough in games and doesn’t shirk contact – as seen in the Lions series – Lynagh has also became known as a flighty trainer, who is hyper-aware of any tweak or injury niggle he feels in his body. One theory at Ballymore is that Lynagh’s past life as a schoolboy cricketer may have contributed to a propensity for back tightness.



Whatever the reason, a wary Lynagh often sat out sessions and could not complete a full week of training. Given Joe Schmidt rigidly demands as much to be selected, the blond No.10 fell out of the Wallabies reckoning. Edmed, a no-frills but durable type, was called up, and Gordon was also poached back from league (only to also start picking up injuries). This year, the Wallabies’ long-standing problem at No.10 hasn’t gone away. If anything, it has become more acute. Harry McLaughlin-Phillips trained with the Wallabies in Perth in July. Getty Images The Wallabies’ forwards have improved hugely but the backline’s work - and game management in particular - has gone the other way. Ryan Lonergan has been outstanding at halfback but the work of several options at No.10 has been B-grade. The Wallabies’ ability to exit their half via the boot has been mostly dire this year, and the game direction has gone from mediocre to muddled as Tests have worn on.



It comes with a very obvious fitness caveat, but Lynagh at his best presents as the solution: a tough, long-kicking five-eighth, with a strong voice and the heads-up composure to run a game. Related Article NRL 2026 PNG Chiefs in war over name as NZ Rugby threatens legal action So getting Lynagh back on the field and keeping him there is the name of the game. If any coach can do it, it’d be Kiss, who managed him effectively in the first half of 2025. If Kiss can get Lynagh back into that same shape and mindset, the 23-year-old could be a key factor in the Wallabies’ campaign at the Rugby World Cup. “I’m really enjoying Tom in a playmaker role and a decision-maker within the team,” new Reds coach Vern Cotter said this week. “He’s got a great head on his shoulders. He sees the game well. He’s calm and decisive, so I’m looking forward to having him run the game for us.”



Just to be “careful”, Cotter said he’ll give Lynagh 40 minutes at Ballymore and then everyone will wait and see how he pulls up. There may be crossed fingers.

World.title: Police conduct welfare checks after dozens of Triple Zero calls fail due to Optus outage
World.content:
Updated NationalVictoriaEmergency services Police conduct welfare checks after dozens of Triple Zero calls fail due to Optus outage James Costa Updated September 12, 2026 — 7:01am ,first published 9:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dozens of Triple Zero calls struggled to connect to the Telstra national emergency line because of an Optus outage on Friday, Triple Zero Victoria says. “Just before 7pm, Optus has provided details of 39 calls that experienced difficulty connecting to the Telstra national Triple Zero (000) emergency call person,” Triple Zero Victoria chief operations officer Paul Santamaria said. Optus confirmed an outage on Friday afternoon. Getty Images Victoria Police confirmed on Saturday morning its officers had completed about 40 welfare checks on affected callers across Victoria following the outage. “There were no adverse outcomes or issues of note,” a police spokesman said.



Earlier on Friday, Optus confirmed it became aware of an outage at “approximately 1.30pm AEST and immediately mobilised technical teams and restored services as quickly as possible”. Optus confirmed later on Friday evening that the outage lasted for one hour and 16 minutes, and affected some customers in Victoria, South Australia, Tasmania and the Northern Territory. The telco said that a network issue resulted in intermittent call dropouts, and it had referred failed calls to police for welfare checks. “We are still determining whether calls were able to connect to a different network and this will be established in coming days,” an Optus spokesperson said. The Tasmanian Department of Police, Fire and Emergency Management said Optus had advised it of an outage that affected three Triple Zero calls in Tasmania.



“Police subsequently contacted the callers, and it was determined they did not require immediate police or emergency services,” the department said. Related Article Updated

Telecommunications Optus sued over Triple Zero outage linked to two deaths Some Optus customers took to social media earlier in the day, stating they had lost service or were unable to make or receive calls. Optus sent a text message to customers saying that in Victoria, South Australia, the Northern Territory and Tasmania, “Optus has loss of coverage due to this outage”. “Emergency service calls can be accessed where other mobile provider coverage is available or are able to call via Wi-Fi,” the text message said.



In July, Australia’s communications regulator sued Optus over last year’s Triple Zero outage, alleging the telco failed to connect emergency calls on 1005 occasions and exposing it to penalties of more than $500 million. The Australian Communications and Media Authority filed civil penalty proceedings in the Federal Court against Optus Mobile over the September 18 outage, when a bungled firewall upgrade blocked calls to Triple Zero across South Australia, Western Australia, the Northern Territory and far west NSW for about 13 hours. The outage was linked to two deaths. With Ashleigh McMillan Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: They’re an AFL powerhouse. So why can’t Collingwood’s women’s team find success?
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFLW They’re an AFL powerhouse. So why can’t Collingwood’s women’s team find success? Hannah Kennelly September 12, 2026 — 6:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For nearly four quarters, Collingwood captain Ruby Schleicher was on the verge of an unwanted statistical milestone. With just three minutes left in last weekend’s game against Carlton, her career-high personal tally of three goals and four behinds would ordinarily have been cause for celebration. But the disappointing fact for Schleicher and her Magpies was that she had contributed 100 per cent of her team’s score. Ruby Schleicher during Collingwood’s clash with Carlton Getty Images Teammate Georgia Knight offered a reprieve with a behind, followed by a goal to Dominique Carbone, which made the 39-point loss to the undefeated Blues sting a little less. To put the loss in perspective, the injury-marred Pies were missing key players, including last-minute drop-outs from star Ash Centra and Jemma Rigoni and were facing Carlton – a team that made finals last year and will likely to do the same in 2026.



Still, Sunday’s defeat marks their fourth consecutive loss —a streak that, compounded by several years of poor results, should be sounding alarm bells at Collingwood headquarters. In 2019, this masthead published a piece, titled ‘What’s wrong with Collingwood’s AFLW side’, which examined the club’s poor performance after high-profile players Jasmine Garner, Moana Hope, Emma King and Jess Duffin defected to North Melbourne during W’s rapid expansion period. Collingwood coach Sam Wright and his team. AFL Photos At the time, critics questioned the Pies list management, draft and recruiting strategy. Staff turnover was also cited as a concern, after the club had employed three women’s football operations managers in three years. That was seven years ago. Even the brightest of optimists and diehard Pies fans would concede not enough has changed since then.



Collingwood are currently second-last on the ladder and – like Essendon, St Kilda and West Coast – yet to record a win ahead of their match on Saturday against Gold Coast at People First Stadium. Related Article AFL 2026 Jeremy Howe changed his mind on retirement. Now his mate’s daughter is a Collingwood clubmate So why single Collingwood out, when three other clubs have the same 0-4 start? Essendon, St Kilda and West Coast entered AFLW at later stages of the competition, with the latter two reaching finals for the first time last year. Collingwood are one of the inaugural teams of the competition, but – despite showing glimpses of promise – seem to have gone backwards.



Their first and only preliminary final was in 2021 against the Brisbane Lions, followed by a semi-final appearance in 2022. Since then, Collingwood have finished 11th in 2023, last in 2024 and 15th in 2025 with only three wins. Collingwood should be a successful AFLW club. They have up-to-date facilities and a strong history of success in the men’s program, plus a large membership pool to tap into. View post on X The Pies have also been adamant they are improving. Coach Sam Wright told media after their round 12 loss in 2025 the Pies would have a “tough and prescriptive” off-season. “While we only got the three wins this year, we don’t feel like we are far away from progressing,” he added. So why can’t Collingwood’s AFLW program find success?



The club has had steady leadership over the past few years, poaching Wright from North Melbourne in 2023 and promoting highly regarded performance analyst Jess Burger to general manager of women’s football in 2024. Burger and Collingwood declined to comment for this article. However, support from Collingwood’s upper echelons has been less straightforward and more cautious. Collingwood CEO Craig Kelly has been publicly and privately vocal about the financial risks of expanding the AFLW program. Collingwood Football Club chief executive Craig Kelly. AAP Last year, the AFL met with all 18 clubs for a conference exploring the priorities for the future of the AFLW for its 10-year anniversary. Columnist Caroline Wilson, reported Kelly urged the league to consider the heavy cost of expanding the AFLW competition too quickly, arguing the game should not invest too heavily in the women’s competition at the expense of upgrading the MCG, creating better facilities for the game across Australia and improving the AFL experience for fans. AFLW commentator Chyloe Kurdas said it was important for clubs to remember the women’s game was still “playing catch-up” to the men’s – a chase that requires investment in staffing, resources and most importantly mindset.



“I can’t speak specifically about Collingwood, but I think what is a problem is that not all 18 clubs have got a consistent mindset across the whole club of the value of the women’s program and the level of investment that’s required to ensure that there’s success in it” she said. Kurdas – a former AFL Victoria football development manager – said the most successful AFLW clubs established cultures that the best players wanted to be a part of, pointing to the long-term success of Brisbane, Adelaide and reigning premiers North Melbourne. View post on X “You can throw lots of money at a program, but if it’s not part of your heart and soul, and ... you don’t believe in its capability, then it doesn’t matter how much money you spend,” she said. From a list perspective, Collingwood are lacking key players in their forward line. The Pies have consistently struggled to find a consistent path to goal, arguably since Chloe Molloy’s departure in 2022. Superstar Molloy signed with the Sydney on a five-year-deal – the longest contract in the history of the competition.



After receiving a list assistance package from the AFL Commission in 2025 – including two additional spots for the 2026 season and one for 2027 – Collingwood’s list went under an extensive turnover Eleven players left the program and 13 new players were introduced; including delisted free argent Jemma Rigoni and two cross-code Super Netball players Maisie Nankivell and Olivia Lewis. The recruits have helped build versatility and height in Collingwood’s list, but the Magpies still lack experienced players in their forward line. Through the 2025 draft, the Pies brought in six young players, injecting a noticeable boost of energy into their side. But it’s also left the overall playing group relatively inexperienced and young. Kurdas said, while Collingwood’s young players looked exciting and the team had shown some improvement this year, the Pies needed to recruit more A-grade quality players.



“Collingwood probably just don’t have enough depth of mature-age elite level talent, and they need more of those in each zone,” she said. There’s also concern about Collingwood ability to retain senior players. The club has strong leadership from veteran captain Schleicher, but it’s worth noting she and a number of senior players come out of contract this year. Collingwood coach Sam Wright is in his third year as senior coach. Getty Images Schleicher has been offered a deal, but is yet to sign, while, Tarni White, Sarah Rowe, Mattea Breed, Lauren Butler and Bri Davey are others coming out of contract. Vice-captain Jordyn Allen signed a three-year deal in 2024, but tried to seek a trade to Brisbane last year. After their loss to Carlton last weekend, Wright conceded the Pies were “under some duress from a list point of view with injuries”, but said there were opportunities for young players to step up.



When asked specifically by this masthead, what was missing from the Collingwood program and list, Wright said Collingwood were still working that out. “It certainly throws some challenges when you’ve got this many injuries to significant key players as well,” he said. “As a club, we are working through it right now, to put our finger on it, but certainly part of it is luck. But the other part [is] we want to be the best program we can be in that area, and we are working really hard. “In terms of list, it’s more around just continuing to get our processes right, push our processes.” Both Richmond and Carlton initiated comprehensive independent reviews into their AFLW’s programs after periods of poor performance. Carlton’s review in 2022 led to the departure of coach Daniel Harford and other key staff, while Richmond’s review at the end of 2025 prompted the departure of senior coach Ryan Ferguson.



Since then, Carlton have surged, playing in the finals last year and opening thisd season with four straight wins. It’s too early to examine Richmond’s progress, but the Tigers have got two wins on the board so far this season. Related Article AFL 2022 ‘A global reckoning is coming’: The toll of trolls on footballers No one can dispute Collingwood’s desire to get better. As Wright put in his press conference, “I think every player in our program and every staff member is committed to winning”. Kurdas said Collingwood have “the potential to be a great W side”, and said any club that wasn’t getting the success they wanted should consider evaluating their program. “The ability to self-reflect honestly; that’s a non-negotiable ingredient of being successful,” she said.
