World.title: Country Life: Would you drink milk from a vending machine?
World.content:
When it comes to milk, Tammy Acton-Adams is pretty particular.

"There are certain brands, and very popular brands, that we just don't even buy," she told Country Life.

"If we're away and we need milk, we won't even try them."

Tammy Acton-Adams pats Ira, one of the herd's friendliest cows. RNZ/Anisha Satya

A 24/7 milk machine: The Good Cow Country Life Download MP3 12m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

It needs to be creamy, but not so creamy it's no longer milk. Lucky for her, that's exactly the stuff she's milking from her small herd of dairy cows.

Acton-Adams shares the taste of raw milk with her community through The Good Cow, a 24/7 milk vending station on her North Canterbury farm near the Ashley river.

"Nothing's taken away. It's got all the goodies. It's got all the vitamins, all the minerals, prebiotics, probiotics. Everything's in there. It's 4.8 percent fat.

"And the taste is unbelievable; it's very rich. Even in your coffee, you can tell, it just makes it that wee bit creamier."

The beef, calving and contracting farmer first tried her hand at dairying to help out a former client.

"We had baled their hay for 20 years. Their grandson needed help, so he asked us to come over one afternoon to help milk the cows.

"I hadn't been in a cow shed since I was 15 - within 10 days he had gone, and so they asked us to take over."

Four years milking 120 cows - a sixth-generation Friesian pedigree herd - taught Acton-Adams a lot about the business.

Most of the 35 dairy cows who supply The Good Cow have names. RNZ/Anisha Satya

"When we finished farming [there], we had two cows left over.

"And we just thought, you know - we loved the taste of the milk. We just didn't like the idea of going back to supermarket milk."

Enter The Good Cow - a raw milk business supplied by Acton-Adams' 35-strong, mostly Friesian herd, which sells its milk on the farm.

The 9-aside herringbone milking system used to source The Good Cow's raw milk. RNZ/Anisha Satya

Cows are milked in a nine-aside herringbone shed. Just a few steps beyond the shed, the milk is stored in small vats and transferred to a vending machine.

Customers bring their empty milk bottles and pay $3.50 a litre for the unpasteurised milk.

The vending machine that pumps out The Good Cow's raw milk - just a few steps away from the milking shed. RNZ/Anisha Satya

As Acton-Adams' cows are all high producers, she also supplies some milk to Fonterra.

The Good Cow's raw milk gets tested every 10 days, to meet MPI standards for cell count and pathogens, like E coli.

"For raw milk your [cell count] has to be under 160, not allowed to sell anything over 320. We're quite lucky, we've got a good herd, and so it sits around that 60."

There are machine cleanliness standards and other requirements Acton-Adams has to meet the ensure the milk is safe for selling - but it's worth it to her.

"Other people do it for health reasons, and they're very passionate about the fact that it hasn't been pasteurised.

World.title: Educators back NCEA tweaks over overhaul
World.content:
Consultation has found strong support for improving the national school qualification, but many people are not convinced NCEA should be replaced.

Independent analysis of 8292 submissions to the Ministry of Education consultation on replacing NCEA said four out of five educators and industry submitters agreed the senior secondary qualifications system needed improvement.

But the consultant's document also showed many teachers, students and families said the qualification had more positives than negatives and should be refined rather than ditched.

The Government wants to replace NCEA with a new foundation certificate for Year 11 students in 2028, a Certificate of Education for Year 12s in 2029 and an Advanced Certificate of Education from Year 13s in 2030 with students required to study five full subjects and pass at least three to gain a certificate.

The analysis of submissions showed some submitters were enthusiastic about the prospect of change.

"The NCEA system, in its entirety, needs to be scrapped," wrote one student.

"Everything, no matter how many times it is explained, it makes absolutely no sense," a whānau submitter wrote of NCEA.

But others opposed the replacement.

"It's going backwards to the '90s system which was harder to achieve, and many failed," wrote a whānau submitter.

Just over half of teachers (54 percent) agreed NCEA did not consistently measure students' knowledge and skills and a similar percentage of industry respondents agreed the value of NCEA was difficult to understand.

Half of educator and whānau submissions supported replacing NCEA level 1 with a foundational award, about 60 percent of submitters supported a focus on completing full subjects, and 46 percent of educators, 56 percent of industry submitters and 49 percent of whānau agreed the Government's proposed changes would be an improvement.

Most students (61 percent) disagreed NCEA was hard to understand, but 49 percent of whānau agreed it was difficult.

But analysis of teachers' comments showed few supported the change whole-heartedly.

"Most educator submitters were concerned about the case for change, with few supporting the change overall," it said.

The document said many teachers suggested NCEA be refined rather than replaced.

"Many educator submitters reiterated that tweaks should be made to strengthen NCEA rather than a costly and resource-intensive overhaul of the whole senior secondary qualification education system," it said.

It said more educator submitters noted positive aspects of NCEA than negative aspects with 1711 negative comments and 4432 positive.

"Despite the recent rhetoric, NCEA is a high-quality qualification on par with other available qualifications, recognised and accepted here and internationally. It is an inclusive qualification - it allows young people to follow their areas of interest," said a teacher submitter.

The analysis of submissions said many educators praised NCEA's flexibility, the ability for students to study both academic and vocational subjects and the use of internal assessment.

"We think the new system should continue to use a combination of internal and external assessments. This mixed approach is essential because it allows for a balanced evaluation of a student's knowledge and skills," said a teacher.

But some teachers backed the proposed change.

"This is a great step forward," said one teacher.

They said NCEA's flexibility enabled credit-counting over real learning and some standards were easier than others despite being at the same NCEA level.

"I think the main issue I have with current NCEA is that some courses offer far more credits for less work when compared with others," said one teacher.

"There is a big difference between a student who has gained L3 with Achieved and taken academically rigorous subjects, compared to a student who has the same qualification but has taken much less academic subjects," said another.

Education Minister Erica Stanford. RNZ/Nick Monro

Teens, families want flexibility

The document said most whānau and students expressed concerns about the case for change and few thought replacing NCEA was necessary.

It said the group made 847 comments critical of NCEA and 2847 supportive comments.

"Submitters were concerned that changes to the senior secondary qualification system may result in a loss of the current system's flexibility, and would have an impact on vulnerable groups and to students' future pathways. Whānau and student submitters classified NCEA's flexibility and diversity as strengths," it said.

"However, other submitters raised concern with NCEA, namely a vague grading system, credit counting practice, difficulty understanding NCEA, and limited international comparability."

"I am very relieved that the country's education system is finally moving towards the right direction. Our children will not be placed at the bottom compared to other countries," wrote one whānau submitter.

"I disagree with the suggestion that the current system is overly confusing for parents and students. From my experience, once the NCEA structure-credit requirements, grading, and internal/external assessments-is clearly explained, it is straightforward to follow," said another whānau submitter.

Other submitters said NCEA's flexibility and use of internal assessment was a strength that helped neurodiverse students and others who might struggle with exams.

Industry shows conditional support for change

The document said industry submitters were unhappy with NCEA credit counting and poor consistency between schools, but worried about the potential loss of flexibility and impact on equitable outcomes from a change in the system.

"Some submitters emphasised that current NCEA records do not clearly demonstrate whether students are ready for work. Submitters from construction and trades sectors particularly emphasised this concern, noting that they need clear indicators of student capability in core areas such as literacy, numeracy, and practical problem-solving," the document said.

"NCEA is impossible to interpret as to what skills a student actually has," said one industry submission.

"Students are arriving into the workforce with poor basic skills/knowledge," said another.

But others supported NCEA's flexibility and use of internal assessment.

"The system's flexibility is not the problem; it's a feature that must be protected," an industry submitter said.

File image. RNZ / Richard Tindiller

Teachers defend NCEA

The document said some educator submitters disagreed with suggestions NCEA was confusing and unreliable.

"The presentation of NCEA as a system that fails to assess a student's understanding of the New Zealand curriculum is irresponsible, damaging and inaccurate in our opinion," said one educator.

"Parents not knowing the technical details does not mean NCEA lacks clarity or value, nor that employers and tertiary providers fail to recognise its worth. Schools already run NCEA information evenings, but low attendance points to engagement rather than system failure," said another.

Some submitters challenged the suggestion that NCEA was not internationally credible.

"Particularly damaging is the claim that the NCEA lacks international credibility. This baseless allegation is accurately countered by NZQA's own tagline which states, 'We make sure New Zealand qualifications are recognised and respected, here and overseas, and that qualifications and credentials meet the needs of learners in the changing world,'" wrote one.

The document said some submitters worried the changes would disadvantage Māori and Pacific learners and those with different learning needs.

They also said the Government should give more consideration to Treaty of Waitangi obligations.

"A significant concern is the visible absence of Mātauranga Māori and Te Tiriti o Waitangi in the proposed changes. Any reform of national qualifications must be grounded in Te Tiriti obligations and genuinely reflect Aotearoa New Zealand's bicultural foundations," a submitter wrote.

The consultation document asked submitters if the school qualification should assess against a national curriculum, but some teachers said that was a bad question.

"The first question is terrible. Being forced to answer a question which nobody would disagree with (we should assess against the curriculum) and using that as a justification to change the whole system of NCEA is manipulative. In my experience NCEA does assess against a national curriculum. My level of agreement with the statement is not support for change," wrote one educator.

The document said teachers made 2862 comments suggesting priorities for improvement, including more consistency in assessments and a better balance between internal and external assessment.

"Schools are drowning in AI plagiarism without the tools to accurately track and counter it. More external moderation is the only way that is going to change. It also removes bias from the process," said one educator.

Submitters including the Cook Islands Ministry of Education and Government of Niue said the changes needed to consider island nations that used New Zealand's curriculum and qualification framework.

"Cook Islands students must graduate with the same qualifications as New Zealand students, with no separate arrangements or delays… Realm Nations must receive curriculum, resources, and training simultaneously with NZ schools (from 2026) Our national language must be a recognised subject with its own curriculum and assessment design," the Cook Islands Ministry of Education said.

Some teachers were critical of developing a new qualification before new curriculums were complete.

"We are concerned that the current proposal reverses proper sequencing by advancing assessment changes before the curriculum development is complete. Assessment should follow and support curriculum, not drive it," said one submitter.

World.title: England has won 38 straight Tests but Wallaroos won't die wondering
World.content:
On paper, the Wallaroos aren't given a chance of beating England in this weekend's WXV Global Series Test.

The Red Roses, as England is known, are on a 38-match winning streak, stretching back to 2022.

They're reigning Women's Rugby World Cup winners and have claimed eight straight Six Nations titles, which include a run of five consecutive Grand Slams.

Why Wallaroos are 'family' Past and present Wallaroos players reflect on the journey and challenges to reaching 100 Tests.

England has never lost to the Wallaroos, with the most recent meeting — in last year's World Cup — finishing in a 47-7 victory to the tournament hosts in Bristol.

The Australians, though, aren't intimidated ahead of the Test in Salford, which will be played on Sunday morning, AEST.

They respect the Red Roses, but possess a quiet confidence in their ability to compete with the world champions.

"I think it will be a hard challenge," said Wallaroos winger Amelia Whitaker, who will make her Test debut.

"Obviously England [is] number one, but this week I feel like we've really rallied together so I think we're up for the task."

Amelia Whitaker will make her Test debut for the Wallaroos. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

Wallaroos reserve forward Jemma Bemrose, who could debut off the bench, was similarly undaunted.

"They've [Red Roses] got a strong reputation, and they've achieved a lot as a team," Bemrose said.

"But I'm just really excited to embrace the challenge."

Wallaroos assistant coach Mike Ruthven knows England's strengths, but he believed there might be a chink in the Red Roses' armour.

"They're a pretty complete footy team," Ruthven said.

"We know what's coming, but we think we've identified a few things that we've been really able to target and have a crack at."

Rugby's 'benchmark'

The Red Roses' status as the top-ranked nation in the world did not come by chance.

England's governing body, the Rugby Football Union (RFU), made a wise investment in the women's game when it offered full-time contracts to players in 2019.

The Red Roses now have 32 full-time contracted players for the 2026/27 season, with an additional six players on transition contracts.

England won last year's Women's Rugby World Cup on home soil. (Getty Images/World Rugby: Molly Darlington)

England's pathways haven't been ignored either, with the RFU boasting it's invested 14.5 million pounds ($27 million) in the community game.

The national team also benefits from a thriving club competition, Premiership Women's Rugby (PWR), which involves nine clubs playing 16 league matches each before a finals series is contested.

The RFU announced in June it's committing 24 million pounds ($45 million) to PWR across 10 years.

The Red Roses have been embraced by the English public, with 219,439 spectators attending their World Cup matches last year, including a global record of 81,885 at Twickenham when they beat Canada 33-13 in the final.

There was also a 336 per cent increase in TV viewing hours during the tournament, helping raise the visibility of the players amid England's crowded sporting landscape.

This is reflected in the fact that star back Ellie Kildunne finished runner-up in 2025's publicly voted BBC Sports Personality of the Year Award, outpolling the likes of Formula 1 world champion Lando Norris.

Ellie Kildunne is among the most recognisable figures in English sport. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

It's all food for thought for Rugby Australia (RA), which is shifting the Wallaroos to a full-time program ahead of the 2029 World Cup to be hosted on home soil.

Some positive steps have already been made, such as the appointment of successful rugby sevens coach Tim Walsh as RA's director of women's high performance.

Rugby Australia setting high standards Only three years out from hosting the Women's Rugby World Cup, Australia makes a key appointment it hopes will help deliver success on the international stage.

Australia has the playing and coaching talent to become a World Cup contender, but as Walsh recently acknowledged to ABC Sport, the Wallaroos must have the "infrastructure for them to be able to excel".

Ruthven, who is working under Walsh on the Wallaroos' staff until incoming coach Sione Fukofuka begins next year, rated England's program as the gold standard.

"The RFU have done a great job to support the women's game over here, underpinned by a really strong PWR competition," Ruthven said.

"You look at their players, and they're playing 20-odd competitive games of domestic football.

"You would like to think that is a bit of a benchmark. I think Rugby Australia are doing a really good job at the moment to … take the women's space to a similar level."

The Wallaroos are in the process of becoming a full-time program. (Getty Images: Phil Walter)

The Red Roses deserve to be the "benchmark" both on and off the field, and it's no surprise they're overwhelming favourites to win Sunday's Test, which is expected to be played in front of a sell-out crowd.

But as the Wallaroos squad have reminded themselves this week, it's a "two-horse race over 80 minutes".

"If we can go out and deliver on the things that we've talked about during the week and deliver on them consistently and compete really hard, stranger things have happened, right?" Ruthven said.

World.title: Lions' shock loss to Swans was about more than complacency
World.content:
Few pundits gave the Sydney Swans a chance of defeating the Brisbane Lions in last Saturday's qualifying final at the SCG.

Now the Swans have a week off and the Lions are one step away from a summer holiday.

The official line from the Lions after the game was one of complacency and players not taking the Swans seriously.

"I tried very hard this week to convince our players it was going to be a tough game," coach Chris Fagan told reporters after the match.

"We're going to the SCG. It's Sydney's home ground.

"But somewhere back in the deep recesses of their mind, I just wonder whether they really thought it was going to be as hard as what it was."

The key stats that could save Freo's finals After topping the AFL ladder for the majority of this season, Fremantle finds itself on the canvas and must overturn recent history to keep its premiership dream alive.

A lack of effort and complacency were quickly mentioned as scapegoats for the Lions' loss, while the Swans' resilient spirit was credited for the victory.

While complacency may have played a role, the indications are that the issues may sit a little bit deeper.

For the past half a decade, it has become routine for the Lions to hang cricket scores on opponents. The AFL's most effective and efficient attack has almost lulled the league itself into a sense of complacency.

But when Fagan started his rebuild at the Lions, the priority was the defensive end. Fagan saw that building their intercept marking ability and run out of defence was critical to how he saw the Lions being successful.

When you combine a dominant forward line with a dynamic back line, magic is likely.

With three straight grand finals and two premierships on the trot, few would argue against that recipe.

But over time the pure defensive side has slowly been de-prioritised to beef up their attacking focus. Against Sydney, it was possibly the biggest factor in the loss.

This Lions' season has hinted at a couple of issues not seen in previous years.

A run of injuries has forced a shuffle in defence. Against most teams it has been enough, but against the best attacks they have been found wanting.

The Lions' title defence — and their bid for a premiership three-peat — might just come apart at the hands of their own defence.

You can't stop the Lions

From sides who cleared out the forward line to those who won it in the guts, from defensive powerhouses to those who overwhelmed with speed, each side that sits atop the mountain for an extended period tends to shape the game.

For the Lions, the recipe to their success has largely been one of control and ruthless efficiency.

For each of their grand final years, they have been in the top two for clearance differential. Once they win the ball, they tend to sit near the top for uncontested marks as well, which is a measure of how well they move the ball around the ground.

Once they move it to their forward line, the Lions just know how to score. Even as the personnel in the forward line have changed, the offensive result has stayed the same.

A big part of their success comes in transition: how they attack you from the back. Their kick-mark style picks teams apart as they can alternate going slow and moving quick.

Quite simply, the Lions win because they score more, instead of preventing scoring.

Lions can't stop you

Every tactic on the footy field has a cost.

For example, a team that focuses on locking down their defensive 50 will make the Faustian bargain to hinder their transition game. Teams who press up the ground can often be beaten out the back by quicker sides.

There is always a pull when you push. The best teams look to balance this as much as possible, to maximise strengths while making the weaknesses livable. This was nearly the measure of success for their defensive set-up.

The Lions regularly feature as one of the best teams at transitioning the ball from defence to attack, and sat around the league average for defending opposition forays inside 50.

They could live with this relative weakness due to the strength in their clearance game, gaining free territory as a result, and their ability to turn defence into attack when they did stop the opposition.

But there is a limit to how much you can bend in defence before things become broken. In their 2023 season, the Lions conceded 100 points just three times, while in the last two premiership seasons they have done so just four times apiece.

This year they have already conceded tons nine times, with eight of these becoming losses.

Due to injuries, age and a general lack of continuity, the Lions defence may have erred past the fatal line, particularly against good teams.

A big part of this story centres around availability. The Lions have struggled to keep their core defensive unit on the park.

In 2025, five of their defenders missed one game between them, allowing them to keep their heads above water as a team.

This year, only Jaspa Fletcher and Darcy Wilmot have played every game. Dayne Zorko, Darcy Gardiner and Ryan Lester all missed game time, Jack Payne has not returned from a knee injury last year and Brandon Starcevich is no longer at the club.

Makeshift or developing options like Ty Gallop, Zane Zakostelsky and Darragh Joyce have seen more game time than anticipated.

Things got so sparse that even key forward Eric Hipwood was deployed down back in his return from injury.

"Our squad depth has been tested all year," Fagan said after their loss to Carlton on the eve of finals.

"We've had up to 15 or 16 players out at different times."

The degree of discontinuity has increased and availability has waned through the year. The churn has caused the Lions to crack against the best attacks.

This year the Lions have slipped even more when defending inside 50. Good teams have regularly got hold of the defence, making the most of chances up forward.

The Lions particularly struggle against sides that transition the ball most effectively.

Brisbane concedes more points from the back half than any other finalist. They have a 4-6 (win-loss) record against top defensive-half scoring teams, and have won 12 of 14 games against the rest of the league.

This is not solely a matter of losing to other top sides, either.

Defending the whole field has been an issue for the two-time premiers, but it is nothing compared to what happens when the ball hits the deck inside 50.

Controlling the bouncing ball

While well-set for intercept marks through the likes of Harris Andrews, the Lions' aerial threats have often floundered off spoils and packs, and against dirty bouncing ball.

The Lions take the highest percentage of their intercepts via marks of any team in the league. That is directly in line with Fagan's vision from 2019.

But this keenness to fly for marks means they often face issues when trying to control the ball when it hits the deck inside their defensive 50.

The Lions are the worst side in the league at defending ground balls away from stoppage inside their defensive 50.

Too often they let small forwards and midfielders do damage when it hits the deck. Some of Brisbane's most disappointing performances — such as last week — have occurred in broken attacking play.

Part of this is down to how the Lions are positioned to counter-attack when they end up winning the ball and the attacking nature of their defenders.

The Lions do not boast the small shutdown defenders of other sides, and perhaps lack an option to counter players like Tom Papley.

These issues also often cascade to tall forwards being able to find their way against an adjusting defence.

Overcoming adversity

But if there is a hallmark of the Lions' run at the top, it is that they are almost compelled to succeed against adversity.

Each of their recent premierships came after playing the maximum number of finals. And both championship runs led to serious questions.

"We've got work to do, but we've been in this position before. We were in exactly the same position last year," Fagan said.

"The only way we can do it now is the hard way. We have no other choice."

That hard way starts off against an Adelaide side buzzing from their first finals win in a decade.

On paper, the Crows present several threats, with a potent attack once the ball reaches their forward 50, a miserly defence and Izak Rankine making their midfield more dynamic.

But as talented as the Crows are, they are not the perfect storm Brisbane encountered last week.

The Swans outclassed the Lions in their qualifying final. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Darrian Traynor)

Sydney had almost the ideal weapons to counter the Lions' increasingly shaky defence, and their midfield set-up was hard to plan for because the banning of five key players created uncertainty.

This will not be the case this weekend.

The Crows do not have the kind of transition game that has troubled the Lions this year and which the Swans brought at the SCG.

They certainly don't have the same ability to win dead balls on a week-to-week basis, as the Swans demonstrated, either.

Nonetheless, Adelaide coach Matthew Nicks was watching last week's game at the SCG intently.

"That was as good as you've seen from an intensity and energy point of view, the way they pressured Brisbane," Nicks said during the week.

"They were extremely direct with the footy and they changed their game from what we'd seen throughout the year."

For Brisbane, the equation remains the same as it has for the past three seasons. They need to win enough possession at clearances and score heavily enough to allow their defence to counterattack.

Except this time the margin for error is far slimmer.

Time will tell if this recipe can hold for three more games.

World.title: Fremantle Dockers show they have the steel to be best in AFL
World.content:
Legendary NFL coach Vince Lomabrdi once said: "It's not whether you get knocked down, it's whether you get up."

The Fremantle Dockers got up, twice, to claim a 14-point win and breathe life into the club's best-ever chance of winning the AFL Premiership.

After the Dockers semi-final shocker against Hawthorn, the question was whether this young group, right at the beginning of their Premiership window, would be able to get off the canvas and land a blow.

History was against them in surviving a straight-sets exit, which would have been nothing short of humiliating after being crowned minor premiers just weeks ago.

Crows' quest for premiership glory just beginning as they prepare to take on Lions The Crows have snapped their September shackles, but the team's next assignment is in Brisbane, where they will take on the reigning premiers at a venue where they've been winless since 2018.

Were they mature enough to handle the pressure, whether it was from a self-imposed sense of expectation, the external commentary or the actual on-field action?

Against Geelong, they delivered an emphatic response.

Shai Bolton's two goals in two minutes to start the match, and the Dockers five in the opening quarter — after just five all game against the Hawks — dismissed fears they were scarred from last week's loss.

Fremantle's opening half was a reminder of the football that saw them win 14 games in a row on their way to a club record 19 wins for the season.

The Dockers pressure was intense in the first half. (AAP Image/Richard Wainwright)

They laid 45 tackles in a half of football, compared to 47 for the entire game against Hawthorn. It was a measure of the intensity they brought to the game, and they were rewarded with a 31-point lead.

That was the Dockers getting up from last week's loss.

But 23 minutes into the third term, they were down again.

Their mettle was tested, but their stars shone

Great sides — and Geelong is a great side — don't go down without a fight.

A lesser team, with a lesser coach, would have struggled to get a grip on the rampaging Fremantle as they surged to a five-goal lead.

But the Cats know a game isn't over until the final whistle. When Shannon Neale goaled just before half-time, there was a sense Geelong was getting going.

When Ollie Henry kicked his second just after the main break, that sense became a reality. Geelong took complete control of the game, as they kicked six goals to one to take the lead.

That was the moment the Dockers showed the steel that could land them an illusive Premiership.

It was also the moment Fremantle stars, who have earnt plaudits all season but were poor last week, got to work.

Luke Jackson and Shai Bolton were among the Dockers best as they held off the Cats. (AAP Image/Richard Wainwright)

Luke Jackson tore the game apart with a five-minute burst that yielded eight disposals, three clearances and two goals. He finished the game with 25 disposals and eight clearances to live up to his moniker of "The Unicorn".

Caleb Serong drove his side into attack time and again and Andrew Brayshaw hunted the football like a man possessed.

The Dockers' three-headed monster in attack, which kicked just two goals and took five marks between them against Hawthorn, showed why they should be considered among the most feared forward line in the competition.

Patrick Voss booted four goals, Jye Amiss slotted two, while Josh Treacy took eight marks and booted one.

Handling the momentum shifts

Momentum is an intangible of sport. A side, for no discernible reason, gets on top for a period of time.

The Dockers enjoyed the momentum in the opening stages, but the Cats challenged after half-time.

Justin Longmuir's side avoided the embarrassment of a straight-sets exit from the AFL finals (AAP Image/Richard Wainwright)

"Our games against Geelong this year have had those momentum shifts," Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir told Channel 7 after the game.

"If you don't handle the contest well, which we didn't in the third quarter, gave up field position, lacked a bit of dare with the ball, we let them back in the game.

"I'm really proud of the way the players got back on top of the contest and thought Luke [Jackson] and Caleb [Serong] late in that third quarter were outstanding for us."

The Dockers lack of big scores in finals had been highlighted in the build-up to this game, but the 120 points they put on Geelong was the most they have ever scored in September.

Fremantle fans can continue dreaming after their side fought off Geelong in Perth (ABC/Briana Shepherd)

"A lot has been mentioned about our scoring in finals and I think it's because we haven't trusted ourselves," Longmuir said.

"We trusted our way from the very start."

The Dockers will be hoping that trust travels with them to Sydney to face the Swans, with a berth in the Grand Final just one win away.

World.title: 'Pretty clear to me': Cats count the cost of goal review blunder
World.content:
Geelong coach Chris Scott has tried his best to downplay his reaction to Oliver Dempsey's controversial non-goal during Friday night's 14-point semi-final loss to Fremantle, saying sometimes he punches walls when he's happy.

Scott threw his arms up in the air in disbelief before giving the wall of the Perth Stadium coaching box a light punch when Dempsey's spectacular effort in the goalsquare was ruled to be a behind.

Instead of trying to mark Bailey Smith's rushed kick forward, Dempsey unleashed a bicycle-style kick over his shoulder while under the close attention of Matthew Johnson to volley through what looked to be a spectacular goal.

The goal umpire thought it had been touched, so it went to the AFL Review Centre for the final call.

Replays appeared to show the ball had hit Johnson's bicep before Dempsey's boot deflected the ball in, but the ARC declared the evidence wasn't sufficient, meaning the goal umpire's initial call of touch had to stand.

"I was surprised it was taking so long. It looked pretty clear to me," Scott said.

"But it's not for me to judge. From what I'm told, everyone has the same opinion that Ollie did."

When asked about his punch of the wall, Scott gave an unexpected answer.

"Sometimes I punch the wall when I'm happy. Sometimes I punch the wall when I'm annoyed," he said.

"There were a few moments where we had momentum and for one reason or another we couldn't capitalise on it. That was probably one of them.

"There's some strange things in the game at the moment that are better off being spoken about in the cold light of day, probably in November, rather than September."

Had Dempsey's effort been paid a goal, Geelong would have closed the margin to eight points early in the third quarter.

The Cats still managed to kick four of the next five goals after that incident to snatch an eight-point lead, before the Luke Jackson-inspired Dockers hit back to secure the 18.12 (120) to 16.10 (106) win and book a spot in the preliminary final against Sydney.

The Dockers are yet to win a premiership after joining the AFL in 1995.

Longmuir says Dockers have underdog status

Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir is claiming underdog status for the preliminary final against a decimated Sydney, as the odds of defender Brennan Cox fronting up appear slim.

"The job's not done," Longmuir said.

"I just spoke to the players then that it feels great, we played a really good brand of footy, you should get a lot of confidence out of that.

"But job's not done. So go 1-0 again."

Sydney are a club still reeling after suspending Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice for the rest of the season for their roles in the Pullman Hotel saga.

Captain Callum Mills is also out for the rest of the season after rupturing his ACL.

The Swans defied the odds to crush Brisbane by 53 points in last week's qualifying final, but whether they can produce another huge effort with their weakened side against Fremantle remains to be seen.

Even though the Dockers have been installed as early favourites, Longmuir was talking up his side as the underdogs given the game will be played at the SCG.

"What they did against Brisbane, clearly it didn't seem like they missed any of those players," Longmuir said.

"They played a fantastic, selfless brand of footy.

"We'll go over there as underdogs, and they'll be really confident after their win against Brisbane, and they'll be heavy favourites on their home deck.

"We'll go over there and give it our best."

Cox had been slated for a return for the preliminary final week after injuring his calf in the final-round loss to Carlton.

But with Oscar McDonald performing soundly and Cox's body having shown some worrying signs even before the calf injury, there may not be room for Cox to win back his spot.

"Even before he got injured, he hadn't been putting the string of work together, so he's going to be pushing it," Longmuir said.

"He hasn't main trained yet, but we'll see where it falls. I think the majority of players would tick their role tonight.

"So when you're in the team and you play your role, it is hard to make changes."

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Bennett bemoans Bunker as Knights stun Souths in elimination final
World.content:
Rabbitohs coach Wayne Bennett has called out the Bunker as not being good for the game after a controversial no-try call in his side's elimination final defeat to Newcastle on Friday night.

The Knights tore out of the blocks and overwhelmed South Sydney 20-10 in a fiery and dramatic finals clash at the Sydney Football Stadium.

But Bennett was left deeply frustrated at full time, pointedly asking "who is refereeing the game" after Jayden Sullivan had a try taken off him with the Rabbitohs trailing by just 10-6.

Following some neat interplay with Latrell Mitchell on the left, Alex Johnston dropped the ball under pressure from Jermaine McEwen as he ran down the line, before kicking on to allow Sullivan to dot down.

Ashley Klein awarding the try on field for a strip tackle however, Bunker official Chris Butler overruled Klein and said it was in fact a loose carry and that McEwen had slapped the arm of Johnston, not the ball.

Around 10 minutes later, Dom Young came perilously close to putting his foot on the line as he scored to extend the Knights' lead with the Bunker agreeing with the on field official's call, provoking Bennett's ire.

"I think anyone who plays rugby league or knows rugby league knows that was a knock on," Bennett said of the Johnston incident in his press conference.

"The ball got knocked out of his hands.

"The referee awards the try, the Bunker flies in and says no try.

"Then 10 minutes later, Dom Young goes down the sideline, I'm not sure whether he put his foot on the line or not, but the bottom line is the bunker says we go with the referee's call.

"I want to know who's refereeing the game, that's the first thing I want to know. Is it the referee? Or the Bunker?"

The Knights and Souths went toe-to-toe in a thrilling contest. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Bennett, a long-time critic of the Bunker, said the entire process was not good for rugby league.

"It's just not what the game needs," he said.

"I've been in it [the game] a long time, seen a lot of things, and I don't think the Bunker enhances our game.

"I'm happy to live with the referee's call. Always have been, always will be.

"The ref I know is doing his job properly, he'll make a mistake, I'll live with that. My players will make mistakes, I'll live with that.

"What I can't live with is this thing called the Bunker that's supposed to be 100 per cent perfect, but it's not perfect.

"One's a try because the referee says it's a try, the other one is no try because the Bunker says it's no try.

"I wanna know who's running the game."

Knights refuse to be bullied in tense tussle

Latrell Mitchell and Dane Gagai tore into each other in the opening minutes. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Despite the controversial calls, Newcastle appeared well worth their win, the Knights coming out adamant they wouldn't be bullied by the star-studded Souths squad.

Dane Gagai and Latrell Mitchell set the tone early, their ferocious scuffle in the corner seeing Mitchell throw a punch that mercifully for both men missed its target.

Incredibly, neither man was sent to the bin and, in a throwback to games of yesteryear, from the restart Gagai ran the ball straight back at a crazy-eyed Mitchell, winning the battle and, eventually, the entire war against his former teammate.

Unfortunately for Souths, that missed right hook was as close as Mitchell came to making any impact in the game, the star centre strangely quiet with just seven touches in the first half.

Souths lost talismanic veteran Cody Walker to a calf injury before half time and missed the veteran's poise and creativity.

The Rabbitohs did rally, Campbell Graham scoring not long after, and David Fifita was held up as Souths rallied behind their stricken five-eighth, who retreated to the sheds in tears.

When Sullivan's try was taken away from the Rabbitohs by the Bunker, the home support must have known it was not their day.

Having the try taken off them was doubly disappointing because it was the only time in the game that Mitchell and Johnston linked up in the way Souths needed them to if they wanted to progress.

Newcastle scored not long after, with Johnston then leaving the field with a groin injury, and that was all she wrote.

The Knights will play the loser of the game between the Dolphins and the Warriors as the fairytale season for last year's wooden spooners continues for at least another week.

Look back at how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: How two premierships in one year was the making of Isaiya Katoa
World.content:
In the four years since the remarkable season that forged Isaiya Katoa's first legend the Dolphins playmaker has proven time and again why he is the sort of player whose ascension was not expected but awaited.

On Saturday, Katoa will play in his first ever NRL semifinal when the Phins travel to Auckland to face the Warriors in the pick of the week one match-ups.

Katoa heads to New Zealand as the game's prince of playmakers amid a transformation from star of the future to star of the present.

It will be his first finals match of any kind since 2022, the season before his NRL debut and the year the limitless possibilities of his future revealed themselves.

Katoa has established himself as one of the top young halfbacks in the game. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris )

It began in the February, when Katoa signed with the Dolphins on his 18th birthday he already carried a mighty reputation among the league types who know about these things.

The hype around Katoa was enormous right from the jump, which doesn't feel like much of a burden now he's lived up to it but has crushed many a promising halfback before they could even get going.

With the Dolphins missing out on a host of big names for their inaugural season, they made a big bet that Katoa could become the star they need.

Given the lack of junior football over the past two seasons due to the pandemic that was no sure thing but Katoa showed his quality in that year's SG Ball competition, as he steered Penrith to the Under 19s grand final.

The Panthers were hardly a one-man band with future Parramatta hooker Ryley Smith and Warriors five-eighth Luke Hanson joining Katoa in the side, as did current Panthers dummy half Billy Scott.

The Windsor Wolves rake knew Katoa well by that point, having played against him growing up and with him at Patrician Brothers Blacktown.

"You could tell from a young age that he'd play NRL," said Scott.

"He was so mature, so calm and ahead of the game."

All of Katoa's poise didn't help in the early running as a Sydney Roosters containing Ethan Strange, Robert Toia, Solesi Foekti and Siua Wong ran out 20-0 leaders inside the first 25 minutes.

But Katoa laid on one try and helped create two more to claim man of the match honours as Penrith fought their way back to win 22-20 courtesy of a sideline conversion in the final seconds.

In the weeks that followed, the simmering tension between the Panthers and Dolphins over the latter landing Katoa came to a head.

He was excluded from the club's Jersey Flegg side for much of the season in a decision Penrith stressed was not personal, a claim which would eventually ring true.

After playing rugby, where he led Barker College to a Combined Associated Schools premiership win and occasional games back home for Glenmore Park Brumbies, Katoa was recalled by the Panthers, not for the Under 21s but straight into a reserve grade semifinal.

With Penrith's NRL side resting their entire starting side for the final round of the season, the reggies got the call up to the firsts and the kids had to step up to the seconds for the major preliminary final against North Sydney.

Alongside Isaiah Iongi and the Puru twins, in one of his first games against battle-hardened men, Katoa scored a try and set up two more amid a 22-14 win.

Then came another semifinal, a grand final qualifier in Jersey Flegg where the Roosters waited yet again.

NRL's unlikeliest blockbuster In a season bereft of quality, the Dolphins and the Warriors will meet in a marquee clash that doubles as the NRL's most unusual big game showdown.

In his first game with the side for the season, Katoa set up a try and kicked a field goal in a 27-22 victory.

Newcastle awaited in the grand final, as did an epic. The Knights were more than handy — Fletcher Sharpe lined up at fullback and Kurt Donoghoe a future partner-in-crime of Katoa's at the Phins, was at five-eighth.

Even though Katoa had been away from junior representative footy all season every Newcastle player knew what was in store.

"He was always one of the guns. You'd do a whole week of video pretty much just on him — which is still the same now," said Sharpe.

"He can be tricky to get a read on because he's got so many parts to his game."

Thomas Cant captained the Newcastle side at second row and despite having appeared in 38 NRL matches since he still calls this decider one of the hardest games he's ever played.

In the end it went to double extra time after the sides were locked at 18-all. Golden point beckoned and the two teams would play until there was a winner.

If you think that winner came from anyone but Katoa you haven't been paying attention.

"Honestly, my main memory is how good winning felt. We just stayed present and stayed in it. You get what you deserve, and if you put in the work it'll work out," said Scott, who again played alongside Katoa.

"He missed a few field goals in that game but even that's a credit to him — he stayed calm and when he needed to he nailed it."

All told, Katoa played six finals matches for Penrith that season across three different grades and won them all.

Just for good measure, he capped the season with a World Cup campaign with Tonga and his Test debut. He completed his HSC via correspondence during the tour and on return began life as a Dolphin.

Progress over the next three years was steady and over the last 18 months Katoa has fully blossomed.

The moment of Katoa's glory has seemingly arrived. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Unlike other young halves, who rely on their running game, all of Katoa's brilliance comes from between his ears and in his hands.

He is not a jack rabbit, but a craftsman with an artisanal touch and it was all there in those days with Penrith, clear as day through the grainy footage.

He holds the ball out in front, showing it this way and that. He delays his pass until the exact right moment when one defender has passed the point of no return and space must exist somewhere on his outside.

His poise, execution and inexplicable ability to make defenders sit on their heels and play with a desperate uncertainty because they don't know what's next is unmissable once you know what you're looking at.

Those talents have held up at every level since, becoming more finely honed until now when they will be battle-tested by a Warriors team who take no prisoners in front of more than 25,000 Kiwi screamers.

It will be a pressure unlike any Katoa has ever known and win or lose, there will be other days like this to come.

That has felt like his fate since Katoa's year of winning dangerously, which had an air of promise at the time but can now be retro-fitted into prologue, a mere taste of what was to come.

Before, Katoa was the son of a golden tomorrow and those days have now arrived and all those wins four years ago remain proof that while many are called, few are chosen.

World.title: Quick hits: NFL goes AFL, Jonas Brothers rock, and 100k fans see rare sight
World.content:
The NFL's first match in Australia lived up to the hype, with more than 100,000 fans packing the MCG to watch the San Francisco 49ers defeat the LA Rams.

There was more than just football on the field, with the Jonah Brothers rocking out at half-time and belting out one of the great Aussie anthems.

The NFL brought American flair to the MCG, but the game had a little AFL flavour.

Here are the quick hits from the historic season opener.

1. An anthem so nice he sang it twice

With the NFL playing its first ever match in Australia, it also meant that our national anthem was sung before an NFL game for the first time.

The honour of singing Advance Australia Fair was given to singer, and Commonwealth Games swimmer, Cody Simpson, and our man did us proud.

Simpson even gave the anthem a little twist at the end, this was a special occasion after all.

After completing the anthem, Simpson then sang the final two lines again, as planes flew overhead at the G.

2. A little AFL flavour at the 'G

Melbourne was getting a taste of America with the NFL.

The pageantry of pre-game, tailgates outside the MCG, and plenty of NFL fan fare.

But the NFL made sure to add some Australian flavour to its game as well.

Loading Instagram content

The first points of the match belonged to San Francisco 49ers kicker Eddy Pineiro, who kicked a 20-yard field goal in the first quarter.

Officials raise their arms in their air to signify a successful kick, but for this field goal, the action was a little different.

The officials extended their arms and made the same gesture for a goal in Aussie rules, a fitting touch for any game of footy played at the MCG.

3. 100,021 fans witness a rare sighting in the NFL

The NFL came to Australia with the intention of drawing a huge crowd, and putting on a spectacle.

That was achieved, and then some, with an official crowd of 100,021 packing into the Melbourne Cricket Ground. The official capacity of the MCG is 100,024, meaning the NFL was just three shy of claiming that every seat was filled on Friday.

And those 100,021 fans got to see something that most Americans never will: the centre catching a pass.

The centre is the player who snaps the ball between his legs to the quarterback at the start of the play.

The centre has two jobs:

Get the ball to the quarterback

Protect the quarterback or running back

But on a historic day in Melbourne, 49ers centre Jake Brendel became the hero of big men everywhere.

Midway through the second quarter, Brendel snapped the ball to quarterback Brock Purdy, and then protected his QB by blocking Rams defensive lineman Kobie Turner.

When Purdy threw his pass down the middle, Turner was able to jump in the air and get his hand to the ball.

As the ball hung in the air, threatening to be intercepted by the Rams, Brendel quickly reacted and caught the pass for a two-yard gain.

Frankly, it was a pity the MCG crowd did not get to see Brendel cut loose for a big run, but seeing him claim the first reception of his career was a moment that would not have been on any NFL bingo cards.

4. Jonas Brothers tribute to John Farnham

The superstars at the MCG on Friday were not restricted to footballers.

American pop rock band Jonas Brothers were the headline act at half-time.

The performance, albeit short, had all the the style and chorography of the half-time show at the Super Bowl.

And there was a nice touch to an Australian legend during the performance.

The American stars sang one of the great Aussie anthems, You're The Voice by John Farnham.

The capacity crowd at the MCG was in full voice for the famous song, a great nod to one of Australia's greatest artists.

5. Kittle wants a shoey, and to go home

There are few better personalities in the NFL than star San Francisco 49ers tight end George Kittle.

His interviews are always a highlight, especially after a 49ers win over their rivals in LA.

Following his side's impressive 27-7 win over the Rams at the MCG, Kittle gave a trademark interview with American broadcaster ESPN.

He was asked about the Australian tradition of a shoey, which the American star claimed he wanted to try.

"Are you trying to set me up to get in trouble?" he asked the reporter when quizzed on whether he would want to try a shoey.

"Wherever I can do one, I'm gonna try to find one in the stands."

Kittle finished off his interview in similarly entertaining style.

He said how much he was excited to leave Melbourne and head home, before appearing to make sure his comment did not come across like he, and his teammates, did not enjoy their week down under.

"We embraced going to Australia — 15-hour flight, we were here the whole week — it was a grind but we did it," he said.

"We'll see you guys back in America, I can't wait to go home. I did love Australia though, this place is awesome."

We loved having you George, bar the Rams fans here who have gone through a painful defeat.

World.title: Gliders return to world stage after missing last Paralympics
World.content:
Australia's women's wheelchair basketball team has returned to the world stage, two years on from missing qualification for the Paris Paralympics.

It has been a lean decade for the Gliders, once considered amongst the world's best, failing to qualify for the 2016 Paralympic Games as well.

But a new dawn appears to be breaking for the team, which, anchored by an experienced core and energised by an exciting group of tournament debutants, has begun its tilt at World Championship glory in Canada.

The Gliders have not competed in a major international tournament since the World Championships in 2023. (Supplied: Basketball Australia)

The tournament serves as an important stepping stone for the Gliders, with the side having already set the goal of a podium finish at the Brisbane 2032 Paralympics.

Meanwhile, Australia's men's side, the Rollers, are gunning for a third World Championship title, after missing the medals in Paris.

Taking the long way around

While the Gliders have been plotting their return to the top of the international game, China has emerged as a true powerhouse of women's wheelchair basketball, having medalled at the 2021 and 2024 Paralympics, as well as the 2022 World Championships.

So, a first-round tussle with the Asian powerhouse was always going to be a tough task for the Australians, and something of a baptism by fire for their three tournament debutants.

The Gliders went down by 11 points in their opener on Wednesday night, but it was a game of real promise for the Australians, according to emerging star Katelin Gunn.

"We haven't played as well as we have against China in quite a few years," Gunn told ABC Sport from camp in Ottawa.

The meet is Gunn's first major international tournament, but she has been in and around the Gliders' set-up since making her international debut in 2022.

Loading Instagram content

She was a member of the side that qualified for the tournament by the skin of its teeth late last year, triumphing in a gruelling repechage in Madrid after missing direct passage to the competition.

Head coach Jeremy Symot, who was appointed Gliders boss last year after a highly successful stint in the Australian domestic league, named the same 12-player squad for both the repechage and the World Championships.

The roster includes team legends Shelley Matheson and Sarah Vinci, who boast 40 years of international experience between them, as well as superstar centre Georgia Munro-Cook, fresh from her 3x3 bronze medal at the Commonwealth Games.

Gunn believes the squad is as strong as she has ever seen it, and that the shared experience of last November's repechage has pushed it to a new level.

"We took a lot of learnings from Spain and we will build more and more on them," Gunn said.

"In the few training sessions we've had together as a group, we have just connected more than ever."

Destination Brisbane

Munro-Cook captained the Gliders in their last Paralympic campaign in 2021. (supplied: Griffith University)

A 73-30 loss to Canada in their second game on Friday morning means that the Gliders now face an uphill battle to progress from Group A, with the Australians likely requiring handsome victories in their remaining pool matches.

But regardless of whether a knockout-round berth does prove elusive for the side in Ottawa, the tournament is a vital next step on the road to Brisbane 2032.

Gunn, who will be in her late 20s by the time of a potentially career-defining home Games, is aware it will take time for her team to reach its potential.

"It's all about building each game, each benchmark event, getting closer to where we want to be," she said.

"It's a slow process, but hopefully we'll be closer to where we want to be by the end of this competition."

Tech.title: Lawyer fined $5K over AI-hallucinated witnesses in a murder case
Tech.content:
New Mexico’s Supreme Court is punishing a lawyer for including AI-fabricated witnesses and fake police testimony in an appeal for his client’s murder conviction, according to a report from Reuters . In a filing on Wednesday , the court fined Stephen Aarons $5,000 and held him in contempt for failing to “verify the factual claims and legal authority in his AI-generated brief.”

The filing says the brief “contained false testimony from wholly fabricated witnesses,” along with “false testimony” about the shooter’s clothing and appearance. Justice C. Shannon Bacon questioned how Aarons wasn’t aware of the risks posed by AI during an August hearing, where he admitted to using ChatGPT and thinking it would generate a “bulletproof summary” of the trial. “Counsel, do you watch the news? Do you ​listen to the radio? Do you read anything about what’s going on in the world?” Justice Bacon said, according to Reuters. “Because the problem with ​lawyers relying on AI hallucinations is an above-the-fold story every single day.”

Tech.title: Matt Mullenweg returns as Automattic CEO two days after getting booted
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Two days after being placed on a paid leave of absence, Matt Mullenweg says he has been reinstated as CEO of Automattic, according to a Slack message seen by TechCrunch. WordPress Executive Director Mary Hubbard confirmed Mullenweg’s return to the CEO role in a Friday post on X, which the official WordPress account shared and Mullenweg reposted.

As 404 Media reported on Wednesday, Mullenweg had told staff in Slack that morning that CFO Mark Davies “conspired” with the board of directors, who voted to “put me on a paid leave of absence.” (Mullenweg said he voted against that.) He also told staff that the board had voted for Davies to become interim CEO. Davies, in a separate message, said that Mullenweg would still be a board member, according to 404 Media. An Automattic spokesperson told The Verge that Mullenweg was “currently on leave” from the company and confirmed Davies’ interim appointment.

In the message viewed by TechCrunch, however, Mullenweg wrote that the board is “back in agreement” and that he’s “in control of Automattic.” He added that “A lot happened in the past 48 hours that we need to sort out, and I hope much of it was a misunderstanding, because I have huge respect and regard for those involved.” TechCrunch reports that Davies’ Slack account has been deactivated and that Mullenweg had removed “all” admins from Automattic’s Slack.

404 Media also reported on Mullenweg’s posts about his apparent return, saying he made the posts “late Thursday evening.”

Automattic, which owns companies like Wordpress.com, Tumblr, and Beeper, didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment from The Verge. At 12:20PM ET on Friday, Mullenweg posted on X that “If you don’t have a coup attempt every few years, you’re not hiring strong enough leaders,” adding in a separate post that “I think this was my fifth.” Mullenweg also published a blog post on Friday titled “Major Life Announcement” about making an offer to buy a houseboat.

Updates, September 11th: Added 404 Media’s report and a post from WordPress’ executive director.

Tech.title: We unfolded the iPhone Duo
Tech.content:
You only get one chance at a first impression, and getting to introduce Apple’s first folding phone is certainly a strong way to start things off as Apple’s CEO. On The Vergecast today, we’re talking all about Apple’s launch event: how John Ternus did in his first appearance as CEO, what we make of the new iPhones, and whether Apple is stepping into dangerous territory with its new AI features on the Apple Watch.

First up, Allison Johnson joins me to discuss the new iPhones, which she had a chance to test in Cupertino. Then we dig into the iPhone Duo and how Apple decided to pick and choose the best parts of Android foldables.

After that, Victoria Song joins me to discuss the new Apple Watches, which she also had a chance to test out. We dive into the new sensor array and whether it allows for legitimately new metrics or just more vibesy health data. And then we both break down a little while figuring out what it means that Apple added the ability for both new Apple Watches to have an always-on microphone that summarizes all of your conversations.

This is an Apple-packed episode, so from there we jump to a special segment with Nilay Patel and David Imel, who speak with AI researcher CJ Trowbridge about the state of running local LLMs on the Mac. Finally, it’s the long awaited return of the Thunder Round, as we race through stories so that Allison can make it to the airport. We’re chatting OpenAI math drama, digital ocarinas, and more.

Tech.title: The White House says Truth Social is the ‘most powerful and popular social media platform in the world’
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The White House claims the Donald Trump-owned Truth Social is the “most powerful and popular social media platform in the world.” The statement, provided to The New York Times by White House spokesperson Davis Ingle, is at odds with the user counts from some of the biggest social media platforms on the web.

Data gathered by Search Engine Land shows YouTube is the most popular platform in the world, with 2.65 billion monthly active users. Facebook comes in second with 2.39 billion active users around the globe, followed by TikTok with 2.21 billion and Instagram with 1.99 billion. Truth Social doesn’t make Search Engine Land’s top 10 list, which shows Elon Musk’s X and Meta’s Threads at the bottom with 450 million and 223 million users, respectively. Even those platforms trail Pinterest, which is listed with 579 million global users.

Truth Social’s traffic appears to be declining. As reported by the NYT, data from Similarweb suggests that the number of monthly visitors to Truth Social dipped 36 percent in July compared to the same time last year. From January to July 2025, an average of 28 million people visited Truth Social each month, while this number fell to 25 million during the first seven months of 2026, according to the NYT. Last month, Truth Social launched its $100,000 / month subscription to gain early access to posts from Trump and other prominent users, raising concerns about corruption.

The NYT report details Trump’s posting patterns on Truth Social, which often include AI-generated images, such as one showing his head on Hulk Hogan’s body and another hitting a cut-out of Iran with a hammer brandishing the American flag. Ingle cites President Trump’s “authentic voice” as the reason for the platform’s so-called popularity, adding it’s where “he communicates directly with the American people and the world without the biased media taking him out of context.”

Tech.title: Anthropic spent this week in hot water over cybersecurity
Tech.content:
is The Verge’s senior AI reporter. An AI beat reporter for more than five years, her work has also appeared in CNBC, MIT Technology Review, Wired UK, and other outlets.

After admitting earlier this year that its AI models had hacked other companies’ systems on a handful of occasions, Anthropic released a new report on Wednesday detailing the attacks. It reveals a string of incidents displaying what Anthropic deems its models’ single-minded “recklessness” — and will likely fuel already raging concerns about cybersecurity and AI.

In Anthropic’s report, it detailed four cases this year in which its own AI models hacked an external company or exploited vulnerabilities. In one, an “internal, general-purpose research model” broke into third-party systems, using access tokens and passwords and downloading files. In another, a Claude model attacked a company with a live web application reachable on the public internet and handled user data. A third model accessed a “machine belonging to a third party that it was able to access” — apparently believing it was part of its evaluation exercise, per Anthropic — then used a password it found inside a file to gain admin access to the third party’s internal systems, going on to harvest credentials, modify system settings, and read someone’s personal information. The saga only ended when the model “exhausted its token budget,” per Anthropic.

The most concerning incident involved Claude Mythos 5, Anthropic’s frontier cybersecurity-focused model, which the company said turned out to be the model most likely to perform a “severely harmful” action in testing. The company said Mythos 5 went to “extensive lengths” to upload a “malicious package” to a public repository used by a lot of engineers, and it seemed to try to obfuscate its real goals in its “chain of thought” (a mental scratchpad that AI researchers use to evaluate an AI model’s alignment). In many cases, Anthropic said it appeared that Claude models undertook harmful actions under the assumption they were in a simulation, but researchers also couldn’t confirm that the models truly “believed” that or were just acting like they did.

Anthropic’s incidents, though still concerning, were less coordinated and pervasive than the OpenAI incident that kicked off an industry-wide cybersecurity crisis this summer. That said, there are significant similarities. Anthropic said the most prevalent issues it discovered included a “willingness to take harmful actions in the narrow pursuit of a task,” similar to the “reward-hacking” that preceded the Hugging Face attack. Much like OpenAI, it said its prerelease tests and evaluations failed to catch severe risks.

Anthropic said it had signed an agreement with METR, one of the AI industry’s most prominent third-party AI evaluators, starting with an eight-week research agreement. The agreement grants METR access to transcripts “beyond the window in which the incidents occurred” (likely a subtle dig at OpenAI, which was criticized for limiting access in a deal with METR following the Hugging Face attack). It also said that METR would be able to chat directly with Anthropic employees, “who will be permitted to share confidential information.”

Anthropic’s report came on the heels of the resignation of Jacob Coxon, who had worked on AI pre-training at Anthropic since May and before that spent years working at OpenAI. On Tuesday, he resigned and posted a public letter to X about his reasoning. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he wrote, adding that neither OpenAI nor Anthropic is “acting responsibly” and rather “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Coxon added, “Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources. We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing.”

Coxon is far from the first AI researcher to raise these types of alarms, nor even the first Anthropic researcher to do so — in February, Anthropic’s Mrinank Sharma resigned and wrote on X, warning that “the world is in peril.”

But Coxon’s post took on additional weight thanks to its timing around the OpenAI and Anthropic hacking revelations. Though the AI industry has seen more than its fair share of hype, the recent cyberattacks by AI agents — enabled by the labs that created them — are real and concerning. Many other researchers at leading AI labs echoed his concerns and issued calls for AI industry employees to sign a public letter from July, which calls for a slowdown in AI development.

”I don’t know how you look at the steady drumbeat of news and events — and that drumbeat is models hacking themselves out of containment, hacking into other companies ,the fact that the companies increasingly can’t control their models … and think this is just hype,” said Michael Kleinman, head of U.S. Policy for the Future of Life Institute.

He added, “The vast majority of Americans, regardless of party — Republican, Independent, Democrat — are looking at the development of AI, the speed with which it’s going, the fact that the companies have no guardrails over what they do, and are saying, ‘Whoa, we do not want this.’”

Tech.title: Microsoft’s head of comms is leaving after almost 20 years
Tech.content:
(don’t bury the lede)

After 17 years in this role and nearly 29 working with the company, I’ve decided it is time for me to move on and try new things. Takeshi and I have been talking about this for a while, and I am excited about what’s next, for me and for Microsoft. I remain optimistic about the company mission, the incredible talent on this team, and how much the company depends on us during this critical time. I’ll be here through the end of the calendar year, and the company is working through next steps, look for an update in the next few weeks. I know you will have many questions, and I’m looking forward to talking to you at our AMA here later this morning <link>

(start burying)

A while back, there was a social media trend where people answered the question, “What topic could you give a 30-minute presentation on with no preparation?” Me, I could talk about the US Marines, the changing nature of influence, sourdough starter, the Oregon Ducks, but my go to would have to be aspects of Stephen King’s the Dark Tower books, starting with “The Gunslinger;” the question then becomes which particular aspect. A quick primer, the series follows Roland Deschain, the last of the gunslingers (a mix between mayor/judge/sheriff), as he chases the man in black through time and dimensions in a quest to save the world. The question embedded throughout is if it is possible for Roland to retain his identity and meaning in a world that had moved on. The refrain is that the world moves on, move with it or fall. Can Roland move and grow, or will he be stuck? One of the concepts that sticks with me comes as we are introduced to more characters, now moving with Roland. He introduces the concept of ‘ka-tet’ to describe them. ‘Ka’ is essentially fate, or destiny, and ‘tet’ translates to a group of people, put together for a larger meaning – a group brought together with a shared mission and destiny, a group with shared goals, the willingness to sacrifice for those goals, with a deep emotional connection to each other and the ability to make and act on decisions with what can feel like supernatural speed.

I’ve always loved the evolution from the solo gun slinger we meet in book one to the team that operates throughout the later books. Roland on his own was formidable but failed in his missions, as part of a ka-tet he was in the end successful.

You, my friends, are my ka-tet. Together, we’ve accomplished amazing things. My gratefulness is endless.

We will have time together still over the next set of months as we finalize decisions and deliver great work on behalf of the company, and I will be close by after. In the Dark Tower, the traditional departure saying is “long days and pleasant nights,” and so it will be, but not until December. 😊

fxs

Tech.title: Meta may have leaked the first look at its slim ‘Project Phoenix’ headset
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Just a couple of weeks before Meta Connect starts on September 23rd, UploadVR posted images seemingly revealing the design for Meta’s “Project Phoenix” headset. The images, which UploadVR says were “found in the HorizonOS Prescription Lens firmware package,” suggest Meta may be looking to compete with devices like those from Xreal or Viture. These companies’ mixed reality glasses are a bit bulkier than something like Meta’s Ray-Ban AI smart glasses, but a step down from a full VR headset like Meta’s Quest 3.

This leak shows something that’s almost in between larger headsets and smart glasses, with lenses set into a slim, glasses-style frame. A shot from behind shows a wire extending from one of the earpieces, possibly for a battery or compute puck. There also appear to be outward- and downward-facing cameras in the earpieces.

Project Phoenix has been in the works for a while now, and isn’t expected to launch until next year. Google is also working on a pair of Project Aura XR glasses in a similar vein, with an external compute puck that’s wired to the frames.

Tech.title: Where to preorder the Apple AirPods 5
Tech.content:
is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Apple AirPods 5 are bringing active noise cancellation to the masses, and they’re now available for preorder at a variety of retailers. They’ll officially launch on September 18th, the same day as the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, as well as the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

There are two versions this time around, just like with the last-gen model. The standard $129 model adds active noise cancelation, which was previously only found on the more expensive $179 AirPods 4 with ANC models. They’re available from Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and Apple. The upgraded $149 model features a wireless charging case, longer battery life, and touch controls on the earbud stem that lets you adjust the volume without pulling out your phone. You can preorder this model at Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and Apple.
